The experimental protocol is appropriate: it contrasts "collapse" vs. random "normal" COUNTERFACT cases across GPT-2-XL, GPT-J, and Llama2-7b; inspects intermediate quantities; and uses ME-PPL50 to quantify instability. Results are consistent with the analysis: denominators are orders of magnitude smaller in collapse cases while numerators are comparable, and enforcing key consistency (C-ROME) removes the perplexity blow-up without otherwise perturbing the model, directly supporting the causal claim.

178.human_review: C-ROME is capable of dealing with collapse cases effectively. The experiment result exemplifies that C-ROME has a significant restorative effect on the edit efficacy metric.
178.llm_review: Result, Evaluation, Experiment: The evaluation is multifaceted, measuring stability (ME-PPL50), edit success (efficacy), generalization, and locality. Empirically, C-ROME prevents collapse (perplexity remains close to the original model rather than exploding as under the original ROME), and adding a random prefix at test time restores high efficacy on collapse cases for GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, while preserving strong locality. The study considers both collapse and normal subsets and reports outcomes across multiple model families, strengthening the result’s credibility.

179.human_review: The relationship between collapse cases and the token length of the edit question’s subject is quite interesting, which was neglected in the previous analysis.
179.llm_review: Analysis: The paper provides a clear mechanistic account linking collapse to the unusual distribution of first-token representations in autoregressive decoders. The t-SNE analyses distinguish prefixed vs. unprefixed key distributions and show that divergence is concentrated in first-token cases; the BOS behavior of Llama2-7b and the non-autoregressive T5-3B encoder serve as informative counterpoints that bolster the interpretation. This yields an insightful, model-level explanation rather than a surface fix.

180.human_review: The experiment of unprefixed k* and prefixed k* lacks of innovation, because the difference in their distributions is intuitive. The representations of k* with prefixes will be integrated with the random-sampled prefixes in the self-attention module. Even if their next token prediction results may be similar at the last layer, their representations still show significant differences in distribution at ROME’s edit layer (17th layer for GPT2-XL with 48 layers).
180.llm_review: Experiment: The empirical scope, while solid, is limited. Most analyses concentrate on GPT-2-XL and GPT-J, with only brief treatment of Llama2-7b’s distinct behavior; newer, larger instruction-tuned or more diverse architectures (e.g., Llama-3, Mistral, Mixtral, GPT-NeoX) are not evaluated. The solution’s sensitivity to the type/length/distribution of prefixes is not ablated, and there is no exploration of multiple or sequential edits, which are common in practical editing scenarios. Quantitative robustness analyses under varied prompting conditions would strengthen the experimental section.

181.human_review: Compared to method ROME, method C-ROME does not present any novel changes over method ROME, indicating that this paper may lack sufficient workload.
181.llm_review: Novelty, Comparison: A core factor—the inconsistent use of prefixed and unprefixed keys—was identified concurrently by prior work (Gupta et al., 2024a), which reduces novelty. While the paper’s analysis is deeper and the fix is simple, the work does not provide thorough comparisons against other editing methods or recent collapse-mitigation approaches (e.g., MEMIT variants, MEND/SERAC, gradient-based methods), nor does it benchmark against alternative implementations that may already address the bug. This makes it harder to position the contribution within the broader model-editing landscape.

182.human_review: The analysis based on Llama is not sufficiently convincing. The experimental results do not demonstrate the improvements of C-ROME on Llama, and the analysis of Llama in the paper is also questionable.
182.llm_review: Result, Experiment, Analysis: The proposed solution has trade-offs: C-ROME alone stabilizes models but substantially reduces efficacy and generalization on collapse cases; adding random prefixes at test time fixes efficacy but only modestly improves generalization and may be impractical for user-facing applications that cannot alter inputs. The analysis relies heavily on t-SNE for distributional claims; additional quantitative measures (e.g., cosine similarity distributions, condition-number analyses) would make the case stronger. Finally, the fix targets first-token cases and may not address other collapse modes (e.g., cumulative effects under sequential edits).

183.human_review: well written, easy to read, easy to follow, introducing the method and experiment to reader fluently.
183.llm_review: Well-motivated and clearly presented plug-and-play preprocessing that targets a real error mode in ABSA (compound sentences). The methodology is coherent (LLM-distilled T5 splitter + preference alignment) and the paper supports it with a reasonably broad experimental suite: multiple datasets (Rest15/16, Laptop16), two quad tasks (ASQP, ACOS), multiple backbones (Paraphrase, MvP) and LLMs (GPT-3.5/4). The oracle analysis and aspect-level error breakdown help justify the design, and the figures make the pipeline and training stages easy to follow. Code availability aids reproducibility.

184.human_review: the ideal is simple yet efficient, fully utilized the LLMs to enhance existing models by providing ABSA models with simplified, clearer sentences as input, the paper demonstrates that ATOSS significantly improves the performance of sentiment quadruplet extraction tasks, such as ASQP and ACOS. This highlights the substantial impact that sentence structure can have on the effectiveness of sentiment analysis.
184.llm_review: Methodologically, aligning the splitter to each target model/dataset via DPO on preferred/dispreferred split outputs is a neat idea that operationalizes "what helps this model most" rather than a one-size-fits-all split. The plug-and-play design that leaves ABSA parameters untouched is practical and increases applicability to closed-source LLMs. The two variants (general vs specific) are sensible and often show complementary benefits.

185.human_review: ATOSS is designed as a "play-and-plug" module that can be seamlessly integrated with various ABSA models, including both fine-tuned and large language models (LLMs). This allows the benefits of the sentence simplification to be leveraged without requiring any modifications to the underlying ABSA models.
185.llm_review: The aspect-term–oriented splitting objective is a focused inductive bias for quad extraction, and the training pipeline has reasonable safeguards: generate diverse candidates, filter with explicit criteria, supervised fine-tuning on split pairs, then preference alignment. Using a small LM (T5-base) for inference keeps overhead modest at deployment compared to repeatedly prompting an LLM.

186.human_review: the Direct preference optimization (DPO) part leads to the decrease of the generalizability of this method, a model-specific training procedure is requirement when it comes a new model. Thus the "play-and-plug" is not applicable on this method.
186.llm_review: Key methodological baselines and ablations are missing or underdeveloped. The paper does not compare against simpler or established sentence/clause splitting approaches (e.g., rule-based, dependency-based, SRL-based, or off-the-shelf clause splitters), so it is hard to isolate the value of the proposed training vs any reasonable splitter. Ablations on each component (LLM filtering, K selection, use of gold aspects during split generation, SFT vs DPO, general vs specific) are needed to understand where gains come from and whether DPO is essential.

187.human_review: Besides, It doesn't look like DPOs have a very big performance advantage, and their complexity is higher, also limits the generalizability of the method. I think it was there simply because the authors want to make the whole method more complex.
187.llm_review: Methodology-result linkage is not fully convincing: improvements are generally small and sometimes inconsistent across datasets and metrics, with a few regressions. Results are reported with a single seed (and single-run LLM prompting), with no variance estimates or significance testing. The use of oracle plots motivates the approach but sets a high upper bound without assessing how close ATOSS gets. More granular error analysis (e.g., by conjunction type, number of quads, clause distance) would clarify when the method helps most.

188.human_review: the method is pretty easy and simple, the workload is small too. This article is more suitable as a short paper.
188.llm_review: The pipeline depends heavily on proprietary LLMs for candidate generation and filtering, and on computing F1-based preferences, which is costly and may not be easily reproducible across users or budgets. It is also unclear how meaning preservation is ensured beyond LLM-based filters; a human evaluation or automatic semantic similarity check targeted at polarity/aspect-opinion consistency would strengthen the claim that splitting preserves intent. Finally, the preference selection appears to rely on gold labels to score F1; the paper should explicitly detail how train/dev/test splits are handled to avoid leakage and overfitting during DPO.

189.human_review: The motivation and method are sound. The expression on KGs indeed differs from daily communications. Thus, adapting the KG subgraphs via an adapter is more reasonable than simply verbalizing them via the labels. Training the adapter with DPO sounds reasonable.
189.llm_review: Methodology and motivation are well aligned: CoTKR reframes knowledge rewriting as an interleaved process of reasoning and summarization, which directly targets the redundancy, omission, and semantic misalignment issues of single-pass KG-to-text or summarization. The preference alignment stage (PAQAF) is well motivated by a plausible preference gap between the rewriter and the QA model, and the use of DPO with QA-driven feedback is a principled way to optimize the rewriter for utility. The paper validates these intuitions empirically, showing that interleaving reasoning with targeted knowledge extraction yields more semantically coherent, task-aligned representations that lead to higher QA accuracy.

190.human_review: The experimental results demonstrate that CoTKR significantly enhances performance across various LLMs.
190.llm_review: Methodologically grounded results: Across two benchmarks, multiple KR LLMs (Llama-2/3, ChatGPT) and QA models (ChatGPT, Mistral), CoTKR delivers consistent gains over Triple, KG-to-Text, and Summary on Acc/Recall/EM. The PAQAF variant further improves over supervised CoTKR, supporting the claim that aligning the rewriter to QA model preferences matters. Additional experiments across retrieval settings (2-Hop, BM25, ground-truth subgraph) show robustness, and the ablation on data augmentation clarifies that PAQAF’s benefits are not solely due to ChatGPT paraphrasing. The triple-vs-natural-language analysis is a useful diagnostic that explains when careful natural language rewriting helps.

191.human_review: This paper is well-presented and easy to read.
191.llm_review: The paper is clearly written and easy to follow: core concepts (KR, CoTKR, PAQAF) are introduced with precise definitions, equations, and a succinct algorithmic description. Figures communicate the pipeline and training flow effectively. Experimental settings, metrics, and baselines are described coherently, with prompts and implementation details referenced in the appendix. The case study concretely illustrates how CoTKR avoids omissions and aligns knowledge with the reasoning path.

192.human_review: The experimental datasets are somewhat limited, as the experiments were only conducted on GrailQA and GraphQuestions from Freebase. GraphQuestions is constructed using fixed patterns, which means the questions are less natural and diverse.  *This limitation is not very severe given that GrailQA is one of the most representative KGQA datasets in recent years.* (please refer to suggestions 1)
192.llm_review: Data/Task scope and experimental framing are limited: evaluation is restricted to two Freebase-based KGQA benchmarks, with the GrailQA dev set used as test, and the setup assumes the subject entity is given (sidestepping entity linking). Retrieval is treated superficially (2-Hop, BM25, and an oracle GS), and the method is trained per QA model, raising questions about generalization across tasks, KGs (e.g., Wikidata), and settings without strong retrievers or provided entities. Heavy use of ChatGPT for corpus generation also limits assessment of performance under more resource-constrained or fully open-source pipelines.

193.human_review: The experiments focus solely on the effectiveness of the rewriting module, and the choice of evaluation metrics does not follow the common computation used in complex KGQA. This makes it difficult to compare the performance of the proposed method with existing KGQA approaches (please refer to suggestions 2).
193.llm_review: Evaluation and comparisons leave gaps: results are not accompanied by statistical significance testing, cost/latency/token-overhead analysis, or sensitivity studies (e.g., number of CoT steps, candidate sample size M, or the semantic-difference selection heuristic). The baseline coverage omits recent stronger KGQA pipelines that integrate CoT or explicit reasoning (e.g., KD-CoT, Keqing) and traditional non-LLM KGQA systems, making it hard to position absolute progress. The PAQAF supervision signal uses ChatGPT to judge QA outputs, introducing potential bias/circularity without a human or automated gold-label adjudication; there is no human evaluation of knowledge faithfulness, and the reported gains are sometimes modest.

194.human_review: **Comprehensive Dataset**: The OEE-CFC dataset is extensive and well-annotated, covering a wide range of event types and argument roles, including complex and shared arguments. This makes it a valuable resource for training and evaluating event extraction models.
194.llm_review: Data/Task and Evaluation: The paper introduces OEE-CFC, a substantially richer Chinese financial commentary dataset for open event extraction, annotated with 21 roles that go well beyond traditional subject–predicate–object, including situational and adverbial roles. The corpus explicitly captures complex phenomena crucial to real-world use (events as arguments, shared arguments, partial overlaps, multi-events per document), and reports clear corpus statistics and inter-annotator agreement (84.88% overall, 91.2% for triggers). The evaluation is thoughtfully designed to probe the dataset’s utility: it uses PAIE with multiple prompt strategies, reports both head- and span-based F1 for identification and classification, and demonstrates that explicit role ordering improves extraction performance, thereby validating that the dataset encodes meaningful role semantics.

195.human_review: **Novel Methodology**: The authors developed a general open event template that includes not only common roles like subject, object, and time but also more nuanced roles such as background, manner, and scope. This comprehensive approach provides a deeper understanding of event semantics and enhances the extraction process.
195.llm_review: Methodology and Novelty: The work proposes a general open event template with 21 roles grounded in linguistic theory and tailored to financial discourse, notably adding adverbial roles that are typically ignored in event resources. The schema explicitly models unconventional entities and complex arguments (including events-as-arguments) and shared argument structures, and it is backed by expert consultation and detailed annotation guidelines. This combination of an open, linguistically motivated role inventory and explicit treatment of nested/overlapping phenomena is a novel and useful methodological contribution for the OEE community.

196.human_review: **Insightful Empirical Results**: The experiments conducted using the PAIE framework and the four designed prompts demonstrate the dataset's practical significance. The explicit continuous prompt, in particular, achieved the best performance, validating the dataset's utility in real-world applications.
196.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result, Experiment: The experimental design links the dataset’s role inventory to modeling choices by constructing role-order and role-quantity prompts within the PAIE framework. The ablation across four prompt types isolates how role-order semantics affect performance, with the explicit continuous prompt achieving the best Span-C F1 (63.47%). These results empirically support the claim that OEE-CFC’s richer role semantics are learnable and beneficial for argument extraction, and the multi-event, shared-argument characteristics highlighted in the corpus analysis align with the observed modeling gains.

197.human_review: **Detailed Annotation Process**: The dataset setup is complex and detailed, making the annotation task more challenging than traditional event extraction tasks. It's crucial to know how annotators performed their tasks and how the quality of annotation work was controlled. This aspect requires a more detailed description.
197.llm_review: Data/Task and Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: Important aspects of the task and schema are under-specified in the main paper, which may hinder reproducibility and consistent use. Criteria for what constitutes a meaningful event trigger (e.g., excluding �18�18�18, �18�18, �18�18) are not formalized, and boundaries among closely related roles (e.g., scope vs. manner vs. background) remain subjective with limited disambiguation guidance. The notion of complex entity (events or qualified phrases serving as arguments) needs clearer operational definitions and boundary rules. Tokenization/segmentation choices for Chinese and the definition of head token are not described in detail, yet they directly affect span/head F1. Several crucial specifications are deferred to appendices (e.g., role motivations, special guidelines), and dataset statistics are inconsistently reported across tables, which complicates interpretation.

198.human_review: **Annotation Cost**: There is no mention of the cost of the annotation work. Providing information on the time and resources required for annotation would help in understanding the feasibility of replicating or extending this work.
198.llm_review: Data/Task: The dataset is single-language and single-domain (Chinese financial commentary), limiting generality and external validity relative to the general open template claim. While the corpus emphasizes multi-events and shared arguments, it does not annotate event-event relations, coreference, or event graphs, constraining downstream tasks that the paper motivates. Role distributions are imbalanced (e.g., relatively few material/placeAdverb instances), potentially challenging robust learning. Data access is promised upon acceptance, and details about licensing and long-term availability are not provided.

199.human_review: **Inconsistent Model Development**: The abstract mentions the development of two event extraction models, but only one is discussed in detail in the subsequent sections. Clarifying this discrepancy and providing details on both models would improve the paper's coherence and completeness.
199.llm_review: Methodology: The empirical validation is narrow. Only one framework (PAIE with BART-Base-Chinese) is tested, with no comparison to strong alternatives (e.g., generative IE, structured decoders, or span-classification baselines), and no trigger detection or end-to-end evaluation despite reporting trigger IAA. Cross-sentence argument extraction and unconventional-entity extraction are central motivations but are not separately benchmarked. There is limited error analysis and no statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess the robustness of observed gains across prompts. More comprehensive baselines and analyses would strengthen the methodological claims.

200.human_review: The paper's three key contributions—SN-Caption, MatchTime, and MatchVoice—are highly valuable. MatchTime offers an intuitive yet effective solution, while the design of MatchVoice is reasonable.
200.llm_review: Clear and multifaceted contribution: (i) a manually aligned benchmark (SN-Caption-test-align) that exposes and quantifies the severe video–text timestamp mismatch in SoccerNet-Caption; (ii) a scalable, automatic video–text alignment pipeline that leverages audio ASR, LLM summarization, and contrastive multimodal matching; (iii) a higher-quality aligned training resource (MatchTime); and (iv) a tailored commentary generator (MatchVoice) achieving state-of-the-art results. Together, these deliver a coherent path from problem diagnosis to resource creation and model design, with measurable downstream gains.

201.human_review: The paper statistically highlights the misalignment issue present in existing datasets and demonstrates the impact of this issue by comparing model performance with and without proper alignment. This robust evidence strengthens the necessity for accurate alignment and solidifies the motivation for the proposed task.
201.llm_review: Methodology is well-motivated and validated on the target task and data: the intuition that live audio narration roughly tracks events justifies the coarse ASR+LLM step, while contrastive CLIP-based alignment provides fine-grained matching. On the data/task, the pipeline substantially reduces temporal error (e.g., Avg|Δ| from 13.89s to 6.89s; percentage within 10s window from 35.32% to 80.73%; within 60s to 98.17%). Results corroborate the value of alignment: both baselines and MatchVoice trained on MatchTime outperform training on the original data, and ablations on alignment level and window size further support the design choices.

202.human_review: The authors provide clear and detailed guidelines for human annotation, ensuring the reliability of their dataset.
202.llm_review: The paper curates task-specific data assets valuable to the community: manual re-annotation of 49 test matches with clear guidelines (continuity, replay handling) produces a more reliable evaluation set (3,267 pairs) and reveals large misalignments (up to 152s, mean absolute 16.63s). The automatic pipeline then scales alignment to 422 videos, yielding MatchTime (29,476 pairs; 26,058 train, 3,418 val). These resources directly address a known bottleneck—temporal mismatch—for soccer commentary generation.

203.human_review: Table 1 clearly illustrates the significant improvements achieved through both pre-processing and alignment training, aligning well with the paper’s objectives and underscoring the value of their approach.
203.llm_review: Methodology and results are presented clearly and supported by ablations. MatchVoice uses a pragmatic architecture—frozen visual encoders, a lightweight Perceiver-like temporal aggregator, and LLaMA-3 decoding via prefix tokens—making the approach efficient (single A100) and reproducible. Results span multiple visual backbones and consistently set new SOTA on the aligned benchmark; for example, with Baidu features trained on MatchTime, BLEU-1/4, METEOR, ROUGE-L, and CIDEr reach 31.42/8.92/26.12/29.66/38.42. Figures and tables crisply illustrate alignment improvements and downstream gains.

204.human_review: I believe MatchVoice to be a reasonable design. However, I am also curious about exploring whether PEFT techniques, such as LoRA or other efficient methods, could serve as alternatives to the prompt-tuning approach proposed by the authors.
204.llm_review: Methodologically, the alignment model is trained on a relatively small manually aligned set (45 matches, 2,975 pairs), raising concerns about coverage and overfitting to phrasing styles in that subset. The coarse step relies on WhisperX and LLaMA-3; robustness to noisy audio, multilingual narration, or non-game chatter is not examined. The fine stage constrains search to a [-45s, +30s] window around provided timestamps, which may miss large offsets observed in the data (up to 152s) if coarse alignment fails. For matches without audio, the method skips the coarse step, but generalization under this harder setting is not analyzed. Finally, freezing the visual and language components limits disambiguation of visually similar events and could bottleneck end-to-end alignment quality.

205.human_review: Given that the soccer game commentary application is both practical and designed for human use, incorporating evaluation metrics that capture human preferences, such as BLEURT, could provide additional valuable insights into the effectiveness of the proposed solution.
205.llm_review: Evaluation leans heavily on automatic text metrics and an LLM-as-judge (GPT-score) without human studies or significance testing. Baseline coverage is limited primarily to SN-Caption variants; comparisons to recent video–LLM systems or strong prompting baselines are missing. The new benchmark is authored by the paper’s team, and while valuable, it is unclear whether the 49 manually aligned matches used for evaluation also serve as the validation split in MatchTime; an explicit statement guaranteeing no leakage would strengthen claims. Cross-dataset generalization (e.g., to the original SoccerNet-Caption test or other sports/commentary styles) and a thorough error analysis are absent, making it hard to assess broader robustness and practical applicability.

206.human_review: It supports a large number of unique watermark IDs due to its use of vocab permutation and orthogonal perturbation methods (Section 3.3).
206.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clear, training-free watermarking operator that perturbs LLM paraphraser logits via (i) n-gram–keyed vocab permutations and (ii) orthogonal perturbation functions. This combination is novel and well-motivated: permutations spread signal uniformly in the watermark space to preserve fidelity, while orthogonal bases reduce interference between different IDs and enable overlap-resilience. The design supports metadata embedding and a verifier that avoids recovering the key/ID, which is desirable for robustness.

207.human_review: Training-free and applicable across multiple text types and languages supported by LLMs (Sections 1, 3.1)
207.llm_review: Methodology: The problem is formulated carefully with explicit desiderata (fidelity, verifiability, robust verifiability, scalability) and a support-set perspective that justifies using LLM paraphrasers to enlarge the space of semantically equivalent texts. The fidelity–verifiability Pareto frontier is an appropriate way to expose trade-offs, and the hash-seeded, n-gram-dependent keying is a plausible mechanism to distribute signal across many carriers for attack robustness while keeping verification lightweight.

208.human_review: High robust verifiability even after various attacks, such as paraphrasing and translation, which are often common to LLM-generated text (Section 4.1, 4.2).
208.llm_review: Result: Empirical results are strong and multifaceted: high AUROC pre-attack (~0.99) with controllable fidelity via kappa, robustness under insertion/deletion/synonym, translation, paraphrasing, overlap-watermark, and in-context prompting; substantial verification speedups over baselines; effective metadata extraction that improves with aggregation; competitive code watermarking with higher verifiability than SRCMARKER; and LLM data provenance where AUROC reaches 1.0 with ~100 queries even with many clients.

209.human_review: Embedding and extraction of metadata, providing additional utility in verifying the provenance of text (Section 4.1, Metadata Extraction).
209.llm_review: Data/Task: The evaluation spans diverse settings—news articles (C4 realnewslike), programming code (MBJSP), and scientific abstracts (arXiv) for provenance—plus a realistic suite of attacks (A1–A4) including cross-lingual translation and LLM paraphrasing. The provenance experiment fine-tunes an LLM on watermarked data, reflecting a practical unauthorized-training scenario. The scalability study tests discrimination against many alternate IDs.

210.human_review: The framework may not be applicable to text types where format or style is critical, such as poetry or very short texts (Section 7).
210.llm_review: Methodology: The security model lacks a formal analysis. Claims of scalability (|V|!·|F1|) are mostly theoretical and do not address key management, collision risk, or independence when the same mechanism is reused across many n-grams and texts. There is no principled treatment of adaptive attackers who know the algorithm and actively minimize correlation with the chosen orthogonal functions (e.g., via targeted paraphrasing/decoding), nor a cryptographic argument about resistance to chosen-plaintext or overlap-removal attacks beyond empirical tests.

211.human_review: The performance depends on the capabilities of the LLMs used for paraphrasing, which may limit its performance with less advanced models (Section 7).
211.llm_review: Methodology, Result: Evaluation coverage has gaps. Fidelity relies on STS without human judgments to capture fluency/style regressions; code fidelity is limited to pass@10 without readability/maintainability metrics. Sensitivity to crucial hyperparameters (n-gram size, hash choices, basis family), tokenizer/LLM paraphraser choice, and multilingual breadth is underexplored. Baselines for text are limited (M-BIT, P-NLW), and the provenance setup uses GPT-2 with LoRA, which may not reflect behavior of modern, larger black-box LLMs; comparisons to alternative provenance defenses are missing.

212.human_review: Large scale deployment studies: While the framework is designed to be scalable, actual large-scale deployment might require additional considerations for managing and verifying a large number of watermark IDs (Section 4.1, Scalability).
212.llm_review: Methodology: Verification at web scale is under-specified. The paper reports AUROC but does not characterize thresholds that achieve very low false positive rates under multiple-hypothesis scanning (billions of documents) or discuss calibration and distribution shift. Assumptions about n-gram carrier independence, tokenizer stability across languages/models, and robustness of the orthogonal basis under different vocabularies are not theoretically justified, raising questions about deployment robustness.

213.human_review: The paper tackles an important research question. It addresses a significant gap in understanding how large language models (LLMs) encode and adapt to task-specific information through instruction tuning. It contributes by identifying distinct layers in LLMs where general to task-specific transitions occur, which extends the understanding of multi-task learning mechanisms
213.llm_review: Methodology/Contribution/Data/Task: The paper adapts MOSSA to the instruction-tuning setting and combines it with CKA to quantify task-specific information layer-wise, offering a principled, architecture-aware analysis. The core contribution—mapping layers of an instruction-tuned Llama 2-7B into shared (1–9), transition (10–15), and refinement (16–32) groups—is novel and actionable for PEFT/MTL. The use of over 60 FLAN tasks organized into clusters enables a broad, task-diverse lens on representational dynamics, strengthening the generality of the insights within the NLP domain.

214.human_review: The paper conducts experiments across a wide range of over 60 NLP tasks, using the Flan dataset, which encompasses both language understanding and generation tasks
214.llm_review: Data/Task/Experiment: The study covers a wide task spectrum (60+ datasets across 12 clusters) with careful sampling and mixing to mitigate imbalance, and includes held-out tasks to assess generalization. Multiple complementary analyses (CKA trends, t-SNE clustering, PCA variance, and readability correlations) produce a coherent picture of where multi-task specialization emerges. Training details (LoRA settings, steps, early stopping, hardware) are sufficiently specified to support reproducibility, and the control-vs-experimental model design is appropriate for isolating task-specific information.

215.human_review: Figure 3 is very interesting and conveys the idea clearly.
215.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is clearly structured around three focused research questions, with consistent narrative flow from methods to findings. Figures are informative and well-chosen (e.g., CKA distributions by layer/cluster, t-SNE snapshots, variance curves, and readability correlations), and equations precisely define CKA usage. The mapping of layer functionalities is concisely illustrated (Figure 1) and reinforced throughout, making the takeaways easy to follow.

216.human_review: Nor the acronym nor the technique were mentioned in the cited paper technique called Model-Oriented Sub-population and Spectral Anal ysis (MOSSA (MOSSA; Zhao et al. 2022),
216.llm_review: Methodology: (1) The analysis relies on last-token representations for decoder-only models, which may underrepresent multi-token instruction/context dynamics; alternative pooling or attention-weighted representations could change conclusions. (2) The exclusive use of linear CKA and t-SNE (with known sensitivity to hyperparameters) risks over-interpreting similarity/clustering; robustness checks with alternative metrics (PWCCA/SVCCA/Procrustes) and multiple random seeds are missing. (3) Claims about functional layer mapping would be stronger with causal/functional tests (e.g., layer ablations, targeted freezing/interventions) or significance testing of CKA differences.

217.human_review: The assumption of uniform data size and the use of single-task control models might oversimplify real-world scenarios where task datasets vary significantly in size and complexity.
217.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task: (1) The generality is limited by using only Llama 2-7B and LoRA (no full fine-tuning), which may shape where task information localizes. (2) Control models are trained for 10k steps versus 100k for the multi-task model, potentially biasing CKA comparisons; sensitivity to training budget and early-stopping criteria is not examined. (3) The evaluation is confined to FLAN 2021 tasks and only seven held-out tasks, leaving open how the mapping extends to other domains (code, multilingual), larger/smaller model sizes, or different instruction corpora.

218.human_review: While the study compares Llama 2-SFT with task-specific fine-tuned control models, it might benefit from additional comparisons with other state-of-the-art models or broader benchmarks to validate its findings across different settings.
218.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Comparison: The work lacks comparisons to alternative analysis frameworks (e.g., probing classifiers, linear probes across layers) and to other instruction-tuning datasets or model families/sizes, limiting external validity. There is no explicit linkage between representational similarity and downstream performance deltas, making it hard to assess the practical impact of the proposed layer mapping. Additionally, comparisons to full fine-tuning or other PEFT methods (e.g., adapters, prefix-tuning) are absent, so the conclusions may be LoRA-specific.

219.human_review: HTL’s unique integration of natural language reasoning with executable code generation, leveraging Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT) methodologies, offers a novel approach to improving mathematical reasoning in LLMs. This method reduces computational errors and incorrect reasoning, common in existing LLMs.
219.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty: The paper introduces HumanThink Language (HTL), a coherent integration of CoT and PoT that is conceptually novel and well-motivated by the identified Code Translation Error (CTE). The Focus Attention mechanism explicitly controls information flow so that PoT generation conditions on the full CoT trace (while mitigating attention-sink via preserved initial tokens), and the adaptive mask coverage reconciles the training/inference mismatch. The error-assessment PPO adds a targeted penalty structure to discourage repetitive reasoning. Together, these components constitute a fresh, human-analogous generation paradigm rather than just another prompting tweak.

220.human_review: The paper demonstrates significant improvements in mathematical reasoning capabilities, particularly highlighted by results on the NumGLUE dataset. HTL’s ability to outperform existing models on diverse mathematical datasets showcases its robustness and effectiveness.
220.llm_review: Data/Task, Result: The evaluation spans eight datasets with varying difficulty and domain overlap (GSM8K, NumGLUE, MATH as in-domain; SimulEq, DeepMind arithmetic, SVAMP, MAWPS, ASDiv as out-of-domain), enabling a credible test of generalization. HTL consistently improves over strong MAmmoTH baselines, with average gains of about +4.1 points for CodeLlama-Base (66.27 vs. 62.20 Hybrid) and +3.0 points for Mistral-Base (71.67 vs. 68.65 Hybrid). Particularly notable are the large gains on NumGLUE (e.g., +8.7 absolute over the CodeLlama Hybrid baseline) and steady improvements on SimulEq/ASDiv, suggesting better handling of language-heavy reasoning and OOD transfer. Results are averaged over three runs, and the paper reports reductions in CTE alongside accuracy gains.

221.human_review: Introducing a focus-attention mechanism to enhance the model’s reliance on natural language reasoning is innovative. This mechanism improves computational accuracy and aligns the model's processing closer to human-like reasoning patterns.
221.llm_review: Methodology, Result: Ablations are informative: Focus Attention alone yields roughly +2 average points, indicating that information-flow control is the main driver; PPO adds modest average gains but reliably helps the long-form, hard MATH set by curbing repetitive generations. The adaptive coverage strategy outperforms fixed masking, and the two-stage variant does not outperform the proposed one-stage, reinforcing that the training-time attention design is key. Error analysis shows reductions in both logical and execution errors, and CTE is nearly halved (e.g., CodeLlama from 8.33% to 3.96%, Mistral from 6.97% to 3.55%), aligning with the method’s stated goals.

222.human_review: Despite successes, HTL’s testing does not include Math23K as its performance comparison. From the last submission, the authors pointed that Math23K is in Chinese for a reason of omission. They stated that LLM's ability in other languages is inferior to that of English. I can see that HTL can be less effective but the baselines also would be experimented in the same setting, so I do not see any reason to omit the Match23K experiments.
222.llm_review: Result, Experiment, Comparison: The empirical study, while broad, omits several important comparisons and analyses. (1) There is no significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis beyond reporting 3-run averages; it is unclear if the improvements are statistically robust per dataset. (2) The baseline suite is missing recent or stronger open-source math models and tool-augmented systems (e.g., specialized math-LLMs, more recent CoT+tool integrations), making it hard to position HTL against current SOTA. (3) Scalability is not demonstrated: only 7B models are tested despite claims that CTE is not resolved by scaling; it remains unknown whether HTL’s gains persist or grow at 13B/34B/70B scales. (4) Inference settings (0-shot vs. few-shot) differ across baselines in places and best-of-n or majority-vote decoding is not explored, which might understate the baselines. (5) The evaluation does not report program-execution reliability metrics (e.g., pass@k or failure modes) or runtime/latency overhead due to extra CoT generation and masking, limiting practical interpretability.

223.human_review: The model’s success heavily relies on the quality and variety of the datasets used for training, potentially limiting generalizability to other domains or less structured problems.
223.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: Several design choices appear ad hoc or weakly validated. (1) The PPO reward function is handcrafted with coarse terminal rewards and no process-level alignment; it encourages outcome correctness but not faithfulness, yet the paper’s claims hinge on improved faithfulness. (2) Focus Attention is trained with a local mask but decoded with standard causal attention, relying on an adaptive schedule to bridge the mismatch; while ablations help, a formal justification or analysis of failure modes is missing. (3) The self-distilled training data links CoT and PoT by correctness rather than step correspondence; without human or automatic process-alignment checks, it risks reinforcing spurious mappings, especially on problems with multiple valid solution paths. (4) The training corpus is relatively small (36k) and drawn from a narrow set of math sources; the claim of broader transferability (e.g., to NLI) is asserted but not substantiated with dedicated non-math benchmarks or analyses. (5) Data provenance and contamination controls are not detailed, leaving uncertainty about overlap between training and test distributions.

224.human_review: This paper studies an important problem: the generalization of truthfulness hyperplane inside LLMs for hallucination detection.
224.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clean, well-motivated probing framework that targets a universal truthfulness hyperplane via linear methods (logistic regression and mass-mean). The representation design is thoughtful: it extracts last-token features from attention head outputs, uses a principled head-location selection procedure (per-head preliminary probes on diverse training tasks), and introduces k-sparse feature selection to reduce redundancy. This balances interpretability, simplicity, and efficiency while directly testing the linear separability hypothesis for truthfulness across tasks.

225.human_review: The paper's approach to scaling up the number of training datasets to over 40, covering 17 distinct categories of tasks, is thorough and ambitious. This extensive evaluation provides a robust analysis of the existence of a general Truthfulness Hyperplane across different domains.
225.llm_review: Data/Task, Evaluation, Analysis: The authors curate an unusually broad suite of 49 datasets spanning 17 task families, carefully structuring training vs. test tasks to probe cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Evaluation is comprehensive: they benchmark against Self-Eval, probability thresholds, and finetuning, and test across multiple base models (LLaMA2-7B/13B, Mistral-7B). Analyses are insightful, including ablations on representation type (attention heads vs residual stream), scaling the number of training tasks, and varying per-dataset sample sizes; the finding that diversity matters more than volume (≈10 samples per dataset suffice) is practically important and well supported.

226.human_review: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The authors provide thorough details of the experiments, making it easier for others to replicate the results.
226.llm_review: Experiment, Presentation: Experiments are extensive and clearly presented, with tables and figures that make the setup and results easy to follow (e.g., reproducing OOD failure when training only on TruthfulQA, then showing consistent gains when training on diverse data). The cross-setting comparisons (cross-task, cross-domain, in-domain) and multi-model results are organized coherently, and key implementation details (hyperparameters num and k, selection protocol, data splits) are documented and deferred to appendices where appropriate, aiding reproducibility.

227.human_review: The authors conduct hallucination analysis over 17 tasks but fail to provide specific definitions of hallucination for each task. It seems like the authors are considering any LLMs' mistakes as hallucination. However, this approach might be quite problematic as the mistakes in different tasks are different in nature. For instance, fabricating a news story and making a mistake in a reasoning task are two different types of errors.
227.llm_review: Data/Task, Analysis: The negative data construction relies heavily on GPT-generated false answers and attribute substitutions, which may introduce artifacts or stylistic biases that probes can exploit instead of genuine factuality cues. The paper acknowledges potential misalignment between model knowledge and ground-truth labels, but there is limited quantitative auditing of label noise or error typology. Moreover, the test coverage, while diverse, concentrates on 3 test tasks (8 datasets) for the main cross-task evaluations; stronger claims of universality would benefit from broader, more realistic, and independently annotated settings, plus analyses that disentangle data-construction artifacts from true generalization.

228.human_review: The experiments are limited to 7B and 13B size models. It would be nice if the authors apply their analysis to larger models, especially given the low-cost nature of the probing method.
228.llm_review: Methodology, Experiment, Analysis: The central claim about a universal hyperplane rests on improved cross-task accuracy (≈70%) rather than causal verification; there are no intervention experiments to test whether moving along the learned vector modulates truthfulness. Important baselines like unsupervised linear probes (e.g., CCS, LAT) are discussed but not compared empirically. The head-location selection involves training many preliminary probes and choosing top positions per validation split, which risks selection bias/multiple comparisons without statistical controls. Methodologically, focusing only on last-token features may miss distributed signals (e.g., multi-token pooling), and the paper does not report robustness to random seeds, confidence calibration, or statistical significance testing. Together, these issues limit how strongly the results can support the universality hypothesis.

229.human_review: The introduction of NNN provides a simple yet effective way to enhance multimodal retrieval performance without the need for additional training. This method's applicability across different models and datasets highlights its versatility.
229.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The paper introduces a simple, training-free normalization that subtracts a per-candidate bias estimated from its top-k most similar reference queries. This additive correction is easy to cache and integrate at inference via an embedding augmentation trick, yielding sublinear overhead. Empirically, it consistently improves Recall@1 over base contrastive models across both directions (image-to-text and text-to-image) and multiple architectures (e.g., CLIP, BLIP, ALBEF, SigLIP, BEiT/BEiT-3) on COCO and Flickr30k, with notable gains such as sizeable R@1 improvements for CLIP on COCO.

230.human_review: The experimental results are comprehensive, showing consistent improvements in retrieval accuracy for both text-to-image and image-to-text tasks. The inclusion of multiple baselines (DBNorm, QBNorm, DualIS) and a variety of models strengthens the validity of the findings.
230.llm_review: Result, Experiment, Comparison, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Methodology: The experimental suite is broad and careful: evaluations span 5+ contrastive models, two standard datasets, both retrieval directions, and in/out-of-distribution reference sets. Comparisons include prior training-free test-time normalization methods (DBNorm, QBNorm, DN), where the proposed method is competitive or better while being substantially more efficient. Ablations on reference set size show robustness, and hubness analyses (kurtosis/MAE reductions, fewer hubs) validate the motivation that per-candidate score inflation drives errors. A fairness case study (VisoGender) further validates the intuition by jointly reducing gender bias and improving precision, all with a methodologically simple additive correction.

231.human_review: The paper addresses the critical issue of gender bias in multimodal retrieval. The ability of NNN to reduce bias while maintaining or improving accuracy is particularly noteworthy and addresses a significant concern in the deployment of AI systems.
231.llm_review: Methodology: The core algorithm is well specified and practically grounded: compute per-candidate bias as the scaled mean similarity to top-k reference queries, subtract at inference, and fold the correction into a standard vector index by augmenting embeddings (r' = <r, b>, q' = <q, -1>). Biases are precomputable and cacheable; top-k search is efficiently handled with IVF in FAISS, making both precomputation and query-time integration straightforward. Hyperparameters (k, alpha) are tuned on a held-out subset, mirroring how competing methods are tuned while being far cheaper than DBNorm.

232.human_review: The method's computational efficiency, with sublinear runtime relative to the reference database size, makes it suitable for real-world applications where computational resources may be limited.
232.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: The method is model- and dataset-agnostic within contrastive retrieval, requiring only embeddings and a reference set, and it works without any additional training. It yields consistent gains on standard retrieval tasks (MS-COCO, Flickr30k) across diverse contrastive models and remains helpful when the reference set is out-of-distribution. Its ability to operate in black-box settings and limited-compute environments is compelling for practical multimodal retrieval deployments.

233.human_review: While the method shows promising results for contrastive multimodal models, its applicability to models with dedicated cross-attention mechanisms remains uncertain. This limitation should be acknowledged and explored in future work.
233.llm_review: Methodology: The correction is a global, query-agnostic bias per retrieval candidate. While effective against hubs, it may overcorrect for genuinely broad or multi-faceted items, potentially suppressing correct matches in certain contexts. The approach is sensitive to k and alpha with no guidance beyond validation search, and it lacks a theoretical characterization connecting the top-k mean correction to an optimal normalization objective. Moreover, the sublinear precomputation relies on approximate nearest neighbor search, introducing an extra approximation layer whose impact is only briefly quantified.

234.human_review: NNN's reliance on a reference database could be a limitation in scenarios where such a database is unavailable or challenging to curate. Exploring methods to mitigate this dependency would be beneficial.
234.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: Performance depends on the choice and composition of the reference set. Although out-of-distribution references can help, the method still presumes access to a sizable, reasonably representative reference database, which may be non-trivial for specialized domains. The empirical scope is limited to two relatively small benchmarks (Flickr30k, COCO) and contrastive architectures; scalability and behavior on truly large-scale, noisy web corpora or multilingual settings are not demonstrated. Some configurations show small degradations, indicating sensitivity to data/model match.

235.human_review: The experiments primarily focus on well-known datasets (MS-COCO and Flickr30k). Including more diverse datasets, especially those with different characteristics or from different domains, could further validate the method's robustness.
235.llm_review: Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Data/Task, Result, Experiment: While the hubness motivation is compelling and supported by distributional metrics, the paper’s claim of outperforming prior normalization baselines is not uniformly borne out across all settings in the main tables, where DBNorm sometimes matches or exceeds the proposed method (e.g., several Flickr cases). Statistical significance is relegated to the appendix; the main narrative focuses on R@1 with limited discussion of R@5/R@10. The fairness validation uses a small VisoGender subset and COCO-derived references, which, while illustrative, is not a comprehensive bias evaluation across demographic attributes or domains.

236.human_review: The need for hyperparameter tuning (α and k) might complicate the method's implementation. Providing more guidelines or an automated approach for selecting these parameters could enhance usability.
236.llm_review: Methodology: The approach is tailored to contrastive scoring via cosine/inner product; the authors note reduced effectiveness or impracticality for cross-attention models that require per-pair forward passes. This limits applicability to a large class of modern multimodal retrieval systems. Additionally, the per-candidate constant shift assumes a stationary bias independent of query distribution shifts at test time; no adaptive mechanism is proposed to update biases online or handle evolving retrieval corpora.

237.human_review: The authors introduce two methods - TOPLA-Weighted and TOPLA-Summary - to create ensembles from a set of underlying LLMs in an efficient manner (through subset selection).
237.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a principled, diversity-aware ensemble framework. The focal negative correlation/diversity definitions explicitly target simultaneous failure modes among component LLMs and are operationalized for selection. A genetic-algorithm-based pruning strategy makes the combinatorial search tractable while aiming to preserve diversity. Two complementary learn-to-ensemble mechanisms are well-motivated: (i) TOPLA-Weighted (stacking via an MLP over calibrated class/answer distributions, including CoT-derived answer-frequency vectors for open-ended short answers), and (ii) TOPLA-Summary (a seq2seq aggregator that generates a new output by conditioning on the query and concatenated candidate responses), augmented with sliding-window sparse attention and selective global attention to scale with long inputs.

238.human_review: Through a set of well designed ablation experiments on 4 evaluation benchmarks (MMLU, GSM-8k, SearchQA and XSUM) and 8 different LLMs, the paper highlights the effectiveness of the LLM-TOPLA framework.
238.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Ablation, Experiment: The study covers three output regimes (MCQ, OEQ, GQ) and evaluates on four benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8k, SearchQA, XSum) with 6–8 modern LLMs, providing a realistic ensemble pool. The experimental protocol is clear: construct D_train by sampling model outputs, prune with focal diversity, and train either TOPLA-Weighted or TOPLA-Summary depending on task type. Ablations probe (a) the effect of pruning versus using all models, (b) the contribution of sliding-window and selective global attention, (c) sensitivity to the number of CoT samples K, and (d) training data size. The paper also reports inference latency and releases code plus a dataset of model outputs, supporting reproducibility.

239.human_review: The paper also proposes a systematic way of pruning a given ensemble of LLMs with equal/more performance compared to the overall ensemble using a genetic algorithm to explore the subset space in a computationally efficient manner.
239.llm_review: Methodology, Result: The focal diversity metric is empirically correlated with performance, and pruning yields smaller sub-ensembles that match or exceed the performance of larger teams and the best single model. The learn-to-ensemble designs translate into consistent gains: +3.5% accuracy over Mixtral on MMLU and +~2% over More Agents on GSM8k, while TOPLA-Summary delivers large improvements on generative tasks (e.g., substantial F1 gains on SearchQA and ROUGE gains on XSum). The GA-based pruning substantially reduces search time (reported ~100x), making the approach practical without sacrificing accuracy.

240.human_review: The performance of LLM-TOPLA-Summary model seems highly dependent on the encoder decoder trained model which the authors use for combining the information provided by each LLM and generating the correct token sequence. I’m curious why the authors decided to train an encoder-decode architecture from scratch instead of fine tuning a pre-existing LLM? Would that not improve the quality of the generated answers (assuming data constrains in $D_{train}$ due to which the encoder-decoder model might be undertrained?)
240.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result: (1) Methodology: Computing focal diversity requires labeled validation data and, for generative tasks, uses a coarse error proxy (missed 1-grams), which may not reflect quality; comparisons to alternative selection criteria (e.g., pairwise disagreement/Q-statistics, submodular coverage, greedy forward selection) are absent, and GA-driven selection risks overfitting to the validation set. The seq2seq aggregator may learn task-specific generation rather than generalizable ensembling, and the TOPLA-Weighted approach depends on multiple CoT passes (K), increasing query cost; details on hyperparameters/training budgets are sparse. (2) Data/Task: Evaluation is limited to four English datasets and a small pool of open models; generalization to other domains/languages and to stronger/closed models is unclear. The approach assumes access to labels to train the ensemble, which may limit applicability in low-supervision settings. (3) Result: Some claims in the abstract appear misaligned with tables (e.g., magnitude of XSum ROUGE-1 and SearchQA F1 improvements), no statistical significance is reported, and comparisons omit strong recent ensemble/debate systems and stronger LLM baselines; end-to-end runtime and cost overheads of TOPLA-Summary (including extra generation) are not thoroughly quantified.

241.human_review: The paper addresses both understanding and generation tasks, promoting a balanced optimization for TOD systems. It introduces step-by-step rewards that offer continuous, incremental feedback, enhancing the learning process.
241.llm_review: Well-chosen and comprehensive task/dataset setup: the work targets classic task-oriented dialogue with explicit DST, DPL, and RG, and evaluates on the most established TOD benchmarks (MultiWOZ 2.0/2.1 and In-Car) using standard task-completion metrics (Inform/Success/Match/SuccF1) that align with the schema-driven nature of TOD. The inclusion of delexicalized responses (a common practice in TOD) and a low-resource training regime further stress-tests the method under realistic data constraints.

242.human_review: The proposed method achieves new state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.
242.llm_review: Across multiple TOD datasets (MultiWOZ 2.0/2.1, In-Car), the results show consistent and sizable gains on task-focused metrics (notably Inform, Success, Match, SuccF1), yielding new state-of-the-art combined scores without pretraining. The low-resource experiments demonstrate robust advantages over strong pre-trained E2E baselines (SPACE-3, GALAXY) across varying sample sizes, indicating strong task generalization under limited data.

243.human_review: This paper also demonstrates decent performance in few-shot settings, highlighting its adaptability and generalizability.
243.llm_review: Methodologically, the step-by-step token-level reward that jointly covers understanding (DST) and generation (DPL/RG) is clean and tightly aligned with task goals, and the use of NLPO with KL regularization provides a stable optimization framework. Empirically, ablations verify that both the understanding and generation rewards are necessary and complementary (removing either substantially degrades combined performance), and the strongest gains appear precisely on task-completion metrics the rewards target.

244.human_review: The improvement of this method (compared to GALAXY) mainly lies in inform and succ., which demonstrates the contribution of the reward for DST. However, does that harm the capability of the generation part (since GALAXY has better BLEU on all three test sets)?
244.llm_review: Contribution, Result, Comparison: (1) While integrating dense, token-level, goal-aligned rewards is sensible, the novelty over prior RL and reward-shaping approaches (including token-level reward designs) feels incremental; the paper would benefit from a crisper positioning versus closely related methods (e.g., fine-grained reward shaping, IRL-driven dense rewards, token-level RL in TOD). (2) Some comparisons are uneven or missing: several RL baselines are reported only on subsets of datasets, and more recent end-to-end or RL-based TOD systems and LLM-agent methods are not comprehensively included. (3) BLEU improvements are limited or sometimes lower than strong baselines, and the reliance on delexicalized responses complicates comparison on naturalness across methods that generate fully lexicalized outputs.

245.human_review: The improvement on MultiWOZ 2.1 is not significant (Comb. score). Considering 2.1 is cleaner than 2.0, I am concerned if this method can still outperform GALAXY on MultiWOZ 2.4
245.llm_review: Significance, Result, Comparison: (1) The reward depends on predefined informable/requestable schema lists, constraining applicability beyond schema-driven TOD (e.g., open-domain or schema-evolving settings), which limits broader impact. (2) The improvements, while strong on Inform/Success/Match/SuccF1, translate less clearly to response fluency (BLEU), and there is limited qualitative/error analysis to contextualize where gains originate or where failures persist. (3) There is little sensitivity analysis (e.g., α/β, weightings, KL strength) or comparison under alternative evaluation setups (e.g., online RL with simulators, robustness to noisy annotations), making it hard to gauge how broadly the reported gains will hold.

246.human_review: The proposed prompt optimization framework is easy to understand and can be applied to both open-source LLMs and proprietary models. Also, the high correlation between the fairness measure and evaluation performance makes this framework somewhat plausible.
246.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes ZEPO, a zero-shot prompt optimization framework that targets preference fairness by minimizing the deviation of the model’s pairwise decision distribution from a uniform prior. The objective is simple, label-free, and operationalizable with black-box access, using an LLM paraphraser plus greedy search to iteratively refine instructions. The approach is orthogonal to existing calibration/debiasing methods and, in principle, scales beyond binary comparisons to multi-class settings.

247.human_review: This work mentions the connection and difference between the proposed preference fairness measure and other confidence measures or bias measures, which facilitates more comprehensive research on the robustness and fairness of model evaluation.
247.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation: The study first diagnoses prompt sensitivity and connects it to biased decision distributions, then leverages this insight to optimize prompts. The empirical evaluation across three meta-evaluation benchmarks (NewsRoom, SummEval, TopicalChat) with Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B shows consistent average gains over pairwise baselines, often recovering large drops seen with manual prompts. The correlation analysis indicates the fairness metric tracks human alignment better than alternative zero-shot proxies (confidence, calibration), supporting the methodological choice with clear evaluation design and quantitative evidence.

248.human_review: Only two open-source LLMs are used in this study, which makes the generality of the prompt optimization approach questionable. Adding more Open-source and proprietary models will make this approach more convincing.
248.llm_review: Methodology: The fairness objective implicitly assumes a uniform ground-truth prior over A/B outcomes and may encourage a 50/50 split even when the true distribution is skewed (e.g., one candidate set is generally better). This risks optimizing for balance rather than correctness and could incentivize near-random behavior if not countered. The approach also relies on accurate estimation of decision distributions, which can be sample-inefficient, and uses a relatively weak search (paraphrasing + greedy), leaving open whether stronger optimizers or search spaces would materially change outcomes.

249.human_review: Although other confidence measures are compared with the proposed approach in terms of their correlation with evaluation performance in Figure 3, it is unknown how well they are used as the optimization objective. There is no guarantee that a low correlation with evaluation performance will result in bad performance when used as the prompt optimization objective.
249.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation, Comparison: The experimental comparison omits recent automatic prompt optimization/search baselines and stronger debiasing/calibration variants, making it hard to attribute gains specifically to the proposed objective versus the search procedure. Statistical significance is not reported, and there are regressions on some aspects (e.g., small drops in Mistral REL), with no error bars or robustness checks across seeds/prompts. The evaluation focuses on Spearman only, lacks cost/runtime analyses for optimization, and does not test portability to other judges or settings, limiting comparative and practical conclusions.

250.human_review: The authors claim their preference fairness measure can indicate "fairness", but it is subject to the label distribution of datasets. Therefore the proposed preference fairness measure does not have theoretical advantages over context-free confidence.
250.llm_review: Data/Task, Theory: The evidence is restricted to summarization and dialog meta-evaluation, leaving out other common generation tasks (e.g., QA, MT, factuality/safety) where label priors and bias profiles may differ. The central claim that fairer preferences improve human alignment is supported empirically but remains correlational; there is no theoretical characterization of when the uniform-prior fairness proxy should align with human preferences or how task/data skew affects it. This limits the theoretical grounding and external validity of the fairness-human alignment link.

251.human_review: The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the ATM system in generating accurate answers while resisting irrelevant or misleading documents. The authors provide detailed analyses of the Generator's performance, robustness against positional shuffling, and the Attacker's ability to generate increasingly aggressive fabrications across iterative tuning rounds. These empirical findings offer valuable insights into the behavior and capabilities of the proposed system.
251.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment, Analysis: The paper introduces a clear and novel multi-agent adversarial tuning framework for RAG that optimizes both a Generator and an Attacker. Methodologically, the Attacker is trained via DPO using the Generator’s perplexity on the golden answer as a misleading signal, while the Generator is trained with a new MITO objective that combines SFT on attacked inputs with a token-level KL regularizer between normal and attacked contexts. The two-stage process (multi-task SFT with rule-based perturbations followed by iterative adversarial tuning) is well-motivated for today’s noisy, LLM-saturated web. Empirically, the approach yields consistent and sizable gains over strong baselines across NQ, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, and PopQA, with improvements reported in Subspan EM, EM, and F1; e.g., on NQ, the ATM Generator improves by >20 Subspan EM points and ~8 EM points over LLaMA2-7B-chat/REAR settings, and shows generalization to PopQA. The iterative analysis is informative: performance typically improves from Iter0 to Iter2 before slightly regressing at Iter3, and the positional robustness study (20 random shuffles) shows higher mean and reduced variance, indicating improved stability. Additional analysis of Attacker strength via log-loss/PPL histograms across iterations supports the claim that the Attacker becomes more challenging while the Generator becomes more robust.

252.human_review: The iterative adversarial tuning process and the multi-agent system involving two large language models (Generator and Attacker) may have significant computational requirements and scalability challenges. The paper does not provide a detailed discussion on the computational costs, resource requirements, or the scalability of the proposed approach to larger language models or datasets.
252.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: The evaluation data construction and training signals may introduce biases that complicate interpretation. The test-time setting injects fabricated documents from a strong LLM, but it is unclear whether all baselines were evaluated under exactly the same attacked document lists and retrieval pipeline, raising fairness concerns. Core retrieval details (retriever model, corpus snapshot, number of retrieved docs nd, number of fabrications nf, document length limits, and prompt formats) are under-specified, making it hard to assess reproducibility or diagnose where gains originate. The Attacker’s DPO objective uses the Generator’s PPL on the golden answer as the preference signal; this may not always correlate with actual answer correctness and could encourage reward hacking (e.g., increasing difficulty without truly misleading), so a direct misanswer-based signal and calibration analyses would strengthen claims. The method is trained and evaluated primarily on KiQA with synthetic attacks; robustness to naturally noisy or conflicting web documents, to unseen attack generators, and to different retrieval qualities is not thoroughly tested. More component-level ablations (e.g., MITO vs SFT-only, rule-based vs model-based attacks, KL weighting α) and dataset/corpus specifications would improve methodological clarity.

253.human_review: The proposed framework provides a novel engineering solution to the identified problems of KG verbalization.
253.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty: The paper introduces an evidence-focused fact summarization framework that is explicitly conditioned on the QA task, combining (i) LLM distillation from a teacher to produce targeted, high-density summaries and (ii) preference alignment via DPO with two task-grounded criteria (helpfulness for QA and faithfulness to facts). The broad-to-specific paraphrasing guided by gold answers during preference-pair construction is a novel touch that steers the summarizer toward highlighting answer-bearing evidence without relying on QA-time gold information.

254.human_review: The overall structure of the paper is clear and well-elaborated. The authors have clearly formulated the research questions and answered them by presenting the experimental results.
254.llm_review: Experiment, Result, Presentation: The empirical study is broad and clearly presented, spanning two KGQA datasets (WebQSP-WD, Mintaka), three QA LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo, Flan-T5-XL, Llama2-7B-Chat), multiple token budgets (L=200/400), different numbers of retrieved facts (K=10–150), and several retrieval strategies (random, popular, MPNet). Results are systematically organized in tables/figures and demonstrate that the proposed method is competitive or best in many realistic settings, especially under strict context-length budgets.

255.human_review: The provided analysis of evidence density proves the presence of more intensive and useful information in the context instead of arbitrary usage of the noisy triplets. The experiment design provides sufficient support for the choice of the methods.
255.llm_review: Result, Experiment, Analysis: The work addresses three research questions with targeted analyses: (RQ1) density—via length constraints and compression/duplication statistics; (RQ2) clarity—via answer-level vs summary-level accuracy curves as K varies; (RQ3) preference alignment—via helpfulness (summary-level accuracy) and faithfulness (hallucination rate) metrics. The analyses (Figures 2, 4, 5) link the design choices to observed gains and provide insight into why the approach improves QA.

256.human_review: The provided framework is robust over different scenarios such as the number of context tokens, the number of the retrieved triplets, and the choice of the retrieval in addition to enhancement of the quality compared to the previous work.
256.llm_review: Methodology, Result: Training an open-source summarizer with distillation plus DPO produces summaries that are both more helpful for QA and more faithful to the retrieved facts, leading to accuracy gains over baselines in many settings, particularly with Flan-T5-XL and GPT-3.5 under limited token budgets. The method also shows robustness to noisier retrieval (random/popular), indicating it can prioritize salient evidence even when input triples contain noise.

257.human_review: The authors indicated the research gap in choosing better retrieving methods and choice of metrics for generative KGQA.
257.llm_review: Methodology, Evaluation: The evaluation goes beyond raw QA accuracy to include summary-level accuracy and hallucination-based faithfulness, and probes robustness across retrievers, token budgets, and K. Comparisons include linear triple verbalization (KAPING), KG2Text, and LLM-based free-form rewriting, and the paper releases code for reproducibility, strengthening the methodological evaluation.

258.human_review: The absence of comparison of the proposed method with graph-based approaches for KGQA (e.g. GNNs, KG embeddings like in [1]).
258.llm_review: Methodology, Comparison: The preference alignment relies on LLM-based judgments—G-Eval for faithfulness and QA answering for helpfulness—raising concerns about evaluator bias and circularity (especially when the same or similar LLM families are used for both filtering and final QA). There is no human evaluation of faithfulness/fluency. The comparison set omits several recent strong baselines in KG-augmented LLMs and graph-aware prompting/fusion approaches, and does not quantify computational cost/latency or token-savings trade-offs relative to baselines. The use of gold answers during paraphrase-based preference construction, while confined to training, deserves clearer justification to avoid perceived leakage advantages.

259.human_review: The modest improvements on multi-hop KGQA.
259.llm_review: Result: Improvements are not uniform. For example, on Mintaka with GPT-3.5-turbo, EFSumdistill underperforms the no-knowledge baseline (e.g., 0.474/0.449 vs 0.540 in Table 1), and with Llama2-7B-Chat on WebQSP, simpler formats (e.g., KAPING) sometimes perform better. This sensitivity to the QA model’s preferred knowledge format weakens the claim of universally improved zero-shot QA and suggests the need for significance testing, variance reporting, and deeper failure analyses.

260.human_review:
The paper would benefit from providing the information on costs of the API calls of closed-source model to additionally support the paper claims.


[1] Anton Razzhigaev, Mikhail Salnikov, Valentin Malykh, Pavel Braslavski, and Alexander Panchenko. 2023. A System for Answering Simple Questions in Multiple Languages. In Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 3: System Demonstrations), pages 524–537, Toronto, Canada. Association for Computational Linguistics.
260.llm_review: Related Work: The discussion under-represents adjacent lines of work, including RLHF/DPO-style training for factual summarization/faithfulness, recent graph-aware prompting and GraphRAG-style methods, and broader KG-to-text literature beyond the chosen baselines. A more thorough positioning against contemporary knowledge-augmented LLM strategies and faithfulness evaluation frameworks would clarify the paper’s distinct contribution.

261.human_review: The introduction of a coarse-to-fine visual view tree (CFTree) and the use of tree-based Shapley values is quite inspiring and through experiment the author confirms that the proposed method could actually provides a robust mechanism for optimizing visual-token matching, enhancing the precision and reliability of the model's outputs.
261.llm_review: Methodology and Experiment: The paper proposes a training-free, plug-and-play decoding framework that organizes visual evidence into a three-level coarse-to-fine view tree and then uses a cooperative game to select optimal visual granularity during autoregressive generation. The design is concretely instantiated with RAM/Grounded-SAM for entity extraction, BLIP-based visual-text scoring, and an adaptive contrastive decoding scheme, making the approach implementable without model retraining. Experiments span four benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE, MME, LLaVABench) and three LVLM families (LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, mPLUG-Owl2), with careful ablations showing each component (CFTree layers, TSV, adaptive factor) contributes to performance.

262.human_review: GTHM is a plug-and-play, training-free decoding algorithm, making it easy to implement without the need for additional training data or computational resources, which enhances its practical applicability.
262.llm_review: Methodology: The CFTree provides a principled multi-granularity organization (event–relation–entity) that unifies objects, attributes, and relations under a single search space, addressing limitations of prior decoding approaches that focus mainly on objects. Modeling view selection as a cooperative game and introducing a tree-based Shapley value (TSV) to score entire view paths is a neat way to capture coarse-to-fine interactions. The adaptive, TSV-weighted contrastive decoding integrates naturally with beam search and POS filtering, enabling token-specific, vision-aware adjustments without retraining.

263.key_points: Strength: Result, Comparison, Data/Task, Analysis, Theory
263.human_review: The paper provides comprehensive theoretical analysis and comparisons with STOA methods through multiple benchmarks, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods in mitigating visual hallucinations.
263.llm_review: Result, Comparison, Data/Task, Analysis, Theory: Results show consistent, sometimes sizable reductions in hallucination metrics (e.g., CHAIR-s/i and POPE Acc/Prec/F) across LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, and mPLUG-Owl2, outperforming strong baselines including HALC, VCD, and post-processing methods. Evaluations cover caption-style hallucinations (CHAIR), probing-based object presence (POPE), and object/attribute subsets of MME, demonstrating breadth across data/task types. Analyses include TSV–PDM correlations, TSV vs. sentence length trends, and extensive ablations on tree layers, payoff definitions (BLIP vs. Shapley vs. TSV), and contrastive factors, which together support the design choices.
