455.human_review: The studied task is crucial for adapting LLMs to specialized domains, as it addresses the challenges of optimizing model performance in specific areas such as clinical applications.
455.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clear, staged adaptation pipeline for clinical LLMs that juxtaposes continuous pretraining, instruction fine-tuning, NEFTune, and prompt engineering. The training recipe is thoughtfully engineered to mitigate instabilities common in continual pretraining (e.g., linear warmup and a blended in-domain/general corpus to reduce forgetting). The study also operationalizes practical choices—response-only loss for alignment, explicit system/prompter/assistant formatting, and a reproducible noise-in-embedding setup for NEFTune—that make the methodology both implementable and broadly useful.

456.human_review: The proposed method demonstrates excellent performance, showing significant improvements in various clinical tasks through techniques like continuous pre-training, instruct fine-tuning, NEFTune, and complex prompt engineering.
456.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result: The authors curate a sizeable and domain-relevant pretraining corpus (~50B clinical tokens mixed with 15B general tokens) with explicit parsing, multi-stage deduplication (MinHash and exact), and chunking; and a 500M-token instruction dataset assembled from medical forums and medical segments. Evaluation spans standard clinical QA benchmarks (MedQA, USMLE, MMLU-medical, MedMCQA). Results show consistent gains from the proposed pipeline: for Mistral-7B, accuracy improves from 42.89 to 62.69 on MedQA and from 48.18 to 63.98 on USMLE after P+N, with similar upward trends for Mixtral (e.g., 52.55 to 68.34 on MedQA). These results substantiate that domain-adaptive pretraining plus alignment and NEFTune yield measurable improvements on established clinical QA tasks.

457.human_review: The authors provide a analysis of the experimental results, highlighting the impact of each technique on model performance and offering insights into the effectiveness of different fine-tuning strategies.
457.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment, Analysis: The experimental design is comprehensive: the paper tracks multiple pretraining checkpoints, then instruction-tunes them to isolate the marginal effect of continued pretraining; it contrasts standard fine-tuning with NEFTune; and it layers in progressively stronger prompting (CoT, few-shot CoT, dynamic retrieval, and ensembles). The analysis is insightful—showing that pretraining alone can depress MCQA performance but creates a stronger substrate for instruction tuning; that NEFTune likely regularizes and improves generalization; and that MedPrompt-style prompting can further boost Mixtral-Instruct from 52.55% to above 75% on MedQA—demonstrating how these components interact and compound.

458.human_review: It is not clear which part of the proposed method are from prior works and which parts of the work is proposed by authors.
458.llm_review: Methodology, Related Work: The methodological novelty of continuous/domain-adaptive pretraining is under-positioned relative to prior work (e.g., DAPT/TAPT and follow-ups on catastrophic forgetting and stability). The paper does not adequately situate its approach within this literature or discuss alternative stabilization strategies (e.g., regularization, adapter-based continual pretraining). Key design choices—such as the 50B:15B in-domain/general mix, 4 epochs, and NEFTune alpha=5—lack principled justification or ablations, limiting clarity on why these settings are preferred over known alternatives in the literature.

459.human_review: Some analysis are too shallow and are discussed in prior works, such as the usage of NEFT (L517-539), as well as the benefits of using prompt engineering (L540-L562).
459.llm_review: Methodology, Related Work, Analysis: The analysis focuses almost exclusively on multiple-choice QA accuracy and does not examine calibration, clinical safety, bias, or factual consistency—central concerns in clinical NLP. There is no statistical significance testing, uncertainty quantification, or error analysis by category/item difficulty. The modified Harness likelihood computation (full answer text) is not benchmark-standardized, yet its implications are not analyzed. Data contamination risks (e.g., overlap between pretraining and evaluation QA) are not assessed, and the practice of generating and verifying CoT with a strong model could introduce label/format leakage. The related work does not engage with evaluation methodologies that address these concerns.

460.human_review: It would be better to study the effect of different pretraining corpus (e.g. Pubmed, medical textbook) and compare their performance.
460.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Comparison: The comparative picture is incomplete. While some larger clinical baselines are reported, many comparisons are not apples-to-apples (parameter counts, training regimes, or prompting). The study does not include strong alternative adaptation baselines (e.g., LoRA/adapter tuning, other regularizers, or other prompting frameworks beyond MedPrompt variants), nor does it provide compute/efficiency-to-gain trade-off analyses—crucial given the heavy cost of 260B-token pretraining versus the relatively marginal gains on the larger Mixtral. Claims about outperforming prior models would be stronger with matched training budgets, significance tests, and ablations that isolate cost-effectiveness.

461.human_review: The dual-stage approach of KnowTuning—combining fine-grained knowledge augmentation with coarse-grained knowledge comparison—is novel and addresses a clear gap in the existing LLM fine-tuning practices.
461.llm_review: Methodology and novelty: The paper proposes a two-stage, knowledge-aware fine-tuning pipeline that is clearly distinct from prior work. The fine-grained stage identifies difficult atomic facts via perplexity and rewrites QA pairs to target those facts; the coarse-grained stage constructs preference pairs along completeness, factuality, and logicality using principled transformations (delete, revise, shuffle) and optimizes with DPO. This explicit, multi-aspect design goes beyond single-dimension approaches like FactTune and generic preference optimization (RLAIF), and the use of atomic knowledge units to structure both augmentation and preferences is a neat and novel unifying idea.

462.human_review: The paper thoroughly evaluates the effectiveness of KnowTuning across two datasets and compares its performance with baseline models, providing both automatic and human-based evaluations.
462.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result, Evaluation: The approach is applied to two distinct QA datasets (Dolly and MedQuAD) and two LLM scales (Llama2-7B/13B), demonstrating robustness across domains and model sizes. Results consistently favor KnowTuning over Base, SFT, RLAIF, and FactTune on GPT-4 judged completeness, factuality, and logicality; human pairwise evaluations also show significant wins over FactTune. The evaluation is comprehensive: automatic and human judgments, fact-level analysis (#Correct, #Incorrect, %Correct), and ablations isolating each component. Overall, the experimental design convincingly supports the claimed benefits of improved knowledge awareness.

463.human_review: KnowTuning demonstrates a tangible improvement in LLMs' ability to generate answers that are not only more factual but also complete and logically structured.
463.llm_review: Methodology and result: The ablation study is well-aligned with the method’s design, showing targeted degradations when removing fine-grained augmentation (-KA) or any of the coarse-grained comparison sets (-KCC, -KFC, -KLC), and a large drop when removing all (-KC). Fine-grained facts evaluation further substantiates the method’s effect, with higher %Correct and more correct facts than baselines, indicating the pipeline improves both the quantity and accuracy of factual content.

464.human_review: The method's reliance on filtering and rewriting QA pairs, along with constructing and training with comparison sets, may be very time-consuming and costly.
464.llm_review: Methodology: The supervision relies heavily on closed-source LLMs for extracting, rewriting, and revising atomic knowledge, which may inject annotation bias and style artifacts into both augmentation and comparisons. The use of model perplexity as a proxy for "difficult" facts may select rare phrasings rather than genuinely challenging knowledge, and there is limited analysis of this design choice or of sensitivity to the α, β hyperparameters. The logicality dimension is operationalized by shuffling facts, which captures ordering but not deeper discourse coherence or reasoning; similarly, delete/revise operations may produce overly trivial negatives. The DPO pairs always prefer a rephrased answer over disturbed variants, which could bias the model toward a particular style and incompletely reflect nuanced human preferences.

465.human_review: While the paper showcases improvements particularly in medical and generic QA tasks, it's less clear how this method performs across a broader range of knowledge-intensive tasks. A more comprehensive evaluation on knowledge-intensive tasks such as the KILT benchmark (https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.02252) is encouraged.
465.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, Evaluation: The empirical scope is limited to two datasets (with filtered categories), leaving out other knowledge-intensive domains (e.g., legal, scientific, long-form multi-hop) and settings such as retrieval-augmented baselines. Results rely strongly on LLM-as-judge (GPT-4) with limited reporting of absolute scores or inter-rater agreement; human evaluation compares only against FactTune rather than all baselines and lacks detailed protocol (sample sizes, annotator agreement). There is no robustness or OOD analysis, nor cost/efficiency reporting for the multi-stage pipeline. These choices limit claims about generalization and practical applicability across broader tasks and evaluation regimes.

466.human_review: S1. This work effectively combines multiple findings and presents a practical approach to reducing the high computational cost of text-centric visual models.
466.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clear, pragmatic pipeline for building efficient VLMs focused on text-rich images. The enhanced vision encoder is obtained via a targeted text-reading fine-tuning stage and then stabilized through uniform weight averaging (“model soup”) over 12 independently fine-tuned encoders, striking a balance between text-centric accuracy and general visual capability without increasing inference-time complexity. The token-efficiency choice of CLIP-Base with AnyRes keeps vision tokens capped while preserving high-resolution coverage, directly addressing inference bottlenecks.

467.human_review: S2. In particular, the method of training an image encoder with a small VLM to improve its performance for a specific task (OCR task) and averaging it with the original model would be beneficial to many readers in the community, as it has the potential to improve model performance while maintaining inference cost.
467.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The study conducts thorough, multi-scale ablations (1B–13B) isolating the contributions of the encoder variants (C1–C7) and the Read-and-Reason supervision (R1–R4), and reports latency/memory along with accuracy across diverse benchmarks. Results show consistent gains on text-centric tasks with markedly lower token counts (≈98–637 vs. up to 2880), and favorable latency/memory compared to LLaVA-NeXT under constrained token budgets. The evaluation uses standardized toolkits (e.g., VLMEvalKit) and includes sensitivity analyses (e.g., token-reduction in LLaVA-NeXT), supporting the core efficiency and effectiveness claims.

468.human_review: S3. The authors plan to publish models ranging from 160M to 13B parameters, which could be useful for a variety of applications.
468.llm_review: Methodology: The Read-and-Reason training strategy is a simple, well-motivated supervision design that first compels text transcription before downstream reasoning, improving learning signals for visually-situated NLU without incurring inference-time overhead. The broader training schedule—curriculum emphasizing text understanding, plus selective inclusion of diverse datasets (e.g., VisionFlan, RefCOCO, VG, CORD)—is coherent with the objective of maintaining generality while optimizing for document understanding. The intent to open-source models and data further strengthens methodological reproducibility.

469.human_review: W1. I am concerned about the lack of explanation about the small VLMs used when learning REncoder. There seems to be no mention of the small VLM used. It would also be better if conditions such as whether it is better to use the same series of LLMs as the subsequent LLMs or whether models of the best possible quality should be used are discussed.
469.llm_review: Methodology and Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: Some critical methodological choices are under-explained. The uniform model-soup averaging over 12 encoders lacks analysis on stability, variance, and why particular averaging ratios were chosen over alternatives (e.g., greedy/weighted soups). The AnyRes configuration and grid settings are not fully justified with respect to optimality across task types. Claims about reduced hallucinations and improved reasoning would benefit from a deeper, quantitative error analysis and statistical significance reporting. Finally, cross-model fairness (e.g., controlling total compute/token budgets and encoder capacity across baselines) could be articulated more rigorously.

470.human_review: W2. The largest improvement in Figure 1 is achieved by adding the open-source training dataset, but detailed discussion, such as data sampling strategy and the process that led to that recipe, is limited.
470.llm_review: Data/Task and Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation and Result: The new resources raise validity and generalization concerns. CORD-Instruct is small (≈680 samples) and synthetically generated with GPT-3.5, risking stylistic bias and unclear licensing/contamination; its impact on performance is not isolated. Parsing-Bench is tiny (≈30 images) and relies on LLM-as-a-judge, which is known to be variable and can misalign with human judgments; hence conclusions from these results are fragile. More seriously, several benchmarks used for evaluation (e.g., DocVQA, ChartQA) also appear in the training mixture; without explicit split hygiene and leakage audits, reported improvements may overestimate true generalization. OCR-augmented results conflate core model ability with external tool quality and latency, complicating interpretation of the gains.

471.human_review: The method section describes the proposed method and its components in detail. Especially, each component is explained thoroughly and supported by appropriate citations.
471.llm_review: Methodology and interpretation are clearly articulated: the paper defines "attributes" as interpretable compositional concepts and integrates them into prompt tuning via three coherent components—(a) an attribute extractor that predicts text-encoder embeddings of attributes, (b) instance-conditioned context tokens built with a cross-attention module, and (c) a regularization toward a pool of attribute-enriched textual templates. The narrative justifies each component’s role in aligning attribute-level inductive biases with class embeddings and provides intuitive interpretations (e.g., higher cosine similarity to "A photo of [a] [cls]") that connect the learned prompts to human-readable concepts.

472.human_review: Utilizing BLIP-2 model for attribute generation is an interesting idea. This external knowledge may offer information not easily captured with only a few-shot examples.
472.llm_review: Methodologically, the framework is well designed and modular: it learns attribute embeddings from image features using a lightweight MLP trained on BLIP-2–derived attribute labels; strengthens visual representations via deep visual prompting (learnable tokens injected into early transformer layers without updating backbone weights); generates instance-conditioned prompts with multi-head attention rather than simple additive conditioning; and uses a knowledge-guided regularizer based on diverse attribute-aware templates. The losses (classification, attribute prediction, and template regularization) are complementary and align with the stated goal of interpretability-aware tuning.

473.human_review: Both base-to-novel generalization and domain generalization experiments are conducted.
473.llm_review: The methodology translates into consistent empirical gains: across 10 datasets in a 16-shot base-to-novel setup, the proposed instance-conditioned, attribute-aware prompts achieve higher HM (80.75) than prior prompt-tuning methods (e.g., +1.27% over LFA). The domain generalization study from ImageNet to V2/Sketch/A/R shows the approach is competitive or best on average (60.71). Ablations substantiate design choices (deep visual prompting and attention-based conditioning outperform shallow or additive variants), and a negative control (swapping attributes) produces a large drop on ImageNet-1k (−11% HM), supporting the claim that learned attributes are functionally meaningful.

474.human_review: There is no need to limit the BLIP-2 model to generate in “one-word” because the answers from BLIP-2 will be encoded to a single embedding vector and used as a target for the Attribute Extractor. This raises the question about the necessity of ‘single-word prediction’ (which seems to be the key contribution).
474.llm_review: Contribution-wise, the novelty feels incremental: the method combines existing ideas—visual prompt tuning, instance conditioning akin to CoCoOp, and knowledge-guided regularization—augmented with pseudo-labeled attributes from a large VQA model. While the integration is thoughtful, the margin over strong baselines is modest on average (e.g., ~1–1.5% over recent SOTAs), and the interpretability claim is primarily supported by embedding similarity rather than human-centric or task-relevant interpretability evaluations.

475.human_review: The demonstration of cosine similarity (Figure 3) alone is not sufficient to show that the attribute extractor effectively extracts information predicted from BLIP-2. The performance of the ‘oracle’ setting, using BLIP-2 embeddings (i.e., the target of L_attr loss) instead of predicted ones, should be presented. Also, a direct comparison between estimated and BLIP-2 embeddings is necessary.
475.llm_review: Methodology, results, and comparisons raise questions: reliance on BLIP-2 for attribute supervision introduces dependency on a very large external model (with potential bias/noise), and the assumption that a single attribute embedding per image is sufficient is not scrutinized. Improvements, though consistent, are small on many datasets and lack statistical significance testing. Comparisons appear to omit some relevant prompt-generation or concept-based methods (e.g., CuPL, prompt ensembling, concept-bottleneck variants), and evaluations are limited to CLIP ViT-B/16, leaving scalability across backbones underexplored.

476.human_review: Based on the ablation results (Table 3), adding attribute information does not appear to be a critical factor for performance improvement. In other words, visual prompting, instance conditioning, and regularization contribute significantly more.
476.llm_review: Ablation/detail gaps limit insight into results: the paper does not isolate the contribution of each loss term (e.g., removing Lattr or Lreg), tune or analyze the impact of key hyperparameters (number/depth of visual prompts, number of synthetic templates N, loss weights), or report sensitivity to the number of shots beyond 4/16. There is no analysis of computational overhead/latency introduced by deep visual prompting and the attribute extractor, and no human study quantifying attribute correctness or consistency across datasets.

477.human_review: Novel approach using semantic representations to improve AVQA. It uses source-wise learnable tokens to extract semantic features from audio and visual inputs and employs a source-aware semantic representation block to align audio-visual features. In addition, it also applies multi-modal spatial and temporal attention to focus on relevant regions, with integrated features using a fusion network for final answer prediction.
477.llm_review: Methodology and novelty: The paper proposes Source-wise Learnable Tokens (SLT) that act as category-aware anchors for associating audio sources and visual objects, together with a Source-aware Semantic Representation (SaSR) block that performs cross-attention between tokens and modality-specific embeddings. The design is complemented by auxiliary losses (presence BCE, token regularization CE, and a match/mismatch loss) that explicitly encourage the tokens to encode source semantics. Coupled with multi-modal spatial and temporal attention, the architecture provides a coherent and novel pipeline for source-aware grounding and reasoning in AVQA.

478.human_review: Comprehensive experiments and comparisons with existing methods. It outperforms existing AVQA methods on the Music-AVQA dataset, especially for complex question types. It also achieves 89.9% accuracy on the AVQA-Yang dataset, surpassing previous methods. Ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed components.
478.llm_review: Data/Task, results, experiments, and comparison: The method is evaluated on two established AVQA benchmarks (MUSIC-AVQA and AVQA-Yang), covering both open-ended and multiple-choice settings. On MUSIC-AVQA, SaSR-Net achieves 74.21 average accuracy, outperforming strong audio-visual baselines (e.g., A VST, PSTP-Net, TJSTG) by ~0.7–3 points, and on AVQA-Yang it reaches 89.9 (+0.9 over the best baseline listed). Ablations isolate the contributions of SLT and SaSR (+3.9 combined) and of spatial/temporal attention (+2.18 combined), and qualitative visualizations of SA/TA help corroborate the claimed mechanisms. The comparisons span unimodal and multimodal baselines, indicating gains specifically in audio-visual reasoning.

479.human_review: Visualization of model attention helps interpret results.
479.llm_review: Methodology, results, explanation, and presentation: The paper articulates a clear end-to-end architecture with modular blocks (SLT, SaSR, SA, TA), provides equations for self- and cross-attention, and motivates each loss term by the role it plays in enforcing source-aware semantics. The pipeline from raw features to answer prediction is well structured, and the ablations plus attention visualizations aid interpretation of where improvements come from. This organization helps readers understand how semantic tokens enable better alignment and how spatial/temporal attention exploit those semantics for reasoning.

480.human_review: The authors focused on Source-wise Learnable Tokens to extract semantically compact features from videos and employ Source-aware Semantic Representation to align these with visual and audio features. Visualizing and comparing the features in latent space would be helpful to demonstrate SaSR-Net as a better representation method.
480.llm_review: Methodology, presentation, and comparison: Several notational and specification inconsistencies reduce clarity and raise correctness concerns. Examples include an unclear token count ("192" appears without justification), ambiguous or possibly incorrect loss equations (e.g., Lmatch appears to use the same variable for positive and negative terms), and imprecise preprocessing details (e.g., audio sampling rate reported as 16 Hz, conflicting segmenting/sampling descriptions). Some symbols (e.g., LN) are introduced but not used consistently. The paper also omits complexity/runtime analysis and does not compare against the most recent or stronger AVQA systems (e.g., MUSIC-AVQA v2 results or newer parameter-efficient AV-LLM style methods), limiting the methodological and comparative context.

481.human_review: From Table 1, SaSR-Net seems to perform poorly on single-modality questions. I would like to see further elaborations on potential reasons.
481.llm_review: Results: The reported improvements over strong baselines are modest on MUSIC-AVQA (often <1 point over the best prior) and only +0.9 on AVQA-Yang. In addition, there are arithmetic/typo issues and mismatches between some textual claims and table values, which make it difficult to fully trust the magnitude of gains. The paper does not provide statistical significance testing or confidence intervals, so it is unclear whether the reported differences are robust.

482.human_review: Computational costs should be discussed and compared for multi-modal experiments.
482.llm_review: Experiment and comparison: The experimental analysis lacks robustness and sensitivity studies (e.g., effect of the number of tokens C, auxiliary loss weights, or alternative backbones), and there is no evaluation under noise/occlusion or with unseen/long-tail source categories to validate the claimed source-awareness. Ablations toggle whole blocks but do not probe design choices within them (e.g., token supervision granularity, negative sampling strategy). The work mentions MUSIC-AVQA v2 in related work but does not evaluate on it, and broader comparisons to recent AVQA/AV reasoning methods are limited.

483.human_review: The paper introduces a unique approach to TKG reasoning by addressing the asynchronous evolution of events, which has not been adequately considered in previous works.
483.llm_review: Methodology and novelty: The paper introduces a target-entity-driven, natural division of history into explicit and implicit patches, which directly operationalizes asynchronous event evolution—an aspect largely overlooked in prior TKG reasoning. The dual-level aggregation (intra-patch relation-aware GNN plus inter-patch attention with positional encoding) is a coherent and novel architecture that both enriches local representations and adaptively weights distant history. This design enables long-range temporal modeling while remaining query-aware through patch selection tied to the target entity.

484.human_review: The proposed dual-level aggregation framework is well-designed and effectively captures both local and global temporal dependencies, improving the accuracy of entity representations.
484.llm_review: Methodology and results: The relation-aware GNN for intra-patch encoding and the inter-patch attention together yield strong, consistent gains across datasets. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on six benchmarks, with especially large average improvements on ICEWS datasets (e.g., roughly +11.7% MRR, +17.6% Hits@1 over the second best). Ablations carefully isolate each component (implicit patches, connected subgraphs, positional embeddings, inter-patch attention, relation-aware GNN), and the observed drops validate the methodological choices.

485.human_review: Extensive experiments on six datasets show that NEDA significantly outperforms existing methods, providing strong empirical evidence for its effectiveness.
485.llm_review: Methodology, data/task, and experiments: The study targets extrapolation entity prediction on widely used TKG benchmarks (ICEWS14/18/05-15, GDELT) and introduces two new ICEWS-based datasets (ICEWS22/23), evaluated under time-aware filtered metrics (MRR and Hits@k). Experiments are thorough: comprehensive baseline comparisons, ablations, sensitivity analyses (L and n), and limited-data tests that demonstrate robustness. These choices align the methodology with the task’s requirements (long life cycles and asynchronous evolution) and provide strong empirical coverage of design decisions.

486.human_review: The framework's complexity might lead to scalability issues when applied to very large TKGs. The paper could benefit from a discussion on the computational efficiency and possible optimizations.
486.llm_review: Methodology: The explicit/implicit patching is based solely on the presence of the target entity, which may overlook relevant context windows where the entity is absent but influenced by distant interactions not captured by the sampled neighbors. The inter-patch attention employs a learned global query vector rather than a relation- or query-conditioned query, potentially limiting relation-specific weighting of patches. Within-patch modeling assumes a dominant topic per patch, which may be restrictive when multiple concurrent topics are relevant to the query.

487.human_review: The proposed method is evaluated only on TKG reasoning tasks. It would be interesting to see its applicability and performance on related tasks, such as temporal link prediction or temporal knowledge graph completion.
487.llm_review: Methodology and evaluation: The evaluation focuses only on entity prediction under extrapolation, omitting relation prediction—even though many TKG works report both—so the generality of the approach remains partially untested. Comparisons on the two newly constructed ICEWS22/23 datasets rely on the authors’ preprocessing; while grid searches are mentioned, reproducibility and fairness would be stronger with full release and documented pipelines for all baselines. Additionally, there is no runtime or memory profiling to quantify the overhead of per-query patch construction and dual-level aggregation, making it hard to assess practical scalability.

488.human_review: The natural division strategy for patch selection is not deeply analyzed. Further discussion on its limitations and potential improvements could strengthen the paper.
488.llm_review: Definition/description/detail/discussion/explanation/interpretation, result, and analysis: Some technical details are underspecified or ambiguous, such as how implicit-patch neighbor sampling is operationalized when the target entity is absent, how connected subgraphs are formed in practice across time, and the precise mechanics of the temporal GNN in Eq. 2 (e.g., indexing and adjacency semantics). The paper defers the dual decoder to prior work with minimal explanation, and figure/text artifacts hinder readability in places. On the results side, while ablations quantify importance, the analysis is mostly high-level; there are no qualitative case studies, attention weight visualizations, or failure-mode diagnostics to interpret when and why specific patches or components drive gains (or fall short, e.g., on GDELT).

489.human_review: The proposed method effectively combines the content-based filtering capability of LLMs with collaborative filtering. It outperforms both LLM-based baselines and collaborative filtering baselines.
489.llm_review: The paper proposes a training-free progressive enhancement of prompting (PepRec) that composes personal preference summaries with iteratively aggregated preferences from sampled similar users within a cluster, approximating collaborative filtering inside an LLM pipeline. This methodological design yields strong quantitative gains over both deep learning recommenders and prompt-based baselines on two Amazon domains, as measured by AUC and Logloss, indicating that the combined content- and collaborative-filtering signals materially improve ranking quality.

490.human_review: The proposed method is tuning-free, which saves the expensive cost of fine-tuning LLMs.
490.llm_review: Methodologically, PepRec introduces a preference generator that extracts and refines both likes and dislikes from a user's recent interactions via structured prompts and a two-pass LLM summarization, then enhances this personal summary with bootstrapped batches of similar users identified via sentence-embedding–based K-Means clustering. A cosine-similarity-based convergence test regulates iteration, enabling a parameter-light, tuning-free procedure that operationalizes collaborative cues without finetuning the LLM.

491.human_review: The proposed method provides better explainability to the recommendation results.
491.llm_review: The method explicitly encodes interpretability by turning interaction histories into concise, human-readable likes/dislikes and progressively appending salient attributes drawn from similar users; this yields explanations that align with recommendation decisions (e.g., surfacing product features such as 'healing ointments' or 'refrigerator parts' as the prompt evolves). This explanatory mechanism is integrated into the core pipeline rather than added post hoc, and the paper illustrates how these interpretable summaries co-occur with improved predictive outcomes.

492.human_review: The authors conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the method and the necessity of each component.
492.llm_review: The paper complements the method with targeted experiments: an ablation cleanly isolates the contribution of (i) including dislikes, (ii) the preference generator, (iii) adding similar-user information, and (iv) iterative bootstrapping, showing monotonically improved AUC/Logloss as components are added. A hyperparameter study further probes cluster count and sampling sizes, suggesting the approach is reasonably robust to these choices.

493.human_review: PepRec requires a significant amount of LLM calls to predict a user's preference on one item. This is computationally inefficient and can incur a high latency. Although this is an inherent limitation of LLM-based recommendation and the authors also note this in the Limitations Section, the iterative prompt enhancement (each iteration requires two LLM calls) in PepRec makes it worse.
493.llm_review: The methodological stopping rule relies on cosine similarity between sentence-transformer embeddings of textual summaries, which is only a proxy for informational gain and may not correlate with recommendation utility; this could prematurely halt or over-extend bootstrapping. Moreover, the clustering pipeline averages textual encodings of user histories and then applies K-Means; such averaging can blur multi-faceted preferences, and the 'training-free' claim is somewhat overstated given the fitted clustering and dependence on a pretrained encoder.

494.human_review: PepRec can only capture users' recent preference given the context-length limitation of LLMs.
494.llm_review: The approach presumes access to both positive and negative feedback and uses an LLM to infer fine-grained attributes that may not exist in the structured data, risking hallucinated or spurious preference features without a verification mechanism. The methodology does not specify how negatives are constructed on implicit-feedback data or how to guard against LLM inconsistencies, and its dependence on a proprietary GPT-4 model complicates methodological reproducibility and may entangle external world knowledge with the evaluation task.

495.human_review: This paper is well-written and motivated, accompanied by many nicely drawn figures and tables illustrating the major information of the paper.
495.llm_review: Clear motivation: the paper targets two concrete gaps in multimodal math evaluation (diagnosing why models fail and where they fail across problem types). The rationale for open-ended format and for adding process evaluation is well articulated and justified. Validation is supported by a human baseline, discriminative performance across difficulty/grade/knowledge, and interpretable error taxonomies. Presentation is coherent, with an overview figure and well-structured narrative that connects design choices to the research questions.

496.human_review: Fully open-ended problem evaluation instead of other formats like multiple-choice, avoiding LMM to guess an answer, which has been a serious problem in other current evaluation benchmarks.
496.llm_review: Data/Task: a sizable benchmark (5,929 items) of open-ended, visual middle-school computation problems with multi-dimensional metadata (difficulty, grade, fine-grained knowledge taxonomy). Tasks are standardized to a uniform open-ended format with aligned step-by-step solutions. Evaluation: both outcome and process are systematically handled (answer boxing, numeric tolerances, SymPy simplification, interval normalization), plus manual spot-checking of the outcome pipeline. The process evaluation defines concrete error types and reports results across multiple dimensions, enabling fine-grained diagnosis.

497.human_review: Fine-grained meta-information annotation, including difficulty, grade level, and problem type. This information can help LMM developers better understand their model’s weaknesses.
497.llm_review: Methodology: introduces LMM-as-a-judge for process evaluation that aligns model solutions to ground-truth steps and identifies the first error, categorized into four interpretable types (diagram misinterpretation, reasoning, calculation, textual misunderstanding). The scoring rules for different answer forms (numbers, expressions, intervals) are specified and operationalized. Data/Task: careful conversion of source items (MathML to LaTeX, symbol normalization), translation to English with manual verification, and difficulty assignment based on student accuracy make the benchmark structured and analyzable.

498.human_review: Process evaluation with error identification helps people know better about model’s error categories, clearly shown in Figure 4.
498.llm_review: Presentation and Evaluation are tightly integrated: the evaluation protocol is explicit, with prompts, parsing rules, and comparison procedures described. Results are presented along difficulty, grade, and knowledge dimensions (e.g., Table 3), and error distributions are visualized (Figures 4–6), making weaknesses easy to interpret and compare. The text-only vs. multimodal setup is clearly explained and reported side-by-side.

499.human_review: Comprehensive experiments on the most powerful and popular LMMs demonstrate they need help with MM-Math.
499.llm_review: Experiment: broad and balanced evaluation across 10 models (open/closed) under both text-only and multimodal settings, including a human baseline. The findings are robust and insightful (e.g., minimal gains from images, large gap to human performance, sharp degradation on hard items), and include analyses per difficulty, grade, and knowledge types, as well as error breakdowns.

500.human_review: Great insights with detailed examples of LMMs’ errors on the MM-Math. Example figures are clearly drawn and give reader a better deeper view of model’s behavior on the benchmark
500.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Presentation: the end-to-end pipeline (collection, normalization to LaTeX, translation with manual checks, open-ended reformatting, standardized answer boxing) is thoughtfully designed and well-documented, facilitating reproducibility and consistent comparison across models. The fine-grained taxonomy and uniform problem format make the dataset practically useful for targeted analysis and future training.

501.human_review: The process evaluation still requires GPT4-o in the loop. Considering the size of the benchmark (5929), running GPT4-V on all the examples of the benchmark for process evaluation can be quite expensive.
501.llm_review: Data/Task: the scope is limited to middle-school computation problems from a single regional source and time window, which may constrain external validity and diversity. The conversion from multiple-choice/composite to open-ended could alter difficulty or reduce genuine visual dependence. Evaluation: process evaluation relies on GPT-4V as a judge and the "first-error" assumption; the reported misidentification rate (~9%) and lack of inter-annotator agreement or external auditing introduce uncertainty about the exact error-type proportions. Using a proprietary LMM as judge while also evaluating some of the same family of models raises potential bias concerns. The small text-only vs. multimodal gap could reflect insufficient visual necessity in some items or limitations in image parsing prompts/protocols.

502.human_review: The category of the problems in the MM-Math might be homogeneous, though Figure 2 clearly shows the detailed category. About 78% of the problems are shape-related (Properties of Shapes, Shape Transformation), thus making the tested ability in the benchmark easy to be optimize by incorporating more domain-related data.
502.llm_review: Data/Task: representativeness and balance are unclear—problems come from one platform (2021–2022) and exclude proof/drawing types, potentially narrowing the skill coverage. The knowledge taxonomy is expert-defined but lacks reported agreement measures. Difficulty is inferred from student scoring rates that may be platform-specific and noisy. Translation and rephrasing may introduce subtle shifts in semantics, and the degree of diagram fidelity, resolution standardization, and licensing/availability details are not fully specified.

503.human_review: The paper analyzes biases in sign language understanding models, covering various demographic and lexical features.
503.llm_review: Methodology and Analysis: The study designs a multi-level analysis that disentangles participant-level (age, gender), sign-level (ASL-Lex frequency, iconicity, phonological complexity, neighborhood density), and video-level (length, image quality via BRISQUE, pose distances to a seed signer, and a proxy for signing speed) factors. The use of per-sign normalization (standard deviations from the sign-level mean) to control for sign identity when assessing video length and speed is methodologically sound, and the combination of Spearman correlations, mutual information ranking, and bucketed analyses provides a coherent analytic framework. The inclusion of qualitative inspection to identify video artifacts (lighting, mouthing, repetition) complements the quantitative analysis.

504.human_review: It implements and evaluates multiple bias mitigation strategies, such as training on single-gender subsets, label shift approaches, and weighted resampling.
504.llm_review: Methodology and Evaluation: The paper evaluates two widely used baselines (I3D and ST-GCN) on the ASL Citizen dataset and reports Top-1/5/10 accuracy, along with a fairness-oriented gender parity metric (female/male accuracy). The evaluation employs sign-level bucketing by standardized video length and speed, computes Spearman correlations with p-values, and ranks feature importance by mutual information, offering triangulated evidence. The debiasing experiments are assessed with consistent metrics and controlled training (e.g., 25 epochs), allowing straightforward comparisons against the baselines.

505.human_review: The empirical evaluation utilizes established models (I3D and ST-GCN) and performs detailed statistical analyses to understand the impact of various features on model performance.
505.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation, and Analysis: The work compares several mitigation strategies (single-gender training, label-shift reduction to binary, and weighted resampling) and transparently reports both negative and positive outcomes. The weighted resampling based on standardized video length yields measurable gains (e.g., at least +2 percentage points in Top-k accuracy over ST-GCN) and improves gender parity (with the female-only resampling variant achieving the largest parity improvement), while the label-shift method is appropriately reported as not helping. The analysis coherently links these results to the finding that video-level factors dominate in mutual information, strengthening the methodological narrative that targeting video-level quality/length distributions can reduce disparities without sacrificing accuracy.

506.human_review: The analysis of how various features (demographic, lexical, video-level) impact model performance enhances the understanding of model interpretability.
506.llm_review: Methodology, Definitions/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Results, and Analysis: The paper clearly articulates research questions, defines all features (e.g., BRISQUE, seed-signer pose distance, Frecht-based speed), and leverages ASL-Lex attributes in a principled way. The discussion is careful about potential confounders (e.g., lighting affecting skin tone detection) and constraints arising from the small test cohort. Unexpected findings (e.g., negative correlation between sign frequency and accuracy) are acknowledged and interpreted cautiously. The inclusion of limitations and ethical reflections, along with releasing participant demographics, enhances interpretability, transparency, and future reproducibility.

507.human_review: The paper does not discuss the potential trade-offs between accuracy and fairness.
507.llm_review: Result: Several reported effects are small in magnitude (e.g., Spearman |rho| often below 0.06), raising questions about practical significance despite statistical significance. The mitigation outcomes are mixed: label-shift reduces gender parity relative to the baseline, single-gender training yields low absolute accuracy, and improvements from resampling, while positive, are modest and demonstrated primarily on ST-GCN. Some key results (e.g., debiasing impact on I3D) are not reported, and confidence intervals or variance across multiple runs are generally absent, limiting robustness claims.

508.human_review: Why is RQ1 (How is the ASL citizen data distributed demographically and linguistically) important? This essentially reflects the data characteristics collected by the Microsoft Research Team and may not be considered a strong contribution to the work. The analysis, however, is important, but I feel it should be in a ‘Data’ section and not individually represented as a research question that the authors investigate.
508.llm_review: Data/Task and Significance: The study focuses on a single dataset (ASL Citizen) and a single task setting (isolated sign recognition for dictionary retrieval), with only 11 test participants, which constrains generalizability. Critical demographic attributes like race/ethnicity are missing, leading to reliance on an external skin-tone classifier that is sensitive to grayscale/color settings and lighting, which reduces interpretability of those findings. The narrow task scope and dataset dependence limit broader impact; replication on other SLP datasets and tasks (e.g., continuous signing) is needed to strengthen significance for the wider *ACL community.

509.human_review: The findings related to participant-level differences are interesting; however, the work basically uses existing models and runs them to compare scores between ASL demographics (Similarly, existing bias mitigation strategies have been used and compared) if I frame it in a simplified view, and thus it is unclear to me from the current text how or why this is new or important.
509.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The analysis is largely correlational without multivariate controls, making it hard to disentangle confounds (e.g., video quality vs. signer demographics). The feature-importance assessment via mutual information is non-causal, and there is no regression-based or causal modeling to jointly account for factors. The resampling probability formula is under-specified/ambiguous in the text, and there is no sensitivity analysis (e.g., different sampling schedules) or robustness across seeds. The "speed" metric relies on pose extraction that may introduce noise, and mitigation results are not evaluated across diverse architectures or accompanied by uncertainty estimates, tempering confidence in the reported gains.

510.human_review: A novel method named TWIST is proposed to achieve robust and scalable text style transfer in low-resource scenario.
510.llm_review: Methodology: TWIST presents a clear, model-agnostic two-stage framework that reuses LoRA-based weight increments from source styles via a structured weight pool and an adaptive retrieval mechanism. The multi-key memory (cluster-level and instance-level keys) plus SVD-based merging to select top-q singular vectors is a principled way to reduce parameter interference while providing strong initialization for low-resource targets. Ablations (w/o adaptive retrieval, w/o multi-key, w/o SVD, w/o LoRA-init) substantiate that each component contributes meaningfully to the overall gains.

511.human_review: A multi-key memory network and an adaptive retrieval mechanism are designed to capture task- and instance-level information in weight increments.
511.llm_review: Data/Task: The paper evaluates on four datasets spanning nine styles, including sentiment, formality, a writing style (Shakespeare), and multiple role-specific dialogue styles (Genshin). It tests both encoder-decoder (T5-Large) and decoder-only (LLaMA2-7B) backbones, and systematically explores low-resource regimes (1%, 2%, 5%, 10%). The rotation protocol to keep each target unseen from the pool mitigates leakage, and a small-scale human evaluation complements automatic metrics.

512.human_review: A clustering-based weight pool is constructed to identify similarities between source tasks for more effective style knowledge transfer.
512.llm_review: Methodology: The use of spectral clustering to organize source increments, a KNN-driven key update for instance alignment, and a convex combination of task- and instance-level queries for retrieval is a coherent design. The SVD-based interpolation offers a tunable sparsity control (via q) that is analyzed both in isolation and within the interpolation module, with empirical guidance on how q trades off information retention and interference.

513.human_review: There are some unclear and imprecise parts in the Method section. (1) How should we understand the similarity and its calculation in the Multi-Keys Optimization section? q is a semantic feature, while k is a weight. Why can cosine similarity be used to measure the similarity between them? (2) How is q^{task} obtained? Why is its dimensionality c? (3)  The calculations in equation 5 are imprecise or wrong.
513.llm_review: Methodology: The learning and optimization of keys are under-specified and appear weakly supervised (cosine-alignment updates without a clear end-to-end objective or stability analysis). It is unclear how gradients propagate to keys through downstream losses, how lambda, W, and q are selected, and how robust the retrieval is to the frozen BERT encoder mismatch with the generative backbones. The computational overhead of the retrieval/memory components is only qualitatively discussed.

514.human_review: The related work is not comprehensive. More PEFT algorithms should be discussed because the core of this paper is reusing weight increments.
514.llm_review: Methodology, Related Work: The positioning relative to closely related parameter-merging and reuse methods (e.g., model soups/LoRA-soups, AdapterFusion/AdapterHub, HyperFormer/Task Arithmetic, prompt ensembling) is limited, and there are no direct comparisons to these families. The claim that SVD reduces interference would benefit from deeper theoretical or empirical connections to prior work on interpolation and sparsification beyond brief citations.

515.human_review: The comparison algorithms are insufficient and outdated (considering T5-Large as the backbone network).
515.llm_review: Methodology, Comparison: Baseline coverage is dated on the T5 side (e.g., CrossAligned, Delete&Retrieve, B-GST) and lacks strong modern PEFT and weight-merging baselines (Prefix/Prompt tuning, P-Tuning v2, Adapters/AdapterFusion, LoRA soups, task arithmetic with attention). On LLaMA2, comparisons to stronger supervised/PEFT variants are missing, and the few-shot ChatGPT baseline is not strictly comparable to supervised training. There are no significance tests, and classifier-based ACC fairness and calibration are not thoroughly examined.

516.human_review: The hyperparameter settings are not described. Moreover, what is the impact of the parameter r in the LoRA model? And what is the impact of different combinations of r and q?
516.llm_review: Methodology: The evaluation protocol relies heavily on Self-BLEU for content preservation, which is known to penalize legitimate paraphrases; more semantically grounded metrics (e.g., BERTScore/BLEURT) are absent. The style ACC uses in-domain classifiers trained on the same datasets, raising concerns about domain overfitting. Human evaluation is small-scale and ranking-based, with limited error analysis and no inter-annotator agreement reporting or per-style qualitative breakdown.

517.human_review: The presentation needs further improvement. There are many very long sentences that affect readability. What is the 'source key'?
517.llm_review: Presentation: Important hyperparameters and design choices (e.g., lambda, number of clusters, key dimensionality, K in KNN, retrieval window W, q selection procedure) are scattered or not specified in the main text, making replication difficult. Some notation is dense (mixing task-, instance-, and cluster-level keys) and figures/tables are referenced without sufficient in-text explanation, which hampers readability.

518.human_review: The proposal of Incompleteness to KGQA is novel, well motivated and seems very reasonable in real-world tasks. Previous methods thoroughly tested in incompleteness setting, great ablation is performed with varying the degree of incompleteness.
518.llm_review: Novelty and Ablation: The paper introduces an IKGQA benchmark that more realistically stresses the integration of internal LLM knowledge with external KGs by deliberately removing crucial triples. The design leads to meaningful stress-tests that conventional KGQA does not provide. The ablation suite is thoughtful: performance is reported across multiple incompleteness levels, with and without the Generate action, and with varying numbers of related triples used in generation. These ablations concretely validate the claimed benefits of integrating generated triples and show how subgraph context size affects accuracy.

519.human_review: Despite proposed method being constructed from previously used Ideas, it is indeed novel and effective. The use of Think-Search-Generate, akin to ReACT is a powerful technique to elicit reasoning abilities of LLM, resulting in best performance across multiple settings and datasets.
519.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty, and Result: The proposed Generate-on-Graph (GoG) framework is a training-free, dual-role approach that treats the LLM both as an agent (for targeted KG exploration) and as a KG (for generating missing triples), operationalized via a clear Thinking–Searching–Generating loop with verification and entity linking. This design distinguishes GoG from prior agent-only methods. Empirically, GoG consistently improves Hits@1 over strong prompt-based baselines under both complete and incomplete KGs, and scales well across multiple LLM backbones (notably strong gains with GPT-4), supporting both methodological novelty and practical effectiveness.

520.human_review: The method and motivation of paper is well described, figures help understand the paper and code is open sourced. The method is also well ablated
520.llm_review: Methodology, Motivation/Validation, and Presentation: The motivation—to evaluate and enable genuine internal–external knowledge integration when KGs are incomplete—is clear and well-justified. The method is intuitively grounded in decompositional reasoning (Thinking), targeted KG interaction (Searching), and knowledge supplementation (Generating), with an LLM-based verification step to mitigate hallucinations. The presentation is accessible: figures illustrate the agent loop and contrast with semantic parsing and path retrieval paradigms; prompts, tool use, and entity linking are described sufficiently to follow the pipeline; and validation across datasets and model backbones substantiates the design choices.

521.human_review: IKGQA is presented as a novel task with no "datasets readily available". However, there  exist multiple papers solving the IKGQA task (without LLMs), however, they do not formulate the task "officially". Moreover, they also generate datasets based on WebQSP, however, I do not find the citations and comparison of the datasets or dataset creation process
521.llm_review: Novelty and Data/Task: The IKGQA datasets are constructed by randomly dropping "crucial" triples (and all relations between the affected entities), which may not faithfully reflect the structure and noise patterns of real-world incompleteness. This synthetic deletion scheme risks biasing the task toward methods that can generate single missing links from local context and may not capture systematic gaps (e.g., type-specific sparsity, long-range missing edges, or relational skew). As a result, external validity to naturally incomplete KGs remains uncertain.

522.llm_review: Related Work: The discussion of prior art underplays recent lines on LLM-assisted KG completion and triple verification, retrieval-augmented knowledge refinement, and LLM-as-knowledge-base paradigms that also attempt to generate and validate missing facts. Positioning GoG more explicitly against these LLM-driven completion and verification approaches—both conceptually and empirically—would clarify the incremental contribution.

523.llm_review: Related Work: Beyond citing a few earlier KGE-based approaches for incomplete KG QA, the paper does not sufficiently engage with modern link-prediction and rule-based completion methods that could serve as strong, complementary baselines when triples are missing. A deeper comparison to contemporary KGE/link-prediction models or neurosymbolic completion in a QA pipeline would strengthen the case that generating triples via an LLM is preferable in IKG settings.

524.human_review: According to ablation method heavily depends on the LLM.
524.llm_review: Methodology and Ablation: The Generate action relies on the same LLM for both proposing and verifying triples, which risks confirmation bias; there is limited analysis of factual precision/recall of generated triples or hallucination rates. Additional ablations are needed: sensitivity to the number of generation samples n, search depth and top-N relation filtering, the choice of retriever (BM25 vs. dense retrieval), and the impact and accuracy of the entity linking module. A detailed failure analysis and cost/latency breakdown would also improve methodological rigor.

525.human_review: Is it not clear whether the fine-tuned approaches for comparison were run by the authors themselves or the numbers were taken from previous papers (for CKG)
525.llm_review: Methodology and Comparison: While results are strong, baseline parity and coverage could be improved. Some baselines are re-run with different evaluation protocols, and it remains unclear whether all methods use identical backbones, prompt budgets, and step limits. Comparisons to agent variants augmented with generation, to SP systems with fallback strategies, and to QA pipelines that incorporate link prediction would provide a fairer test. Reporting inference cost and step counts per question would contextualize GoG’s practicality relative to alternatives.

526.human_review: The paper is well written and clearly explains the methodology used with comparisons to popular baselines such as DPO. It effectively addresses the shortcomings of earlier methods and builds on existing literature to mitigate them.
526.llm_review: Methodology/Related Work/Comparison: The core idea—redefining the trust region in online DAP to be centered on the behavior policy πβ that generated the data—is well-motivated by RL literature on behavior regularization and trust-region methods. The paper situates BPO clearly relative to offline DAP (DPO/IPO/SLiC) and online DAP, and contrasts it with TR-DPO, articulating why setting πref = πβ is more principled in online preference collection. Comparisons are broad across three prominent DAP losses (DPO, IPO, SLiC), and the study fairly controls the total annotation budget when comparing offline/online/on-policy regimes, making the empirical comparisons credible.

527.human_review: The dynamic adjustment of the trust region during training is a significant contribution.
527.llm_review: Methodology/Contribution: BPO is an algorithmic wrapper that can be plugged into multiple DAP losses by simply swapping the static reference with the behavior model, providing a practical and general recipe for online preference learning. The paper further contributes a stabilization mechanism via LoRA ensembling and a data-collection-frequency study (F) that demonstrates strong performance even with low annotation frequency, which is valuable for realistic human-in-the-loop deployments.

528.human_review: The authors conduct a thorough ablation of their proposed method. The analysis with variable time step intervals and comparison with a gold model provide very interesting insights. The use of ensemble LoRA to stabilise training was particularly noteworthy.
528.llm_review: Methodology/Comparison/Ablation/Analysis: The ablations are thorough: (i) varying collection frequency F under a fixed budget demonstrates robustness to sparse annotation; (ii) a strong reference baseline (πref = πgold) shows that dynamic proximity to πβ matters beyond reference quality; (iii) stability analyses (single vs. ensemble LoRA, EMA reference) reveal why the proposed ensembling is needed; and (iv) head-to-head win rates and aggregate metrics (median/IQM/mean with bootstrap CIs) strengthen claims of consistent gains across tasks and seeds.

529.key_points: Weakness: Methodology, Novelty, Related Work, Comparison
529.human_review: Although the paper claims this to be a novel methodology using a dynamic reference policy, there has been some related work [1] that uses DPO iteratively. It would be beneficial to compare their methodology and include a citation for this work.
529.llm_review: Methodology/Novelty/Related Work/Comparison: While centering the trust region on the behavior policy is sensible and supported by RL precedents (e.g., behavior-regularized methods), the novelty over recent dynamic-reference or trust-region variants (e.g., TR-DPO and other online DAP formulations) is somewhat incremental and lacks a stronger theoretical justification (e.g., convergence guarantees or bounds under preference noise). Comparisons omit several strong baselines, such as PPO-based RLHF under the same budget, other recent DAP variants (e.g., ORPO, NCA/DPO variants), or behavior-regularized RL surrogates adapted to preferences, which would better position BPO’s relative merit.

530.human_review: There is a missing citation for the use of LoRA ensembling. Additionally, it would be helpful to have a discussion on why the authors chose to use 5 LoRA weights.
530.llm_review: Definition/Description/Explanation/Interpretation + Related Work: Important design details are under-specified. The behavior policy πβ update rule and exact timing (K vs. F) are only briefly sketched, with limited discussion of how sampling temperature, decoding strategy, and pair sampling (y1, y2) affect the effective trust region. The LoRA ensembling mechanism lacks specifics (e.g., when weights are added/merged, diversity promotion, and its interaction with optimizer dynamics). The related-work discussion could better connect to behavior-regularized off-policy RL (e.g., BRAC/IQL-style constraints) and recent online preference optimization frameworks to clarify conceptual overlap and distinctions.

531.human_review: The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion on the computational cost of the proposed BPO method in comparison to existing techniques. This would provide a clearer understanding of its practical applicability.
531.llm_review: Methodology + Definition/Description/Explanation/Interpretation: The evaluation exclusively uses a single open-source reward model (RM-deberta) both as annotator and as evaluator, which risks reward overfitting and circularity. There is no assessment of robustness to rater choice, reward hacking, or evaluator bias. The claim of equal annotation budget is good, but the paper does not formalize how overlap, replay, and depletion of D are handled over time, nor how sample reuse impacts effective on/off-policy ratios. Additionally, the fixed β across settings may conflate trust-region effects with optimization sensitivity, and no sensitivity analysis is provided.

532.human_review:
Since this strategy uses on-policy learning, it would be very difficult to incorporate humans in the loop for preference annotation. This could limit the applicability of the method in scenarios where human feedback is essential.

References
[1] Self-Rewarding Language Models. Yuan et al.
532.llm_review: Data/Task: The study covers three tasks (TL;DR, Anthropic Helpfulness/Harmlessness) and a relatively small base model (Gemma-2B), all evaluated with the same reward model trained on overlapping domains, limiting generalizability. There is no human evaluation, no out-of-domain tests, and no larger-model validation. The setup does not probe safety/harmlessness beyond the proxy reward or test failure modes when the preference simulator disagrees with humans, which weakens claims of broad applicability.

533.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
533.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: The paper introduces a clean, plug-and-play design that trains lightweight binary classifiers (value heads) on frozen LLM hidden states to judge four orthogonal criteria (intent-, knowledge-, time-, and self-awareness). This avoids full model fine-tuning, shares the same input encoding as generation, and is easy to integrate into existing RAG pipelines. On the data side, the authors curate AR-Bench with controlled, criterion-specific binary subtasks and also evaluate on six diverse downstream datasets spanning knowledge-, time-, and self-aware scenarios, with some OOD coverage. The unified design plus targeted datasets make the study comprehensive and practically relevant.

534.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
534.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Result: The motivation for multi-criteria active retrieval is well-argued, with clear examples of where single-criterion methods fail (e.g., time-sensitive or intent-driven queries). The UAR-Criteria decision procedure operationalizes this intuition in a simple priority pipeline. The paper validates design choices via ablations (single-classifier vs unified pipeline; value head vs whole-LLM classifier) and shows that the proposed unification yields strong end-to-end results while keeping inference overhead minimal. Empirically, UAR consistently outperforms baselines on AR-Bench and delivers the best overall downstream performance across varied tasks, which substantiates the central claim.

535.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
535.llm_review: Result: UAR achieves large gains in active retrieval accuracy on AR-Bench (overall accuracy around mid-80s vs mid-50s to low-60s for baselines on both 7B and 13B settings). On downstream tasks, it obtains the best overall scores and strong per-dataset outcomes: near-perfect retrieval triggering on time-sensitive datasets (e.g., TAQA) and competitive or superior accuracy on static QA (TriviaQA, WQ) while reducing unnecessary retrieval calls. Additional analyses (impact of document number; comparison to single-criterion heads and whole-LLM classifiers) provide further empirical support.

536.human_review: Limited exploration in the dimensions: the authors did not explore or discuss the completeness of the four criteria of retrieval, i.e. is there any possibility of existence of a new criterion, or these four criteria is complete? Further, the authors chose benchmarks specialised for these criteria, which may lead to selection bias for testing.  The authors can possibily argue by experimenting their method on a general dataset and analysize the failure cases.
536.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: Several data and evaluation choices may limit generality and fairness. AR-Bench is author-constructed with balanced classes and synthetic components (e.g., intent-aware data derived from ten seed intents via Self-Instruct), which may not reflect real-world distributions or linguistic variability. The grading of TAQA and FreshQA relies on ChatGPT, introducing potential bias and reproducibility concerns. Baseline comparability is imperfect (e.g., Self-RAG fine-tuned on base models vs chat models here; SKR uses a BERT classifier vs UAR’s Llama-based value head), and the study is limited to Llama2-7B/13B. There is no end-to-end latency/throughput evaluation, and the framework is only tested with single-shot retrieval, constraining conclusions about efficiency and scalability.

537.human_review: Classfier training: Training classifiers rather than training LoRA modules or few-shot prompting needs justification. LoRA or fewshot prompting requires little computation but may achieve comparable or better performance.
537.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Result: The claim that the four criteria are orthogonal and the specific priority order in the decision tree are not thoroughly justified or stress-tested. The pipeline invites cascading errors, yet the paper does not quantify how misclassifications at earlier stages affect overall retrieval decisions or task performance, nor does it explore alternative orders or joint/multilabel formulations. The assertion of negligible extra cost is plausible but unsubstantiated by wall-clock or token-level latency measurements. Empirically, the unified pipeline underperforms the corresponding single classifiers on AR-Bench per-criterion accuracy, and on DROP with 7B the method triggers retrieval incorrectly at a high rate, suggesting fragility in harder regimes.

538.human_review: Failure cases unaddressed in TAQA and FreshQA. Performance of UAR on TAQA and FreshQA is worse than that of Always-Ret. For these tasks, does it mean we can simply set to always retrieval and omit the classification? Especially when the retrieval rate if TAQA if UAR is near 100%.
538.llm_review: Result: The improvements are not universal across tasks. Always-retrieve remains stronger on some time-sensitive benchmarks (e.g., FreshQA), and on non-knowledge tasks UAR can underperform never-retrieve (e.g., DROP with 7B). On several datasets, gains over strong baselines are modest, and reliance on LLM-based judging for some tasks complicates interpretation of absolute scores. These patterns indicate that UAR’s practical advantage may be scenario-dependent and sensitive to classifier accuracy and retrieval quality.

539.human_review: The experiments are well-organized and reasonably comprehensive, effectively supporting the insights and conclusions drawn in the paper. It is particularly intriguing for this reviewer to observe the efficacy of granularity expansion in achieving these positive results.
539.llm_review: The experimental evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough. The paper reports results on the AGGREFACT benchmark across its standard splits, uses balanced accuracy with validation-set thresholding as in prior work, and includes ablations for key components (without granularity expansion, without atomic facts). The single-threshold setting with 95% confidence intervals adds robustness, and the analysis systematically probes design choices: different LLMs for atomic fact generation, varying document granularity sizes, and the impact of coreference resolution. The baselines are diverse (NLI-based, QA-based, and LLM-based), and FIZZ achieves the top average performance, with improvements that are corroborated by multiple analyses.

540.human_review: Although the task performance results would depend on the quality of the generated atomic facts, its impact on the task performance is not discussed.
540.llm_review: Data/Task and Result: The evaluation is restricted to English news-style summarization via AGGREFACT, leaving out other domains (dialogue, biomedical, long-form, multi-document) and languages; this limits claims about generality. While the method attains the best average, it is not consistently strongest on all splits or datasets, and gains over strong NLI baselines are modest in some cells. Some baselines are adapted (e.g., FACTSCORE/FACTOOL treating Wikipedia as the source) in ways that may not be strictly comparable to document-grounded summarization, potentially confounding the relative improvements. The paper asserts interpretability benefits but does not quantify them (e.g., by human studies or user-centric metrics), so the claimed practical impact on error analysis remains unverified.

541.human_review: Similarly, the performance outcomes could also vary with an NLI model utilized. Nevertheless, almost no discussions are presented that makes comparisons with models other than SUMMAC and/or substantiate the adoption of SUMMAC.
541.llm_review: Methodology, Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Result, and Comparison: Several design choices lack precise specification or justification. The definition of an "atomic fact" is informal and tailored to NLI without clear operational criteria or annotation guidelines; no human validation of atomic fact quality is provided. The filtering uses the same NLI model as the final scorer, which risks circularity and bias, and the thresholding rule for "exceptionally low entailment" is underspecified. The final score is the minimum across atomic facts, a brittle choice that can over-penalize summaries due to a single noisy fact (as the paper’s own failure case shows); alternative aggregations (e.g., top-k, soft-min, or calibrated combinations) are not explored. Details on the coreference pipeline (mT5 model variant, domain fit, and error rates) and its error propagation are limited, despite it being a critical step that can alter entity mentions. Comparisons could be strengthened with statistical significance testing across splits, stronger recent NLI systems, and more discussion on the fairness of comparing to ChatGPT-style baselines that lack tunable thresholds.

542.human_review: The criterion for expanding the context, namely that max(e_k, c_k, n_k) ≠ e_k, may seem intuitive, but it might be overly simplistic. This hypothesis should be experimentally validated.
542.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, and Experiment: The intuition for key components needs deeper validation. Using the minimum atomic-fact score as the summary score is motivated by worst-case detection, but the paper does not test whether this aligns with human judgments of summary-level factuality or show that alternative aggregations hurt performance or interpretability. The adaptive granularity expansion is plausible for multi-sentence reasoning, yet evidence is limited to aggregate gains; a targeted analysis (e.g., on multi-sentence entailment cases) would better support the claim. The NLI-based filtering of LLM-generated atomic facts is sensible, but the paper does not show how often incorrect facts survive filtering or how sensitive results are to the filtering threshold. There is no human evaluation of atomic-fact correctness or interpretability, and no robustness tests under noisy coreference or adversarial atomic fact generation. Finally, the method’s computational cost is acknowledged as high, but end-to-end runtime and scalability analyses are not quantified against baselines.

543.human_review: While query expansion and entity retrieval are standard techniques to enhance RAG system ability, combining these is non-trivial. MiRAG uses the K*M combinations of retrieved passages to jointly train the answer generator, passage retrieval and entity retriever.
543.llm_review: Methodology: The paper introduces a clean, principled multi-level RAG pipeline that first retrieves entities (via cross-modal CLIP) and then performs query expansion before DPR-style passage retrieval, with a joint end-to-end objective that conditions generation on both entity and passage selection. The design avoids ad-hoc score fusion by training the retrievers and generator together, with gradients flowing into the entity and passage query encoders, and freezes only the entity text encoder to keep indexing tractable. This formulation directly targets the KB-VQA setting where entity disambiguation is pivotal, and is a methodologically coherent extension of RAG to multi-granularity retrieval.

544.human_review: Comparisons w/ existing VQA RAG baselines are fair and complete, and MiRAG achieves consistent and obvious performance improvements on ViQuAE KVQAE benchmarks. Qualitative examples in the appendix show that MiRAG is able to refer to relevant entities and generate correct answers conditioned on the augmented passage.
544.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, Comparison: On the ViQuAE KB-VQA benchmark, the approach delivers new state-of-the-art results, outperforming strong literature baselines (e.g., DPR v+t, ECA/ILF) and even PaLM (540B) in EM/F1 while using a much smaller generator. The comparisons are careful: the authors control for total retrieved contexts (K_train × M_train) to ensure fairness and evaluate with standard EM/F1, plus retrieval metrics. MiRAG achieves 36.6 EM / 41.2 F1 with BLIP-2 and 29.8 / 34.1 with T5-large, consistently beating RAG and multimodal score-fusion (SBF+RAG) baselines, demonstrating clear gains on the target task.

545.human_review: Ablation studies in Tables 1, 4, and Section 5.5 validate the effectiveness of enabling gradient flow (a.k.a end-to-end training) in RAG joint training, bringing significant performance gain. Multi-modal retrieval proves to be better than using the uni-modal retrieval method.
545.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Ablation, Result: The core intuition—entity-level retrieval improves disambiguation and guides finer-grained passage retrieval—is well validated. Ablations show that (i) backpropagating through the entity encoder improves EM/F1 versus freezing it, (ii) modest K_train (e.g., 3) is sufficient and K×M has diminishing returns, and (iii) although entity expansion boosts pseudo-relevance retrieval (EExp-DPR), MiRAG’s joint objective prioritizes answer quality even when pseudo-relevance metrics do not rise further.
