Together, these analyses justify the multi-level design and the joint training loss, and explain why answer accuracy improves beyond what pseudo-relevance retrieval alone would predict.

546.human_review: Training Efficiency: in Section 3.5, the authors mentioned that answer generation loss has to be backward for all K$\times$M combinations, leading to the concern of training efficacy. In Appendix A, the authors do not report training GPU hours.
546.llm_review: Methodology: The joint probability factorization in Eq. (6) appears to treat passage retrieval as p_Theta(z|q) rather than explicitly conditioning on the selected entity (despite using entity-expanded queries operationally), which creates a potential mismatch between the probabilistic formulation and the implemented pipeline. The approach relies heavily on pseudo-relevance supervision for passage retrieval, which may bias training and evaluation of the retriever; stronger negative sampling or human relevance labels would better ground the signal. Entity retrieval uses only the image, ignoring the question text that could reduce ambiguity, and passage retrieval remains text-only (DPR), leaving performance on multimodal passage retrieval underexplored. The pipeline may also be vulnerable to error propagation from entity retrieval (K_test=1 at inference), and the paper provides limited methodological analysis of this failure mode or of trade-offs between selecting multiple entities at test time and input-length constraints.

547.human_review: Focuses on highly understudied topic in RAG research i.e. the importance how information is structured is also critical
547.llm_review: Significance: The paper targets a salient failure mode of RAG systems—lost-in-the-middle—by explicitly restructuring retrieved content into semantically coherent sections. This directly improves multi-hop reasoning and reduces hallucination risk, yielding practically meaningful gains (up to 6–7% accuracy on HotpotQA and 2Wiki) while also cutting context length dramatically, which is valuable for both research and deployed systems.

548.human_review: Introduces a training dataset which will be released for future research to enhance RAG models
548.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: The proposed extract-and-restructure pipeline couples verbatim, context-complete extraction with explicit sectioning by information relatedness, training a single decoder-only model via multi-teacher knowledge distillation. The design is well-motivated for post-retrieval QA, and the training procedure (teacher voting, verbatim checks, section restoration) is tailored to the evaluated QA tasks (single- and multi-hop), aligning the method with the data characteristics.

549.human_review: Token reduction / compression rates of Refiner upto 89% which is beneficial for reducing real-world costs
549.llm_review: The approach is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, integrating cleanly into existing RAG stacks without requiring parameter access to downstream LMs. It shows robustness to noisy and long contexts and to different retrieval depths, and it reduces tokens substantially (around 89% on average), making it attractive for real-world use where cost and latency matter.

550.human_review: The reduction and refinement into structured content also adds a notion of explainability
550.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: The paper clearly formulates the output principles (concise, sectioned, succinct) and details the pipeline: prompts, teacher ensemble, filtering/voting, and SFT on Llama2-7B-Chat. It provides extensive implementation detail (hyperparameters, templates), clarifies evaluation setup, and discusses nuances such as the verbatimness ratio and typical failure modes (answering temptation, extracting from query).

551.human_review: Ablation showing resilience to adding extra content, where Refiner is still able to maintain performance partly mitigating "lost-in-the-middle" problem
551.llm_review: Ablation and Result: The ablation removing structural sections shows consistent accuracy drops across most tasks and settings, supporting the claim that explicit structure helps downstream models disambiguate related yet distinct facts. Additional analyses (compression rates, effect of added irrelevant chunks, sensitivity to top-k) triangulate the empirical gains and suggest improved utilization of the compressed, structured content.

552.human_review: New STOA results for multi-hop QA datasets including: HotpotQA and 2Wiki with comparable results on single-hop datasets; its worth highlighting that the gains are significantly pronounced when compared to baseline ChatGPT-3.5-Turbo for multi-hop datasets
552.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, Comparison: The evaluation spans five QA benchmarks (PopQA, TriviaQA, ARC-C, HotpotQA, 2Wiki), compares against advanced RAG (Self-RAG, RQ-RAG) and strong compressors (RECOMP, LongLLMLingua), and tests multiple downstream LMs (Llama2 7B/13B/70B; Llama3 8B/70B). Refiner consistently wins on multi-hop, remains competitive on single-hop, often with far fewer tokens, and even surpasses GPT-3.5-Turbo on several tasks, indicating solid comparative performance.

553.human_review: The organization of paper is such that it becomes difficult to understand the methodology that is introduced by the work, e.g. sections 4.1 and 4.2 in less than a page mentions the main contribution of the paper i.e. multiple teacher KD-based dataset curations
553.llm_review: Methodology, Contribution, Data/Task: While useful, the core idea—extract then reorganize retrieved text—is conceptually close to prior compression/summarization and document reordering methods; the novelty primarily lies in enforcing explicit section structure with verbatim, context-complete spans. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning and stronger baselines that approximate structured grouping (e.g., retrieval-cluster-summarize, cluster-based chunking, or reordering-plus-extractive baselines) to isolate the unique methodological contribution across the evaluated tasks.

554.human_review: Pertaining to above, plenty of effort went into analysis where Table 3 and 4 are too redundant in terms of reporting all numbers for +5 and +10 documents across all datasets to derive a conclusion for a given ablation study
554.llm_review: Data/Task, Ablation, Analysis: Ablations focus mainly on removing sections; other key factors (e.g., varying context radius around extracted spans, impact of teacher count/voting thresholds, different retrieval recall regimes beyond top-5/10, or robustness to adversarially misleading chunks) are not deeply explored. A breakdown by question type/hops and more fine-grained error analysis would clarify where structure helps most. End-to-end cost/latency vs. baselines (including the overhead of running Refiner) is also missing, which is important given the efficiency claims.

555.human_review: Figure 4 in appendix gives detail about the training dataset construction and even it lacks several details like what is "ParseGeneratedContent" and what is "V"? similary there is a "Counter" and an "assignSection" not very clear
555.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Presentation: The custom ARC-C evaluation metric improves precision but complicates comparison to prior work; a side-by-side report of both metrics would improve interpretability. For multi-hop datasets, using provided relevant content (instead of full retrieval) may inflate absolute performance and should be discussed. Some data construction details (e.g., final distilled dataset sizes, imbalance) are hard to parse, and the presentation has occasional typos and formatting issues. Clearer reporting and a reproducibility checklist (including released code/prompts and exact evaluation scripts) would strengthen the paper.

556.human_review: Based on these, it is difficult to assess the contribution of this work as the core contribution seems to be introducing this additional training data which is thin for a full paper
556.llm_review: Methodology, Contribution, Data/Task: The approach relies on multi-teacher LLM distillation and assumes availability of high-quality teacher outputs; potential contamination and bias are not analyzed. Verbatimness is not perfect (87–97%), leaving a nontrivial risk of non-sourced content. Generalization beyond open-domain text (tables, domain-specific corpora) is untested, which limits the demonstrated scope of the contribution. Adding stricter extractive constraints (e.g., span selection with copy mechanisms) or verification filters and testing on non-textual/document-structure inputs would strengthen claims of generality.

557.human_review: The proposed method is effective on in- and out-of-domain unanswerable questions when training sets include unanswerable questions while degrading scores for answerable questions. The improvement in out-of-domain unanswerable questions is significant.
557.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The paper proposes a simple but principled training objective for EQA that avoids the [CLS]-as-null-span hack and introduces a complementary per-token tagging loss; the corresponding inference rule (predict empty when the best span score is negative) aligns with the training signal. Empirically, across three base encoders (BERT, RoBERTa, SpanBERT) and multiple benchmarks, the method preserves in-domain SQuAD 2.0 performance while substantially improving out-of-domain unanswerable performance (e.g., +18.4 F1 on SQuAD AGent on average) and overall robustness to two attack types, cutting the average attack drop from 40.7 to 13.2 F1.

558.human_review: The authors show that the proposed method improves the robustness to two types of adversarial attacks.
558.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The paper carefully disentangles the contributions of the two proposed components. Ablations show the new loss alone drives generalization from adversarial to information-seeking unanswerables ("no synthetic" improves AGent by ~14–16 F1 over default across models), while the synthetic extra answers are the key factor for adversarial-attack robustness (without them, the attack drop does not improve). The training-dynamics analysis (Figure 1) further supports the claim that the default objective overfits to adversarial unanswerables, whereas the proposed loss maintains a stable gap.

559.human_review: It is simple yet reasonable to use 1/n as labels for unanswerable questions, and synthetic answers to avoid overfitting to one answer.
559.llm_review: The work targets a timely and practically important robustness gap in EQA with unanswerable questions, and offers an easy-to-implement solution that requires minimal architectural changes and is broadly applicable across pretrained encoders. The gains are consistent across datasets and models without sacrificing standard in-domain accuracy, indicating good practical utility.

560.human_review: No ablation study is conducted, so it is unclear from the experiments which component of the proposed method (QA loss, sequence tagging loss, synthetic answers, and inference pipeline) has an effect on the improved robustness.
560.llm_review: Methodology, Ablation, Result, Experiment: (1) The experimental comparison set is narrow—only the default cross-entropy baseline is considered. Missing are strong, commonly used alternatives such as a separate answerability head/null-logit calibration, adversarial training or augmentation baselines (e.g., AddSent training), bias-product-of-experts methods, and recent robust QA objectives. (2) Ablations are incomplete: sensitivity to the loss weights (lambda_QA, lambda_Tag) and to the proportion/selection strategy of synthetic answers (fixed at ~20%) is not reported; robustness to different synthetic-answer heuristics is unclear. (3) Robustness is assessed on two attack types (AOS and Negation); broader coverage (paraphrase/semantics-preserving or retrieval-perturbation attacks) would strengthen claims. (4) Tables lack statistical significance tests, and only one figure shows error bars, making it hard to assess the reliability of observed differences.

561.human_review: The motivation to use sequence tagging loss instead of the cross entropy loss is unclear to me.
561.llm_review: Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation: The core design choice of assigning a uniform 1/n label distribution for unanswerable sequences in the softmax-based QA loss, combined with a sigmoid tagging loss that pushes all tokens negative, is only weakly motivated. A clearer theoretical or empirical rationale for why this particular combination is preferable to alternatives (e.g., margin-based null modeling, calibrated null logits, or focal losses) would strengthen the argument. Additional validation via calibration metrics (e.g., ECE for answerability), PR-AUC for no-answer detection, or analyses of confidence distributions would make the intuition more convincing.

562.human_review: The details about synthetic answers are omitted from the main part. I think it should be described in the main part if it is a part of the proposed method.
562.llm_review: Methodology, Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: Reproducibility-critical details are missing or deferred to the appendix, notably the construction of synthetic answers (exact heuristics, span selection rules, quality control, and noise analysis), and the practical implementation of the "negative max span score" decision rule (bias terms, any threshold tuning, and how scores are calibrated across domains). More explicit descriptions of training hyperparameters, data preprocessing, and the proportion of modified examples per domain would improve clarity.

563.human_review: This paper may need justification for using only BERT families in the era of decoder-only large language models such as llama.
563.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation: The claim that the single-answer assumption constitutes a key learning shortcut is plausible, but the validation is indirect (improved attack robustness when adding synthetic answers). A stronger test would use datasets with genuine multi-span annotations (e.g., MultiSpanQA) or controlled synthetic setups where multi-span signals vary, to rule out confounds such as regularization effects from label smoothing. Additional counterfactual experiments (e.g., multi-answer without the new loss, or alternative multi-answer generation schemes) would better substantiate the causal claim.

564.human_review: The experiments seem to lack baseline methods. The proposed method is compared against only a default method.
564.llm_review: Methodology, Experiment, Comparison: The evaluation omits direct comparisons to widely used no-answer modeling strategies (e.g., joint span + explicit no-answer classifier, null-threshold tuning) and to diverse OOD QA suites (e.g., MRQA, NQ test). The custom "overall" metric equally weights answerable/unanswerable and domains, which is nonstandard; reporting standard metrics per dataset alongside macro/micro averages and including competitive prior robust-QA baselines would make the case for impact more compelling.

565.human_review: Improving efficiency in long document tasks is an important research problem.
565.llm_review: Methodology: The study proposes a pragmatic, well-motivated alignment strategy across heterogeneous long-context approaches by benchmarking at matched target compression ratios, standardizing decoding settings, and separating prefill vs. decoding behaviors. The protocol acknowledges cross-school incommensurability and reduces it where feasible (e.g., dynamic kept-token adjustment for token-dropping; consistent quantization bit budgets), enabling more meaningful cross-method comparisons than prior work.

566.human_review: While I am not an expert in this field, it seems that the authors have surveyed, organized and implemented a comprehensive set of methods to reduce memory usage in long sequence modeling. These were applied to several LLMs (where possible) and the results seem to agree.
566.llm_review: Methodology: The paper offers a clear taxonomy spanning KV quantization, token dropping, prompt compression, linear-time sequence models, and hybrid architectures, and pairs this with a minimalistic, extensible, and open-source evaluation workbench. The setup documents system considerations (e.g., custom kernels, FlashAttention compatibility) and reports method-specific hyperparameters, facilitating reproducibility and future extensions.

567.human_review: The methods were evaluated on a large set of 16 long document tasks. As the compression ratios are given, the trade off between compression and performance becomes visible.
567.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation: The evaluation covers 11 methods under 65 settings across seven task categories (LongBench plus a Needle test), with per-category and per-ratio breakdowns and cross-model replication (Llama, Mistral, LongChat, Mamba, RWKV, RecurrentGemma). The results are distilled into actionable, method-agnostic insights (e.g., avoid prefill-time compression for long-input tasks; quantization offers robust average retention; hybrids recover retrieval capabilities), supported by both tabular summaries and visual diagnostics (radar plots, Needle curves).

568.human_review: The experimental results can be useful to researchers and practitioners working with these and related methods.
568.llm_review: Result, Experiment: The empirical findings are informative and consistent: (i) quantization (e.g., KIVI/FlexGen at 4b) closely tracks baselines across categories; (ii) token-dropping methods show strong retention on coding tasks and varying behavior on retrieval (InfLLM > StreamingLLM on Needle, H2O robust on some backbones); (iii) compressing during prefill degrades quality on long-input/short-output tasks; and (iv) hybrid models (e.g., RecurrentGemma) outperform pure linear-time models on retrieval-heavy tasks. These trends are demonstrated across multiple models and compression levels.

569.human_review: The analysis mostly remains on the surface.
569.llm_review: Analysis: While the paper presents compelling qualitative observations (OB1–OB4), the causal analysis is limited. 1) There is little ablation to disentangle algorithmic effects from backbone pretraining/data differences or method-specific kernel optimizations. 2) No significance testing, confidence intervals, or variability analysis is reported to quantify robustness across seeds/prompts. 3) Error analyses are sparse (e.g., when and why token dropping fails on retrieval vs. succeeds on code). 4) Layerwise or per-head attribution/diagnostics for prefill vs. decode compression effects are not explored, limiting mechanistic insight.

570.human_review: For example, an interesting result from Figure 2 is that coding tasks seems to suffer less from compression methods than other tasks (noted in L456ff), but there is no attempt to explain this. Figure 2 itself is mentioned only once in the main text.
570.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Presentation: Some key descriptions and reporting choices impede clarity. 1) The Needle-in-a-Haystack adjustments relative to Gemini 1.5 are deferred to the appendix; the main text could more clearly define scoring and normalization (e.g., the 100.0 reference scale). 2) Figures (e.g., radar plots) are dense and hard to parse without consistent axis scaling and clearer legends. 3) "Sys. Supports?" in Table 1 is underspecified (what kernels, what versions, what runtime stack?). 4) Compression ratio is sometimes reported as theoretical; actual realized memory/speed deltas are not consistently documented alongside accuracy, making interpretation harder.

571.human_review: While Table 2 shows results split into 7 task types, only two of them (Code and Needle) are mentioned in the main text. It would be interesting if there are other task- or instance specific phenomena that can be observed.
571.llm_review: Data/Task, Result: The task suite emphasizes long-input/short-output settings (LongBench) and does not include long-generation or multi-turn dialogue/code-generation scenarios, which are critical for evaluating decode-time behaviors and stability. As a result, the strong recommendation to avoid prefill compression may not generalize to long-generation contexts. Additionally, all backbones are <10B parameters, and code tasks are limited; thus some reported trends (e.g., token dropping on code, hybrid gains) may shift at larger scales or with more diverse programmatic datasets.

572.human_review:
Do the results agree between the different LLMs tested?

(The authors have added analyses to their author response)
572.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Analysis: Fairness and comparability remain only partially addressed. 1) Methods differ in architectural assumptions (e.g., KIVI’s sliding window vs. others), pretraining data, and levels of system optimization; these confounds are acknowledged but not normalized in the reported results. 2) The study focuses on quality metrics without reporting standardized efficiency measurements (latency/throughput, memory footprint under specific kernels), so cost–quality trade-offs cannot be fully assessed. 3) Conclusions would be stronger with unified cost-quality curves and controlled ablations that equalize system stacks (FlashAttention versions, CUDA kernels), making it easier to translate findings into deployment guidance.

573.human_review: PER-PCS significantly reduces computational and storage requirements, achieving 7x faster computation and 38x less storage compared to training individual PEFTs.
573.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clear and novel piece-level composition framework for personalization, where per-layer LoRA pieces from consenting sharers are gated and composed to assemble a target users PEFT without training on the target. The post-hoc gate learning per piece is lightweight, and the assembly uses activation-gate cosine similarity and softmax-weighted mixing to produce per-layer deltas. The approach is modular, compatible in principle with multiple PEFT families (LoRA, Adapters, (IA)3, prefix), and stores only indices and weights for the assembled configuration, which supports ownership, modularity, and efficient deployment.

574.human_review: PER-PCS maintains model ownership and fine-grained personalization for target users. It also shows robustness in terms of the number of sharers, sharer selection strategy, and the number of PEFT parameters shared.
574.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The design choices (post-hoc gating, autoregressive layer-by-layer selection, and index/weight-only storage) translate into strong empirical efficiency: the method achieves near-OPPU performance while being ~7x faster and ~38x more storage efficient in reported settings. It consistently outperforms non-personalized prompting, RAG/PAG-only, and PEFT retrieval baselines, showing that fine-grained piece selection can capture user-specific signals better than whole-PEFT retrieval, with minimal extra machinery.

575.human_review: Extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency. The experiments demonstrate that PER-PCS outperforms non-personalized baselines and PEFT retrieval methods across 6 personalization tasks, with performance comparable to training individual PEFTs (OPPU) but much lower computational and storage costs.
575.llm_review: Methodology, Result, and Experiment: The experimental suite is comprehensive across six LaMP tasks (classification and generation), with solid baselines (non-personalized, RAG, PAG, PEFT retrieval, and OPPU) and multiple analyses. Robustness studies cover number of sharers, sharer-selection strategies, and sharing ratios; a time/space scaling analysis quantifies practical gains; and case studies visualize layer-wise piece weights. These evaluations collectively support the claim that piece-level composition is effective, robust, and scalable.

576.human_review: Overall, the manuscript is well-organized and well-written.
576.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is generally well organized and easy to follow. The problem is clearly formulated, the PER-PCS pipeline is depicted with helpful figures, and the relationship between base adaptation, sharer PEFT/gate training, and target assembly is explicit. The LoRA-based notation and the definition of a piece are clear, aiding reproducibility.

577.human_review: From Figure 3, it seems that increasing the number of users who consent to share their personal PEFT will not help improve performance. I would like to see a more detailed explanation of why.
577.llm_review: Result; Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation; Presentation: The papers claims about safe sharing and privacy are not operationalized: there is no explicit threat model, privacy metric, or formal guarantee (e.g., DP, membership inference resistance). Several important details are under-specified, including LoRA rank(s), per-layer top-k, gate learning hyperparameters (steps, LR), and the exact procedure underlying the '*' significance marks. Dataset split specifics and any seed/stability reporting are limited. Minor presentation issues (inconsistent spacing of PER-PCS, occasional formatting inconsistencies) slightly hinder readability and precise interpretation of results.

578.human_review: In several tasks like LaMP-1, PER-PCS+RAG seems not to contribute and even causes a performance drop (compared with PER-PCS Base). I am curious about the potential reasons behind this.
578.llm_review: Result: While performance is strong, the empirical scope is narrow in key dimensions: only Llama-2-7B is evaluated; compatibility with other PEFT families is claimed but not demonstrated; and personalization is tested on 100 users per task within LaMP, with each user tied to a single task. Some tasks still show OPPU as marginally stronger, and there is no human evaluation for generation quality or user-perceived personalization. The privacy/ownership advantages are argued but not empirically validated (e.g., no leakage tests), and cold-start and cross-domain generalization are not assessed.

579.human_review: In the method section, why are the PEFT pieces selected in an autoregressive way? Can we directly weigh the average/merge all the left parameters with the gating score you have learned?
579.llm_review: Methodology: The selection and mixing mechanics rely on heuristics (cosine similarity between gate vectors and activations, fixed top-k, 1/sqrt(n) scaling, history-level averaging) without theoretical justification or comparison to stronger alternatives (e.g., learned meta-selectors, attention over pieces, regularized or sparse mixtures). Gate vectors are trained per-piece on sharer data with ~50 steps, but convergence/overfitting or stability analyses are absent. The approach presumes sufficient overlap in representational space across users; interference or negative transfer from composing many sharers is not systematically analyzed, and the privacy implications of sharing gate vectors remain unexamined.

580.human_review: MINT offers a diverse set of IR tasks, covering a wide range of domains and document types. This ensures a representative and challenging evaluation of instruction-following abilities across various scenarios.
580.llm_review: Data/Task and Evaluation: MINT offers rare breadth and heterogeneity for instructed IR with 100 distinct tasks spanning 6 domains, 396 collections, 5.23M documents, and 8,839 queries, paired with 776 expert-written instructions (including query-level instructions where needed). The evaluation protocol is thoughtfully designed to isolate instruction-following effects (no-instruction vs +instruction settings), report domain-wise breakdowns, and include per-task analyses. The authors further validate the lightweight sampling (≈100 queries/task) via a correlation study showing >0.95 Pearson correlation with full-test results, and provide task-correlation analyses to substantiate diversity, making the benchmark both comprehensive and efficient.

581.human_review: The manual annotation of 776 detailed instructions provides a clear and specific guidance for each task. This allows for a more nuanced assessment of models’ ability to understand and execute complex retrieval instructions.
581.llm_review: Data/Task: The benchmark aggregates real, diverse retrieval scenarios from established sources (e.g., TREC tracks, BEIR, KILT, SIGIR resource tracks, and contemporary LLM evaluation sets) and unifies them into a consistent format after careful cleaning and deduplication. It covers a wide spectrum of retrieval types—fact checking, entity linking, conversational retrieval, legal case/statute retrieval, product and ToT retrieval, biomedical IR, and code/tool retrieval—capturing long-tail, instruction-sensitive tasks with realistic relevance criteria. Expert-authored instructions specify query, document type, and relevance criteria, reflecting real user intents beyond simplistic task descriptions.

582.human_review: The paper benchmarks a variety of retrieval models, including both traditional and state-of-the-art LLM-based approaches. This allows for a comprehensive comparison of different methods and highlights the strengths and weaknesses of each.
582.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, and Comparison: The paper introduces a pragmatic pipeline—expert instruction annotation (including query-specific instructions), k-means-based query sampling for diversity, and a task-correlation analysis—to construct and analyze a large, heterogeneous benchmark. It positions MINT clearly against BEIR, KILT, FollowIR, InstructIR, and MTEB, demonstrating substantially broader task coverage and more varied relevance definitions. Empirically, it benchmarks a wide range of baselines (sparse, single-task, multi-task, instruction-tuned embeddings, cross-encoders, and LLM-based re-rankers) and shows that instruction-tuned models measurably benefit from explicit instructions, highlighting the benchmark’s value for testing instruction-following behavior.

583.human_review: The paper acknowledges the importance of prompt sensitivity in LLMs but does not extensively explore this aspect. Investigating the impact of different prompts on model performance would provide valuable insights for improving instruction understanding.
583.llm_review: Methodology: (1) The re-ranking evaluation fixes the first-stage retrieval to text-embedding-3-small (top-100), which can conflate first- and second-stage effects and may understate the capacity of stronger re-rankers or bias conclusions about instruction sensitivity. (2) The instruction-annotation process lacks critical detail—e.g., annotator counts, guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, and adjudication—making reproducibility and instruction quality assessment difficult. (3) Document sampling includes random negative sampling and occasional corpus merging across tasks, potentially altering original distributions and task boundaries. (4) There is no audit for training-data overlap between instruction-tuned baselines and MINT tasks/instructions, so some generalization claims might be confounded by leakage. (5) The procedure for injecting instructions into different model families is not fully standardized or justified, which could affect comparability.

584.human_review: MINT primarily focuses on text retrieval tasks. Expanding the benchmark to include other retrieval types, such as image or code retrieval, would provide a more holistic evaluation of LLM capabilities.
584.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, and Evaluation: The current benchmark focuses on English, text-only retrieval, limiting generality to multilingual or multimodal IR. Although the authors validate sampling via model-performance correlation, using ~100 queries per task may still miss rare phenomena; the validation relies on a limited set of baselines and a single correlation metric. Task heterogeneity in relevance schemes is collapsed into nDCG@10, and sensitivity to instruction wording is not explored (single phrasing per task, no robustness analysis). The LLM re-ranking comparison uses a single backend (gpt-3.5-turbo), and fairness to re-rankers is further constrained by the fixed first-stage retriever. Stronger evidence for generalization would come from held-out domain ablations, adversarial instruction variants, and instruction-robustness studies.

585.human_review: TGB significantly improves the temporal grounding capabilities of MLLMs, allowing for more accurate interpretation of long-form videos by efficiently extracting and preserving relevant temporal features.
585.llm_review: Results are consistently strong and well-interpreted across settings: TGB yields sizable gains on seven benchmarks (e.g., AGQA 2.0: BLIP2 54.00 → TGB-BLIP2 61.45 overall; large boosts in temporal categories such as Object-relation 53.72 → 62.27 and Object-action 62.10 → 66.09). On NExT-QA, it improves BLIP2 from 69.6 to 72.1, and on EgoSchema zero-shot it surpasses comparably trained baselines (41.2 vs. Video-LLaVA 40.2 with fewer frames). Temporal question grounding (NExT-GQA) shows clear headroom reduction (mIoU 19.9 vs. prior IGV 14.0). The paper offers plausible explanations for why low-dimension motion features plus multi-span grounding better preserve temporal cues than sparse frame selection, and discusses how extrapolative positional encoding underpins the demonstrated length extrapolation (trained on 4 frames, generalizes up to 16× longer). Efficiency analyses (e.g., TGB(OFs) ~2,950 GFLOPs vs. SeViLA ~13,720) contextualize the practical impact.

586.human_review: The framework’s ability to handle sequences up to 16 times longer than initially trained without sacrificing performance highlights its scalability and effectiveness in real-world applications.
586.llm_review: Methodologically, the combination of a language-guided multi-span temporal grounding module over low-dimensional flow features, multimodal extrapolative positional encoding (RoPE) for length extrapolation, and an annotation-free bootstrapping scheme with Gumbel-Softmax joint optimization is novel and well-justified. Empirically, these design choices translate into clear gains: substantial improvements in temporal categories on AGQA, better zero-shot open-domain QA than larger or more frame-heavy baselines, and top results on NExT-GQA without heavy offline video encoders. The method’s pluggability is validated by consistent gains across multiple MLLMs (ALBEF/VIOLET/SINGULARITY) even when only TGB-grounded frames are supplied.

587.human_review: TGB’s bootstrapping framework eliminates the need for explicit temporal grounding annotations, reducing the reliance on costly manual annotations and leveraging existing MLLMs for improved performance.
587.llm_review: The framework is cleanly modular and parameter-efficient: it treats optical flow as a low-dimensional temporal bridge, uses cross-attention to align motion cues with language, performs multi-span selection via an RC head, and can inject selected frames into standard MLLMs through a Q-Former. The extrapolative positional encoding is a principled way to extend temporal reach without retraining for longer contexts, and the bootstrapping mechanism avoids reliance on temporal annotations while allowing end-to-end joint optimization with pluggable MLLMs. The design choice to make the bridge feature-agnostic (flow can be swapped for other temporal cues) enhances adaptability.

588.human_review: Could the authors provide ablation studies on the different strategies of multi-span selection that are discussed in Section D of the Appendix?
588.llm_review: The ablation suite, while informative (e.g., w/o optical flow, fixed bridge, uniform sampling), leaves several sensitivities underexplored: (1) robustness to the choice and quality of optical flow (e.g., RAFT vs. lighter/faster or learned flows), (2) span count k and selection stability, including overlap union strategies, (3) the effect of the Gumbel-Softmax temperature and sampling multiplicity K on both accuracy and computational budget, (4) granularity of the extrapolative positional encoding (e.g., different RoPE scales or alternative extrapolation schemes), and (5) sensitivity to training context size and extrapolation ratio beyond 16×. Reporting these would clarify which components are most critical and how to reproduce the gains reliably.

589.human_review: It is interesting to see how the number of layers of Transformer in TGB influences the tradeoff between the efficiency and performance on downstream tasks.
589.llm_review: Methodology–Data/Task–Result alignment has a few unresolved issues. The claim of general long-video capability is strongest on AGQA and EgoSchema, but gains are modest on the more causality-centric NExT-QA, suggesting task-dependent benefits and potential reliance on motion salience. Comparisons sometimes differ in frames used (e.g., TGB-augmented methods sampled 6 frames vs. others), which may confound fairness. The bootstrapped pseudo-labeling depends on MLLM predictions and answer similarity to ground truth; noise and bias in these signals can vary across datasets and are not quantified. Finally, the temporal grounding results, while best among baselines, are still low in absolute terms (mIoU < 0.20), leaving open questions about practical temporal localization accuracy in very long, cluttered videos.

590.human_review: Could the performance be further improved when the size of the backbone LLMs grows larger than 7B?
590.llm_review: Some methodological details that bear on correctness and reproducibility are under-specified or deferred to the appendix: the RC head architecture and training dynamics, how the number of spans is determined at inference, and how conflicts/overlaps are resolved in multi-span union. The bootstrapping for open-ended QA leverages ground-truth answers for similarity scoring; although it avoids temporal annotations, it still depends on answer supervision and MLLM outputs, which could amplify errors—yet there is no analysis of label noise or its impact. The efficiency claims are promising but would benefit from more wall-clock and memory profiling on standardized hardware, especially under long-sequence extrapolation and across different MLLMs.

591.human_review: The article introduces a new self-evaluation method that leverages the model's own features, avoiding dependence on external APIs and concerns about privacy leakage.
591.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a simple, training-free, and model-aware self-evaluation framework leveraging glass-box features (softmax entropy/variance, ensemble-based uncertainty, and attention entropy). The methodological focus on leveraging token-level probability distributions as confidence signals is well motivated and directly exploits information available during generation. Evaluation: The study benchmarks these features systematically across two standard LLM evaluation suites and two widely used 7B chat models, using multiple correlation metrics (Pearson, Spearman, Kendall), providing a clear, apples-to-apples comparison against established evaluators.

592.human_review: The experimental results show that the self-evaluation method based on softmax distribution achieves higher accuracy than some existing evaluation methods, validating the feasibility of this approach.
592.llm_review: Experiment, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Result, Evaluation: The central intuition—that sharper softmax distributions reflect higher confidence and thus better response quality—is validated empirically. Across MT-Bench and Vicuna-Bench for LLaMA2-7B-chat and Vicuna-7B, softmax-based features consistently exhibit the strongest correlations with GPT-4 annotations, often matching or exceeding GPT-3.5-Turbo and Auto-J on average. The ablations (uncertainty ensembles and attention entropy) reinforce the intuition by showing weaker or inconsistent correlations when the features are less aligned with token-level confidence. Reporting multiple correlation metrics, plus analysis across feature families, strengthens the evaluation and result interpretability.

593.human_review: This method is not only applicable to existing smaller models (e.g., 7B parameter models) but also holds potential for larger-scale models.
593.llm_review: Methodology: Beyond raw softmax-derived features, the paper introduces two practical reference-aware enhancements—an in-context illustration strategy and a probability calibration via reference log-probability—that further improve correlation. These extensions are methodologically grounded (reducing evaluator bias and aligning distributions via demonstrations) and show incremental gains without requiring finetuning or additional supervision.

594.human_review: Simple Variants: The new metrics proposed (such as entropy and variance of the softmax distribution) are merely simple variants of existing signals, lacking in-depth analysis and explanation of their benefits and drawbacks. These variants do not demonstrate unique advantages in practical applications.
594.llm_review: Evaluation: (1) Gold labels are derived from GPT-4 rather than human crowd or expert judgments, which may introduce evaluator bias and limit claims about human alignment. (2) Benchmarks comprise 80 prompts each, which is small for meta-evaluation; no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported, making it hard to judge robustness. (3) While Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall are reported, tie handling differs across methods and is acknowledged as unfair for ranking metrics; the impact of this on comparative conclusions is not quantified. (4) Baselines are limited to GPT-3.5 and Auto-J; additional open-source evaluators and recent reference-free metrics would strengthen the comparison.

595.human_review: Lack of Comprehensiveness: The article does not provide sufficient experimental evidence to support its conclusions. The experiments mainly focus on smaller-scale models and do not consider a wider range of models and larger datasets, which is not good for the confidence of the conclusions.
595.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, Experiment: (1) The tasks are limited to MT-Bench and Vicuna-Bench, which focus on general dialogue and may not represent diverse generation settings (e.g., summarization, factual QA, reasoning-heavy tasks, coding). (2) Results vary across benchmarks and correlation types; in several cases GPT-3.5 remains competitive, especially on Vicuna-Bench, suggesting the advantage is not uniform. (3) Experiments are restricted to 7B models, leaving open whether findings generalize to larger or smaller architectures and different pretraining/fine-tuning regimes. (4) The uncertainty ensemble uses only 10 forward passes and limited perturbations, which likely underestimates the method’s potential and conflates practicality with under-sampling effects.

596.human_review: Practical Issues: Although the self-evaluation method theoretically has certain advantages, there are still practical issues, i.e., can higher glass-box metric performance provide strong evidence that one model is better than the other on a given task. How can these general evaluations results finally affect the model development remains an issue.
596.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation: (1) The proposed softmax-entropy/variance features may be confounded by response length, decoding temperature, and repetition/degeneracy; controls or length-normalized diagnostics are not reported, making causal interpretation uncertain. (2) SentProb and the definition of word-level log-probability/entropy aggregation could use clearer formalization; some notation is ambiguous, and implementation choices (e.g., per-token normalization, treatment of EOS, vocabulary masking) are not detailed. (3) The probability calibration with references, while effective, presupposes availability and quality of references; this partially undermines the goal of general self-evaluation in open-ended settings. (4) The approach relies on glass-box access, limiting applicability to closed-source APIs; a discussion of partial-access settings (e.g., log-probs only, no attention) and robustness there would improve methodological completeness.

597.human_review: The entry point of this paper (i.e., knowledge inconsistencies) is very novel as well as important. Meanwhile, the introduction of KCA offers a systematic and highly applicable method to reduce knowledge inconsistencies in LLMs.
597.llm_review: The paper introduces a novel framing of hallucination mitigation as reducing knowledge inconsistency between alignment data and a foundation models pretrained knowledge. The use of LLM-generated, knowledge-targeted examinations to probe a models knowledge boundary is original and allows scaling beyond simple QA tasks, while the explicit attribution via reference knowledge snippets improves interpretability over prior instruction/response-only approaches.

598.human_review: The paper provides extensive experimental results across six benchmarks, utilizing different foundation LLMs to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
598.llm_review: Comprehensive experiments substantiate the intuition that inconsistency in alignment data correlates with hallucination rates, and that filtering or reformatting such instances reduces hallucinations. The study spans multiple backbones and sizes (Pythia, Llama-2, Mistral; 7B/13B), six benchmarks covering general instruction following, truthful QA, retrieval-style evaluation, and a clinical domain, and employs both LLM-based and metric-based assessments. Results consistently show reduced hallucination rates across settings and competitive ROUGE on MS MARCO and ACI-Bench. Helpfulness analysis further validates the trade-offs: refusal tuning best reduces hallucination, open-book preserves helpfulness, and discard strikes a balance. Methodologically, the pipeline is applied uniformly across datasets and models, reinforcing generality of the motivation.

599.human_review: The paper meticulously describes the steps involved in KCA, from knowledge requirement classification to the implementation of different tuning strategies, providing clear guidance for replication.
599.llm_review: Methodologically well-specified: the four-stage detection (knowledge requirement classification, reference knowledge generation, examination formulation, and model completion with an accuracy threshold) and three calibration strategies (open-book, discard, refusal) are clearly defined. Prompts, thresholds, and decoding choices are documented; the examination design (3 multiple-choice questions per snippet) operationalizes the knowledge boundary in a way that is auditable and attributable. The discussion section helpfully interprets when each calibration strategy is preferable, offering practical guidance.

600.human_review: The reference knowledge for an instruction is generated by a well-aligned LLM G, but G may also hallucinate and generate wrong knowledge. Hence KCA typically relies on a stronger LLM which stores broader knowledge than the foundation model M (ChatGPT-3.5 v.s. open-sourced LLMs in this paper), which restricts the scalability and makes self-improvement difficult.
600.llm_review: The methodology relies heavily on GPT-3.5/4 to classify knowledge requirements, generate reference knowledge, write exams, and judge hallucinations, raising concerns about circularity, bias, and error propagation. The generated knowledge snippets are treated as ground truth without human verification, and exams have only three questions per snippet with an arbitrary accuracy threshold (0.67); sensitivity analyses for threshold, question count, exam difficulty, and choice of generator/grader are missing. Detection quality for complex, multi-fact instructions is unclear, and the refusal-tuning evaluation excludes refusal samples when computing hallucination rates, complicating fairness; while the paper adds an auxiliary analysis, end-to-end impact under deployment-like conditions remains underexplored.

601.human_review: When evaluating the hallucination rate, the refusal response is not considered in the calculation, so the comparison between refusal tuning and other methods may not be an apple-to-apple comparison. A comparison of different methods on the instructions with non-refusal responses should be provided.
601.llm_review: Baselines are limited. There is no head-to-head comparison with prior data-curation approaches that estimate knowledge boundaries (e.g., uncertainty-appended alignment) or with strong training/inference hallucination-reduction methods (e.g., DoLA, CoVe/self-checking, fact-augmented RLHF, retrieval-augmented or knowledge-graph methods). Ablations isolating each KCA stage, alternative detectors (e.g., simple confidence/perplexity filters), and sensitivity to the LLM judge choice are absent, making it hard to attribute gains uniquely to KCA and to position the approach against the state of the art.

602.human_review: The analysis of over 1.2 million posts allows for robust statistical insights and the development of a well-informed model.
602.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Analysis: The paper presents a well-structured, end-to-end pipeline that scales from 1.51M Reddit posts to a targeted set of drug-related and stigmatizing content via a two-stage LLM filter (GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 validation) and an explanation-enhanced stigma classifier grounded in Link and Phelan’s framework. The decision to focus on non–drug-related subreddits is well-motivated to capture external stigma. The destigmatization component is thoughtfully designed, progressing from a zero-shot baseline to an informed prompt and a stylistically guided variant that preserves tone using emotion detection, syntactic cues, and lexical diversity. The linguistic analysis is multifaceted (entities, subject–verb pairs, topic modeling, emotion analysis), and the LIWC-based comparison supports the claim that the best system preserves psycholinguistic properties while reducing stigma. The release of labeled stigma posts and paired original/rewrite examples adds concrete value to the community.

603.human_review: The use of Informed and Stylized LLMs to transform stigmatizing language into empathetic expressions is innovative and addresses a significant social issue.
603.llm_review: The work tackles a socially impactful and understudied NLP application—destigmatization of SUD-related discourse—offering actionable resources and an approach that can generalize to adjacent stigma domains. The combination of conceptual grounding, practical tooling, and qualitative insights positions the paper as both useful and timely for researchers and practitioners.

604.human_review: The study is limited to Reddit, which may not generalize to other social media platforms where user demographics and discussion dynamics differ.
604.llm_review: Methodology: The pipeline relies heavily on proprietary LLMs for multiple critical stages (topic filtering, stigma labeling, explanation, and rewriting), with relatively limited human supervision beyond small seed annotations and a moderate inter-annotator agreement (kappa around 0.67). This raises concerns about error propagation, circularity between detection criteria and generation prompts, and replicability. The human evaluation of generations is informative but small, and there is little error analysis of failure cases or ablations to disentangle the contributions of instruction, few-shot examples, and stylistic controls. Some analytic choices (e.g., many LIWC comparisons without multiple-comparison correction) risk overstating stability. Finally, the definition of Constitutional AI is loosely framed and may not align with standard usage, which could confuse methodological positioning.

605.human_review: The manual annotation process could introduce biases, particularly in subjective interpretations of what constitutes stigmatizing language.
605.llm_review: Data/Task: The dataset is limited to four English-language subreddits and one platform, which may introduce sampling bias and restrict generalizability. The initial ground-truthing for drug relevance is based on only 200 posts, and the reliance on LLMs for large-scale filtering and stigma labeling may inject systematic biases. Details about annotation guidelines and quality control for the larger labeling effort are sparse, and there is some ambiguity in counts (e.g., directed-stigma totals vs. number of destigmatized pairs), which complicates interpretation. Structural stigma is very underrepresented, limiting insights for that category.

606.human_review: The evaluation of the de-stigmatized content might not fully capture whether the rephrased messages maintain the original intent and emotional tone of the user.
606.llm_review: Evaluation: The human evaluation uses five reviewers and 110 posts without reported inter-rater reliability or statistical significance testing across systems, making it hard to assess robustness. The outcome measures rely on rankings rather than calibrated scales, and there is no user study with affected stakeholders to validate perceived harm reduction. Automated evaluation focuses on stylistic similarity (LIWC) but does not quantify toxicity or stigma reduction with independent detectors, nor does it evaluate downstream effects (e.g., reader perceptions, engagement, or moderation utility). These gaps limit confidence in real-world impact.

607.human_review: Interesting observations on how the LLM refusal behavior changes by decomposing the harmful prompts.
607.llm_review: Methodology: The paper introduces a clear and novel decomposition-and-reconstruction attack paradigm. By breaking a malicious prompt into semantically coherent sub-prompts and implicitly reassembling them via benign in-context exemplars, the method reduces the model’s salience on harmful token combinations while still steering outputs toward the original intent. This design is orthogonal to prefix/suffix/hybrid attacks and constitutes a distinct attack family with a plausible mechanism (lower rejection-token likelihood for fragmented prompts).

608.human_review: The proposed method that uses semantic parsing to decompose harmful prompts appears to be a more effective jailbreaking attack. The authors also build a useful pipeline to finally decompose the harmful prompt into instruction, structure, verb and noun components.
608.llm_review: Methodology: The pipeline is well-specified and largely automated: semantic parsing to label phrases into instruction/structure/verb/noun, templated ICL rules and examples for implicit reconstruction, and a search over sub-prompt variants. The choice to avoid harmful exemplars in ICL and instead use benign, semantically similar examples is thoughtful and reduces the risk of trivially flagging malice during reconstruction. Ablations on semantic similarity and exemplar phrasing (affirmative, step-by-step) substantiate key design choices.

609.human_review: Additionally, the authors find that in-context examples are needed to make the victim LLM fall for the latent intent in these deconstructed harmful prompts. Essentially, the fragments of the harmful prompts are spread across the input to the victim LLM in an obfuscated prompt template.
609.llm_review: Methodology: The level-wise synonym search at the phrase (not token) level is a practical way to shrink the search space, improve query efficiency, and preserve faithfulness while boosting success rates. The attack remains black-box and shows strong cross-model transfer, with additional modules (e.g., word games) and defense-aware tests indicating versatility against multiple guard mechanisms without requiring gradient access or extensive optimization.

610.human_review: Relies on a strong model like GPT4 to craft the attack for several key steps, including semantic parsing, synonym generation, and harmless prompt creation.
610.llm_review: Methodology: The approach depends on external LLMs (GPT-4) for semantic parsing and synonym generation, which introduces circularity, cost, and reproducibility concerns. The synonym search relies on embedding-based scoring and manually crafted target/anti-target heuristics, with limited analysis of sensitivity, failure modes, or robustness to parsing errors. The optional word-game component subtly changes the threat model and may conflate the core contribution with known obfuscation tricks.

611.human_review: Is cosine similarity always sufficient to maintain faithfulness with the original intent, does the human evaluation take this into account when measuring success.-
611.llm_review: Evaluation: Success measurement mixes GPT-based judging with human evaluation where a response is labeled harmful if any annotator flags it, a conservative criterion that can inflate ASR. There is only a single run per method, no variance or significance testing, and some results use older API versions. While AdvBench is standard, the additional datasets are small subsets, and key closed-source details are opaque. Defense coverage is limited (moderation, PPL filter, RA-LLM) with no strong output-filter pipelines, and fairness across baselines (hyperparameters, query budgets, prompt templates) could be more rigorously controlled and reported.

612.human_review:
It is not clear if a stronger defense that looks at the prompt structure [1] instead of generic moderation classifiers will reduce the effectiveness. 


[1] The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13208
612.llm_review: Methodology, Related Work: The new "decomposition-based" taxonomy is promising but not fully disentangled from prior families. Earlier attacks already perform structural obfuscation or nested templating that partially decomposes harmful intents, and recent works (e.g., multilingual, encoding/cipher, many-shot ICL or slot-filling) overlap in spirit. The paper would benefit from a sharper positioning against these and a broader comparison to the latest jailbreak strategies to solidify novelty claims.

613.human_review: The paper studies the importance of fairness of LLMs in processing tabular data, which is of importance to society.
613.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Significance: The paper tackles a timely and underexplored question—how demonstration composition in ICL affects fairness for tabular classification—and proposes a concrete selection strategy that prioritizes minority-group examples. The FCG algorithm (clustering + evolutionary scoring) is a simple, general, and model-agnostic procedure that can be applied to different tabular tasks. Evaluating on two high-stakes, widely used fairness datasets (Adult, Credit) increases the practical significance, and the finding that minority-focused demonstrations improve DP/EO fairness with minimal accuracy loss is actionable for practitioners who rely on ICL rather than fine-tuning.

614.human_review: The paper is well-written and organized. The figures clearly present the framework.
614.llm_review: Methodology, Presentation: The methodological setup is clearly specified: formal notation for (X, Y, Z), explicit definitions of DP/EO (difference and ratio), and a prompt template breakdown. The perturbation framework (flipping Y and Z proportions) is well-motivated and isolates the contribution of sensitive-attribute composition vs. label composition. The FCG algorithm is presented with pseudocode and a stepwise workflow, and the paper includes an ablation to clarify the contribution of clustering and genetic scoring. Tables and figures map cleanly to the stated research questions, aiding readability.

615.human_review: The authors conducted extensive experiments on evaluating LLM fairness on different datasets under various settings. The findings reveal the crucial factors that affect LLM fairness under the ICL settings.
615.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result, Experiment: Experiments span five LLMs and two fairness-centric tabular datasets, comparing zero-shot and several few-shot strategies with multiple random seeds. Results consistently show that prioritizing minority-group demonstrations (S2/S3) improves fairness metrics (higher Rdp/Reo, lower 9dp/9eo) while maintaining or improving F1/accuracy. The perturbation studies provide causal evidence that increasing the minority proportion in demonstrations drives fairness gains, while flipping labels harms both fairness and utility. The proposed FCG selection further improves over random demo selection across strategies, and the ablation supports the necessity of both clustering and evolutionary scoring.

616.human_review: The authors only consider two datsets, which may not be necessarily sufficient for the evaluation of the framework. As there are plentiful tabular datasets, the authors should consider using more datasets.
616.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: The empirical scope is narrow: only two datasets, binary classification, and a single binary sensitive attribute per task. Intersectional fairness, multi-label or multi-class settings, and settings with multiple sensitive attributes are not addressed. For the Credit dataset, the exact sensitive attribute used and how tabular features are serialized to text (which can materially affect fairness) are under-specified. Baselines beyond random selection are limited—there is no comparison to established fairness-aware selection or post-processing methods (e.g., reweighing, threshold adjustments), nor to other demo-selection strategies such as LENS or hard example mining on tabular data.

617.human_review: The authors use various LLMs for evaluation. However, the performance of the framework on smaller LMs, such as LLaMA, could also be important and necessitates investigations.
617.llm_review: Methodology: The FCG scoring relies on repeated LLM evaluations on a development set labeled with sensitive attributes, which risks overfitting demo selection to the dev distribution and may be costly for commercial APIs. Sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (number of clusters n, neighbors m, K shots, b1 trade-off, initial p, iterations) are limited, and the choice to weight prediction and fairness equally is not justified or tuned. K-means on heterogeneous tabular features (potentially mixed types) is a simplistic choice without discussion of preprocessing/normalization or alternative clustering methods. The claim that clustering avoids LLM access addresses only step 1; step 2 still requires substantial LLM calls.

618.human_review: The authors only focus on binary classification tasks. However, the fairness problems of LLMs may involve more classification tasks and even generation.
618.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: Some empirical claims (e.g., fairness gains "without sacrificing predictive accuracy") are not uniformly supported—tables show cases with reduced accuracy or precision, and no statistical significance tests are reported beyond small-seed averages. The fairness improvements may in part reflect shifts in acceptance rates rather than improved equalized performance calibration; there is no analysis of operating-point control or calibration. Robustness to prompt templates, serialization choices, and alternative sensitive-attribute definitions is not studied. The demonstration strategies (e.g., S3 with extreme label proportions) may be unrealistic for some applications without discussing distribution shift.

619.human_review: The paper does a thorough analysis of the memory and time complexity providing insights into how the method scared with increasing datasets and label numbers
619.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Analysis: The paper introduces a clear and practical ensemble framework for extreme multi-label learning by combining label subsampling with tree-based linear models. The key methodological choices—bypassing the level-1 probability estimation, retaining empty-labeled instances to avoid biased negative sampling, and averaging per-label probabilities across overlapping subsets—are well motivated for XML settings with very large label spaces. The analysis includes explicit time and space complexity derivations that explain how per-machine memory and training cost scale with the sampling rate, making the approach attractive for distributed deployment on large text classification tasks.

620.human_review: The papers conducts comprehensive experiments across datasets and baseline comparison.
620.llm_review: Data/Task/Experiment/Comparison: The empirical study spans six established XML datasets, including large benchmarks such as amazon-3m and wiki-500k, covering a broad range of label cardinalities and distributions relevant to real-world text applications. The comparisons are against strong baselines (one-vs-rest and tree-based linear methods with all labels), with multiple runs on four datasets to mitigate K-means randomness, and include ablations (random partitions vs. K-means; partition count vs. overlapping subsampling) that situate the method’s gains and design choices in a fair head-to-head setting.

621.human_review: The evaluation metrics and computational requirements clearly highlight the benefit of the proposed techniques
621.llm_review: Evaluation: The evaluation follows community standards (precision@1/3/5), reports mean±std over multiple runs where feasible, and complements accuracy with pragmatic metrics such as model size and training-time analyses. The ablation on distributed settings is informative, showing that overlapping label subsampling plus bypassing level-1 improves over random partitions, thereby strengthening the internal validity of the evaluation.

622.human_review: Impact of sub-sampling and negative sampling is highlighted and considered during the formulation of random label forests
622.llm_review: The paper is generally well organized and explicit about assumptions and limitations (e.g., effects of removing negative instances and hierarchical label dependencies), and it provides enough algorithmic detail to enable reproduction and adaptation in similar XML pipelines.

623.human_review: In the XML , the paper does not study or highlight the impact on long-tail distribution .
623.llm_review: Data/Task/Significance: The method shows a notable drop on wiki-500k, suggesting reduced suitability for tasks with strong hierarchical or correlated label structures where uniform label subsampling can break label relationships. Across other datasets, improvements over strong tree-based baselines are relatively modest and close to OVR, which tempers the perceived significance beyond the engineering advantages; additionally, the inability to predict labels that are never sampled further narrows the method’s applicability for rare labels.

624.human_review: The paper does not highlight any hyper-parameters and sensitivity of the algorithm towards the same. Details for experimental setup is not-adequate for a fair comparison
624.llm_review: Methodology/Experiment: Sensitivity to key hyperparameters (sampling rate r, number of submodels N, number of partitions K, and overlap degree) is not systematically explored; only limited variation (e.g., r=0.15 on a single dataset) is reported. The choice of simple averaging for ensembling is not compared to alternative weighting/calibration strategies, and there is no quantitative ablation on the effect of retaining versus removing empty-labeled instances. Experimentally, OVR is omitted on the two largest datasets and repeated runs are reported only for smaller datasets, limiting the breadth of evidence at scale.

625.human_review: Table 6 highlights reduction in training time, but does not highlight number of distributed compute used and total compute used to train the proposed algorithm
625.llm_review: Methodology: Uniform label subsampling can bias coverage toward head labels and leaves no guarantee that rare labels are adequately represented; the method offers no mechanism (e.g., stratified or importance-based sampling) to ensure label coverage or to adaptively prioritize hard/rare labels. The equal-weight averaging across submodels also ignores heterogeneous submodel quality or subset difficulty.

626.human_review: The proposed method introduces complexity which is not clearly explained  in the distributed training and label sub-sampling techniques. With the release of the code, it would be hard for the paper to be re-produced.
626.llm_review: Methodology: The distributed formulation requires each machine to process the full instance set for training subtrees, which may shift the bottleneck from label memory to data memory and I/O. K-means is still run per subset and is not itself distributed, and there is little discussion of load balancing, fault tolerance, or communication overhead—practical factors that matter for scaling in real systems.

627.human_review: Paper lacks theoretical proofs/guarantees to support the correctness or covergence of random forest labels method.
627.llm_review: Methodology/Theory: The theoretical support is mostly limited to big-O complexity; there are no generalization or ranking guarantees, no analysis linking sampling rate to P@k degradation, and no formal justification that bypassing level-1 and averaging predictions yields well-calibrated or unbiased estimates. The argument about negative sampling effects is intuitive but not formalized, leaving gaps between methodological choices and theoretical guarantees.

628.human_review: The paper offers a valuable critique of the current research trajectory in AES, encouraging the community to reconsider the emphasis on performance metrics.
628.llm_review: Result and Evaluation: The paper delivers a coherent set of results in the form of concrete, field-level recommendations (e.g., going beyond QWK, evaluating on multiple corpora including ESL/time-unrestricted settings, qualitative and quantitative error analyses, cross-prompt protocols, and trait-based interpretability). Its evaluative synthesis of current practices is insightful: it critiques over-reliance on ASAP and QWK, highlights confounds such as essay length, and calls for richer evaluation (trait-wise, type-wise, minority-class sensitivity, and explainability). These outputs are actionable and, if adopted, would improve the rigor and breadth of AES evaluation.

629.human_review: By advocating for a broader outlook, the authors promote a more sustainable and impactful direction for AES research, which could lead to more robust and generalizable solutions.
629.llm_review: Methodology and Significance: Methodologically, the paper employs a structured, historically grounded reflection that organizes the field by corpora, metrics, and modeling paradigms (heuristic, ML, neural/LLM). The argumentation is supported by targeted literature and well-motivated use cases (cross-prompt scoring, trait-level modeling, LLM-assisted annotation). In terms of significance, the agenda is timely and impactful: it addresses well-known bottlenecks (ASAP overfitting, narrow metrics, corpus scarcity) and proposes community-level actions (shared tasks, multi-layer annotations, domain-specific pretraining). This has clear potential to influence research priorities and practice in AES.

630.human_review: The writing level is relatively clear and the writing quality is good.
630.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is clearly written and well structured, moving from a compact overview of the current landscape to focused recommendations. Key terms (e.g., traits, within- vs. cross-prompt) are explained in context, examples are concrete, and the narrative is accessible to a broad NLP audience. The inclusion of explicit recommendations, limitations, and ethics sections improves readability and transparency.

631.human_review: I think some of the methods you mentioned in your article, such as heuristic or ML baseline , have already been mentioned in the previous work. You don't have to spend a lot of space describing this part. You need to describe more emphatically the evaluation and optimization methods of AES in the era of pre-trained models or even LLM.
631.llm_review: Methodology, Explanation, and Comparison: (1) The reflection lacks a transparent survey methodology (e.g., inclusion/exclusion criteria, coverage analysis), which makes representativeness and potential selection bias hard to assess. (2) Several claims (e.g., ASAP-specific biases, ESL-specific error impacts, length confounds) are plausible but not backed by new quantitative evidence or systematic analyses. (3) Comparison is underdeveloped: there is limited engagement with alternative evaluation metrics and reliability measures beyond QWK, limited contrast with adjacent reflective/survey work, and little synthesis comparing cross-prompt protocols or rubric alignment strategies across datasets. (4) Some constructs (e.g., traits as prompt-independent features) would benefit from more precise definitions and boundary conditions, and clearer differentiation from existing feature-based or multi-trait models.

632.human_review: As a review article, the way the paper is written is too subjective (such as Line 523-559 and Line571-580), contains a lot of speculation, and does not give enough papers and evidence to support it. In addition, the descriptions of existing papers are too brief, which does not allow readers to fully understand the existing work (such as line 561-569).
632.llm_review: Explanation and Result: The recommendations are largely high-level and not accompanied by empirical demonstrations or pilot case studies, making the practical feasibility and expected effect sizes uncertain. For example, the proposals on LLM-assisted corpus creation/annotation and trait scoring lack concrete protocols (prompt templates, quality-control pipelines, cost–benefit analyses) and validation results (e.g., inter-annotator agreement improvements or time savings). Similarly, suggestions for cross-prompt evaluation and qualitative error analysis would be strengthened by at least small-scale illustrations or ablation-style exemplars to substantiate the claimed benefits.

633.human_review: This paper tackles a novel and important problem of prompt optimization in multi-step tasks.
633.llm_review: Methodology/Novelty/Data/Task: The paper introduces a novel prompt-optimization framework tailored to multi-step agent tasks by combining human-designed feedback rules with an LLM-driven candidate generation loop and a learned heuristic score prediction model to reduce evaluation cost. This goes beyond prior one-step or purely LLM self-reflection approaches and directly targets the long-horizon credit assignment issues in agent settings. The work also curates and standardizes 11 diverse, multi-step environments (web navigation, simulated robotics, grid-based planning, etc.) and releases prompts/resources, filling a clear gap for benchmarking prompt optimization in multi-step agents.

634.human_review: The proposed method, PROMST, is well-motivated by important problems of multi-step prompt optimization, such as the difficulty of prompt engineering and automatic reasoning over errors.
634.llm_review: Methodology: The framework is thoughtfully structured with clear modular roles (TaskLLM for execution, PromptLLM for generation, SumLLM for feedback summarization, GenLLM for candidate creation) and a variance/error-aware gating criterion for the score predictor that balances exploration vs. conservative filtering. The optimization loop uses consistent parent selection and expansion, a sliding context window for long histories, and standardized hyperparameters across all methods for fair comparison. Algorithms are described with sufficient procedural detail, and ablations isolate the contribution of SumLLM and the score model.

635.human_review: The experimental results are satisfactory in quality and quantity, as the authors provide results on multiple tasks and LLMs compared to a sufficient number of baseline methods.
635.llm_review: Methodology/Result/Experiment: Empirical validation is broad and generally strong: PROMST outperforms six recent baselines on average across 11 tasks with multiple LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5: 0.32 vs. 0.27 PromptAgent; GPT-4: 0.69 vs. 0.61), and also shows gains on Claude 3 Opus and Mixtral variants. Ablations substantiate each components utility: the score model improves exploration efficiency and convergence, human feedback rules yield sizable gains over no-rules/self-reflection, and SumLLM further boosts performance. Additional studies analyze cross-LLM transfer, complementarity with Reflexion in multi-trial settings, and preference alignment via alternative score functions, supporting the papers core claims.

636.human_review: The formatting for both the text and the visualizations has room for improvement. I have described a few of them in the suggestions, and I would suggest carefully reviewing the paper to fix them.
636.llm_review: Presentation: The papers readability suffers from formatting/typo issues and uneven exposition. Tables contain apparent errors/inconsistencies (e.g., 0.GRIDWORLD 1, missing or malformed entries), notation proliferates (TaskLLM/PromptLLM/SumLLM/GenLLM) without a concise legend, and several crucial elements (error templates, task specifics) are pushed to the appendix, making it harder to follow the main narrative. Equation 3s terms are not fully explained in the main text, and the intuitive rationale for the gating criterion could be clarified.

637.human_review: It seems that some descriptions and experimental results solely rely on the Appendix, which may confuse the readers of this paper.
637.llm_review: Result/Definition-Detail/Experiment: The evaluation protocol lacks statistical rigor and some key details. Results are reported as best prompt scores without confidence intervals or statistical tests; the number of trials per task, random seed control, and variance are not specified, leaving overfitting and stability unclear. The main metric is sub-goal progress, while full completion is only briefly validated in the appendix; stronger evidence of correlation and task-level sensitivity would help. Some tasks show regressions or marginal improvements (e.g., ScienceWorld with GPT-3.5), but this is not discussed. Important choices (hyper_M=0.8, 4:1 train/test split for the score model, early stopping criteria) lack sensitivity analyses, and compute/API budgets per method are not reported, limiting practical interpretability.

638.human_review: Some explanations on tasks that PROMPST underperforms baseline methods would be helpful.
638.llm_review: Data/Task/Definition-Detail/Result: The approach depends on human-crafted score functions and feedback rules, but their coverage, design effort, and potential biases are not quantified. While template paraphrases were tested, there is no accounting of person-hours, inter-annotator agreement, or how well rules generalize across error types. Alignment claims rely on changing score functions rather than user studies or human preference evaluation. Fairness of initial prompts is partly conflated with method-specific prompts; the procedure to ensure identical starting conditions and task distributions across methods is not fully specified. It is also unclear how many unique instances per environment were used and whether prompts generalize to novel configurations.
