639.human_review: Introduction of the PrideMM dataset fills a critical gap in multimodal meme analysis, particularly for LGBTQ+ related content.
639.llm_review: Data/Task and Analysis: PrideMM is a well-scoped, multi-aspect multimodal dataset (5,063 text-embedded images) with four complementary tasks—hate, target, stance, and humor—capturing the nuanced axes along which memes convey meaning. The authors document collection from multiple platforms (Twitter, Facebook, Reddit) over 2020–2024, rigorous deduplication and OCR-based text extraction, and a three-phase annotation protocol with clear guidelines. Inter-annotator agreement is strong and improves across phases (final Fleiss’ κ ≈ 0.74–0.81 depending on task). The paper provides thorough dataset statistics, acknowledges label imbalance (notably in target types), and supplements the dataset with topic modeling (Appendix) and qualitative error analyses, giving readers a solid understanding of dataset characteristics and challenges.

640.human_review: The dataset is well-annotated for multiple aspects, including hate speech, targets, stance, and humor, offering a holistic approach to meme classification.
640.llm_review: Data/Task: The dataset fills a clear gap by focusing on the LGBTQ+ Pride context with multimodal, multi-aspect labels, which is underrepresented in prior meme resources. The design choices—multi-platform sourcing, contemporary time window, explicit treatment of both humor and harm, and inclusion of target and stance—enable richer study than single-aspect meme datasets. The authors employ careful preprocessing (OCR, noise removal) and deduplication, and provide predefined splits, which will facilitate reproducible benchmarking.

641.human_review: Effective use of the pre-trained CLIP model helps in preserving valuable knowledge and improving classification performance.
641.llm_review: Methodology and Result: MemeCLIP is a pragmatic, lightweight framework that leverages frozen CLIP encoders, modality-specific projection layers to disentangle embeddings, per-modality feature adapters with residual mixing to mitigate overfitting, and a cosine classifier with semantic-aware initialization for class imbalance. The end-to-end single-stage training avoids reliance on augmented data from external captioners. Empirically, MemeCLIP achieves state-of-the-art or best-in-class performance on PrideMM (notably in hate and humor) and transfers well to HarMeme, with consistent gains supported by an ablation study that isolates the contribution of each component.

642.human_review: MemeCLIP is designed to be robust against imbalanced data, a common issue in real-world datasets, through the use of feature adapters and a cosine classifier.
642.llm_review: Data/Task and Result: The authors establish strong, carefully controlled baselines across unimodal and multimodal methods and multiple prior frameworks (CLIP, CLIP-Adapter, MOMENTA, HateCLIPper, ISSUES), providing credible benchmarks for all four tasks. Results convincingly show the value of multimodality over unimodal baselines and demonstrate robustness on the imbalanced, four-class target task (best accuracy), as well as competitive stance performance. Cross-dataset evaluation on HarMeme further supports the dataset’s and method’s practical utility.

643.human_review: Extensive benchmarking against unimodal and multimodal baselines establishes strong performance standards for future research.
643.llm_review: Data/Task and Result: The multi-aspect framing enables a comprehensive evaluation of how memes encode different communicative intents, and the results reflect realistic difficulty gradients across tasks (e.g., stance is harder than hate/humor). The observation that image-only models outperform text-only models, yet are surpassed by multimodal models, empirically validates the dataset’s multimodal design and underscores its relevance for developing and stress-testing multimodal classifiers.

644.human_review: Although the PrideMM dataset is novel, its size (5,063 images) might still be insufficient for training highly complex models without risk of overfitting.
644.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty, and Data/Task: While effective, the methodological novelty is incremental—projection layers, per-modality adapters, cosine classification, and semantic-aware initialization are established ideas adapted to this setting. The fusion is simple, and encoders remain frozen. On the data side, the scope is restricted to LGBTQ+-related memes with OCR-derived text, which may limit generalizability to broader meme genres and to settings where on-image text is sparse, stylized, or non-English. The claim of avoiding extraneous models is somewhat undercut by reliance on a commercial OCR pipeline.

645.human_review: The focus on LGBTQ+ related content may limit the generalizability of the findings to other domains or types of memes.
645.llm_review: Methodology: The design choices prioritize simplicity (element-wise multiplication for fusion, frozen encoders), but the paper does not explore richer cross-modal interactions (e.g., cross-attention, region-text alignment, or text-layout modeling) that could be critical for memes. There is limited discussion of the residual-mixing coefficient α (how it is chosen/validated), adapter capacity, or alternative fusion strategies, and there is no analysis of the impact of OCR errors or text layout on performance.

646.human_review: While qualitative analysis of misclassified samples is provided, a more detailed quantitative analysis could offer deeper insights into the model’s performance.
646.llm_review: Methodology, Result, and Analysis: Some comparisons risk confounds (e.g., MOMENTA uses ViT-B/32 while MemeCLIP and most baselines use ViT-L/14), and statistical significance testing is absent despite modest margins on several metrics. The predefined split yields a relatively small test set, yet per-class results, calibration, or cost-sensitive analyses are not reported—important given class imbalance in target detection. On stance, the gains are mixed (accuracy is lower than HateCLIPper), and the GPT-4 comparison uses only 100 samples with a single prompt, limiting interpretability of that result.

647.human_review: The heavy reliance on CLIP might limit the exploration of other potentially effective multimodal representations and frameworks.
647.llm_review: Methodology: The evaluation omits recent instruction-tuned multimodal LLMs (e.g., LLaVA, InstructBLIP/BLIP-2 variants, Qwen-VL, Kosmos-2) and modern OCRless or layout-aware approaches that could be competitive for meme understanding. The study also does not test end-to-end finetuning of CLIP backbones or more advanced fusion mechanisms, leaving open whether the chosen architecture is near the Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. efficiency.

648.human_review: Comparison with similar existing dataset is missing.
648.llm_review: Data/Task and Comparison: Although the paper compares with several meme datasets and evaluates cross-domain transfer to HarMeme, broader comparative analyses are limited. There is no breakdown by platform, time, or subdomains within LGBTQ+-related content to assess domain drift, and no cross-context tests beyond COVID-19 memes. Moreover, comparisons to multi-aspect text-only LGBTQ+ datasets are not leveraged to quantify how much the image modality adds for each aspect.

649.llm_review: Methodology: Semantic-aware initialization uses a generic prompt template ("A photo of {LABEL}") that may misalign with meme semantics and non-photographic imagery; there is no sensitivity analysis to prompt design or embedding choices. Similarly, the paper lacks ablations on adapter depth/width, α sensitivity, or alternative fusion functions, and does not report training efficiency or inference latency, which would strengthen the case for the proposed architecture’s practicality.

650.human_review: The paper introduces a unique method of globally explaining neural relevance models by constructing a "relevance thesaurus," which is innovative and addresses limitations of local explanations.
650.llm_review: Methodologically novel global explanation for IR: the paper formalizes a relevance thesaurus of query–document term pairs and introduces PaRM to learn pairwise relevance, enabling scalable global explanations where direct feature enumeration would be infeasible.

651.human_review: The proposed method is practically implemented by integrating the relevance thesaurus into BM25 scoring functions to enhance ranking effectiveness and fidelity.
651.llm_review: Well-designed two-stage training procedure: (i) distillation from a cross-encoder with partial query/document masking to learn coarse alignments, and (ii) fine-tuning to calibrate term–term scores in [0,1] tied to the BM25 scoring logic so implied matches remain weaker than exact matches. The integration into BM25 (and use of Lucene/Krovetz tokens) preserves interpretability and safety of the augmentation.

652.human_review: The proposed method identifies and demonstrates the existence of biases (e.g., brand name bias, temporal bias, encoding errors) in ranking models.
652.llm_review: Solid methodological evaluation strategy: the explanation is evaluated extrinsically by augmenting BM25 and QL (BM25T/QLT), and via fidelity (score correlations) to multiple neural retrievers, including models not used for distillation. This design assesses both usefulness and faithfulness of the explanation, not just intrinsic metrics.

653.human_review: The paper concludes that the relevance thesaurus is effective for models trained on similar data. However, this suggests the method may not perform as well across different domains or datasets, potentially limiting its generalization ability and practical applicability.
653.llm_review: Methodology: The approach relies on cross-encoder attention heuristics to derive partial document segments and infers word-level alignments without supervision, which may be brittle. The thesaurus is constrained to top-10K/100K terms with an arbitrary score threshold, uses only the single best document term per query term, and ignores multiword/phrase mappings and OOV terms. Key design choices (masking strategy, candidate vocabulary size, thresholding, choice of taking top-1 vs. top-k matches, calibration) lack ablations, and the method may inherit teacher biases by construction.

654.human_review: Although the paper identifies various biases, it lacks a detailed analysis of the real-world impact of these biases on retrieval performance.
654.llm_review: Result/Analysis: While in-domain gains are clear, out-of-domain results are mixed with notable regressions (e.g., Touche-2020, Quora, ArguAna). Comparisons are limited to BM25/QL and one local-to-global baseline, omitting stronger semantic augmentation or translation-model baselines. Fidelity is measured via Pearson correlation on BM25 top-1k candidates, which may bias conclusions and does not establish causal faithfulness. Bias case studies are illustrative but not quantified for impact under realistic document contexts, and there is limited error analysis of incorrect or spurious thesaurus pairs.

655.human_review: The paper introduces a detailed benchmark for evaluating the resilience of language models against subtle and complex shortcuts. This framework categorizes shortcuts into three main types: occurrence, style, and concept.
655.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Result: The paper proposes a clear, systematic taxonomy of shortcut types (occurrence: single-term/synonym/category; style: register/author; concept: occurrence/correlation) and instantiates it into a benchmark across three representative text classification datasets (Yelp, Go Emotions, Beer). The construction includes an anti-test that reverses shortcut-label associations and a tunable parameter (lambda) to control shortcut strength, enabling graded stress-testing. Results are consistently interpretable: across BERT, multiple Llama models, and robust training baselines, performance drops from test to anti-test reveal reliance on the injected shortcuts, with statistical significance and multiple runs supporting the findings.

656.human_review: The paper provides a well-organized review of related literature, positioning the current study within the broader context of research on spurious correlations and model robustness.
656.llm_review: Methodology/Result/Related Work: The work is well-situated within the spurious correlation literature and organizes prior observations under a unified framework, while also highlighting underexplored shortcut types (e.g., synonym occurrence and concept occurrence/correlation). Methodologically, the paper connects this framework to practical dataset construction and testing protocols. Empirically, it yields informative conclusions—that scaling model size or pretraining quality does not guarantee robustness, and that robust training methods can outperform larger LLMs in specific cases—offering nuanced takeaways beyond headline metrics.

657.human_review: The study evaluates a wide range of models, including traditional small LMs, LLMs, and state-of-the-art robust models.
657.llm_review: Methodology/Evaluation: The evaluation is thoughtfully designed: (a) varying lambda quantifies sensitivity to shortcut strength; (b) anti-test sets systematically flip correlations; (c) disjoint country/city name sets avoid leakage; (d) multiple model families (BERT, Llama2/3) and robust methods (A2R, CR, AFR) are compared; (e) experiments are averaged over multiple runs with significance testing; and (f) SHAP analyses corroborate that shortcut tokens contribute strongly to predictions. These choices strengthen the methodological validity of the evaluation.

658.human_review: The benchmark and experiments are focused solely on text classification tasks, specifically sentiment analysis and emotion prediction. This limits the generalizability of the findings to other NLP tasks, such as machine translation or question answering.
658.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Experiment: The benchmark relies on synthetic interventions (trigger insertion and LLM-driven style rewrites) that can introduce artifacts and potential label drift. Sentences like "I wrote this review in [Country/City]" or LLM-generated Shakespeare/Hemingway passages may be unnatural for the underlying tasks, and the paper does not include systematic human validation of fidelity or label preservation. The scope is also narrow—limited to sentiment/emotion classification on three datasets—so it is unclear how the findings generalize to diverse NLP tasks or naturally occurring shortcut distributions.

659.human_review: The use of LLMs to rewrite text for creating style shortcuts may introduce noise or alter the original meaning of the text.
659.llm_review: Methodology: Several design choices may confound causal interpretation of the anti-test drops. The label-dependent probabilities for inserting triggers change surface properties (length, position, lexical distribution) in a label-specific way, making it hard to disentangle shortcut reliance from generic covariate shifts. The assumption that the chosen trigger ("honestly" and its synonyms) is sentiment-neutral is not validated. For concept correlation, pairing palate and aroma reviews with matched ratings constructs an extreme correlation structure that may not reflect realistic semantics or discourse coherence.

660.human_review: The paper lacks a quantitative analysis of the quality of the modified datasets. Although manual checks were performed, a systematic quantitative evaluation would strengthen the validity of the conclusions.
660.llm_review: Data/Task/Evaluation/Analysis: There is no quantitative assessment of the style transfer fidelity (e.g., automatic style classifiers or human judgments), nor checks that labels remain stable post-rewrite. The evaluation focuses mainly on macro F1 and test–anti-test gaps, with limited qualitative error analysis or per-class breakdowns. The SHAP analysis, while useful, is based on a relatively small sample and does not examine alternative explanation methods or robustness of attributions. These gaps weaken confidence that the benchmark reliably captures only shortcut effects.

661.human_review: While the paper evaluates existing robust models, it does not propose new methods to improve robustness against the identified shortcuts. Introducing novel techniques or strategies would add significant value to the study.
661.llm_review: Methodology/Novelty/Result/Evaluation: While the taxonomy is helpful, the overall novelty feels incremental relative to existing spurious correlation and shortcut-learning frameworks; the main contribution is a synthesized benchmark with mostly expected outcomes (larger models still exploit shortcuts; robust methods help but are not universal). The paper does not introduce new mitigation techniques, and the evaluation omits several strong robust-learning baselines (e.g., GroupDRO, IRM variants, Just-Train-Twice, environment inference methods), limiting the strength of the comparative conclusions.

662.human_review: The study could explore the impact of different hyperparameter settings on model robustness.
662.llm_review: Methodology/Result: Comparability across models is under-specified. Fine-tuning details for LLMs, training budgets, and tokenization/sequence-length controls are deferred or not fully standardized, which can affect robustness comparisons. Variance reporting is inconsistent across all settings, and some statistical markers appear only in selected tables. Without tighter control of training conditions and more thorough reporting, it is difficult to fully attribute observed differences to model robustness rather than optimization noise or dataset construction artifacts.

663.human_review: This paper provides a method to balance two critical aspects (quality & diversity) of dataset curation, which is crucial for improving the robustness of language models in following instructions.
663.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Result: The paper introduces QDIT, a principled and simple joint selection objective that linearly combines a submodular diversity term (facility location over instruction embeddings) with a per-example quality score, controlled by a single tradeoff parameter. The greedy optimization is scalable via lazy evaluations and subsampling, and the method is shown to consistently improve robustness (worst-case performance) while maintaining or improving average performance across multiple instruction-tuning corpora and evaluation suites. The study clearly surfaces and exploits the quality–diversity tradeoff to deliver stronger worst-case results, which is a meaningful outcome for real-world instruction following.

664.human_review: This paper offers detailed experiments on how quality and diversity inference the instruction tuning process. It's beneficial for potential researchers in data selection areas.
664.llm_review: Data/Task/Experiment: The experimental coverage is broad, spanning five datasets (small and large), multiple model sizes, and diverse evaluation protocols (LLM-based pairwise judgments across several benchmarks plus a reward-model HH score). The authors evaluate worst-, average-, and best-case performance, randomize judgment order to reduce positional bias, and report results across varied test sets (InstructEval, WizardLM, Vicuna, Koala, curated ShareGPT). This breadth strengthens the empirical case that the observed gains are not dataset- or metric-specific.

665.human_review: The authors conduct extensive experiments across multiple datasets and models to validate QDIT's effectiveness and versatility. These experiments clearly demonstrate QDIT's superior performance in various scenarios, particularly in improving the worst-case instruction-following capability.
665.llm_review: Methodology/Intuition–Justification–Motivation–Validation/Experiment: The methodological choice of facility location is well-motivated as a coverage proxy, and the paper validates this intuition via qualitative verb–noun distribution analysis, alpha sweeps that smoothly trade quality for diversity, and multiple ablations (data size, base models, alternative QDIT variants). The use of different evaluators (Claude-2/2.1, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and a small human study) and a paired t-test for robustness provide converging evidence. The train–test coverage analysis offers a plausible mechanism for why diversity particularly improves worst-case outcomes.

666.human_review: This paper only compares QDIT with random, quality, and QDIT variant settings, lacking comparisons with other instruction data selection methods such as CaR and DEITA.
666.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Comparison: The comparison set for diversity and joint selection is limited. Important baselines such as DPPs, k-center/coreset, MMR/coverage-based selection, or explicit constrained formulations (e.g., diversity constraints with quality objective) are not directly evaluated. The approach relies on a single embedding space and cosine similarity; there is little exploration of alternative similarity functions or task-specific representations, which could materially affect the facility location objective on heterogeneous instruction datasets.

667.human_review: The experiments presented were primarily conducted on LLaMA-7B, leaving the effectiveness of QDIT on larger models (e.g., 13B) and more advanced versions (e.g., LLaMA2/3 7B) uncertain.
667.llm_review: Methodology/Experiment: The computational story needs more rigor. The stated O(|V|^3K) complexity and the reliance on lazy greedy and subsampling are mentioned, but concrete wall-clock times, hardware details, and approximation quality–speed tradeoffs are sparse, making reproducibility of large-scale selection claims difficult to assess. The selection of alpha per dataset is not systematically detailed (e.g., validation protocol, sensitivity under different reward models), and the dependence on a single reward model trained on Helpful–Harmless data may bias both selection and evaluation via HH score.

668.human_review: As shown in Table 3, QDIT does not consistently outperform across various benchmarks; the improvement margins are quite limited, and in some cases, such as the Alpaca-3K benchmark, QDIT performs worse than the random baseline.
668.llm_review: Data/Task/Result: While worst-case gains are clear, average-case improvements are sometimes modest and occasionally mixed across benchmarks (e.g., some datasets/metrics see parity or small regressions), and best-case performance can decrease. The tasks focus on single-turn instruction following; generalization to multi-turn dialogue, safety-critical prompts, or long-horizon planning is not evaluated. Human evaluation is limited in scale, which constrains conclusions about real user utility.

669.human_review: The experiments in the paper are predominantly based on supervised fine-tuning. It is not yet clear if QDIT is equally effective for more complex alignment techniques, such as RLHF methods like PPO and DPO. I suggest that the authors conduct RLHF experiments using QDIT-SFT models and other baselines to demonstrate that models fine-tuned with QDIT can maintain performance superiority during the RLHF stage.
669.llm_review: Methodology/Experiment/Comparison: The study primarily contrasts against random and quality-only selection (plus two QDIT-inspired variants). It omits comparisons to competitive joint quality–diversity strategies and to contemporary curated or GPT-4–distilled datasets at equivalent training budgets, which would better contextualize practical gains. Sensitivity to the embedding model choice for diversity and to the quality scorer choice is not systematically compared against strong alternatives, limiting the methodological generality.

670.human_review: This work addresses the very important issue of assessing a model's performance in a generative setting, where token-level evaluation metrics fall short. While I am skeptical of training a model to evaluate another model, the increase in performance of using the reward model is positively correlated with an increase in the traditional automatic evaluations.
670.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Evaluation: The paper proposes a principled RLHF-style pipeline for causal event extraction, using a DeBERTa-v3-based evaluator as a sequence-level reward in PPO with a KL penalty to preserve format and prevent drift. Empirically, the RL-tuned FLAN-T5 consistently improves over SFT, sequence tagging, and GPT-3.5/4 across FCR, FinCausal, and SCITE, with the paper reporting an average ~4% gain and better Human Proximal scores. The evaluator itself attains high agreement with human judgments (e.g., ~94% agreement and strong Pearson correlation on FCR) and transfers well across datasets, strengthening the claim that the method improves semantic alignment beyond token-overlap.

671.human_review: The experimental design is robust and there is a significant amount of baseline exploration as well as ablation analysis to understand the degree of usefulness of each individual feature of this work
671.llm_review: Ablation, Experiment, Analysis: The study includes informative ablations on the reward/evaluator, contrasting DeBERTa-Valid with entailment, SentenceTransformer similarity, and LLM-as-a-judge, and further dissecting the importance of reference vs. source inputs. The weak supervision analyses (e.g., 30/50/80% labeled subsets with top-75% confidence filtering per class) show that a 50% labeled fraction recovers performance close to the full reward model, demonstrating label efficiency. Additional analyses (e.g., inter-annotator agreement, the w/o-EM metric to capture semantically correct but non-exact spans) and comprehensive baselines across three datasets enhance the credibility of findings.

672.human_review: The authors tested for domain transferability bay using different datasets and cross-evaluating models
672.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Evaluation: The approach is well-tailored to the task’s ambiguity in span boundaries by optimizing for semantic validity rather than exact string match. A dedicated human-feedback collection platform yields binary valid/invalid labels that are used to train a compact evaluator, which is then integrated into PPO for sequence-level rewards. The method is evaluated on three causal span-from-source datasets (FCR, FinCausal, SCITE), shows cross-dataset evaluator transfer, and introduces a weak-to-strong framework to reduce annotation needs while maintaining high agreement with human judgments.

673.human_review: Using weak supervision for generative causal relation extraction appears to be a promising avenue
673.llm_review: The paper addresses an important and timely problem, articulates the limitations of traditional metrics clearly, and offers a practical, reproducible solution (with code release) that should be useful to researchers building robust, semantics-aware extractors.

674.human_review: I would like to see more analysis on the discrepancies between human annotators and the trained reward model. The authors mention two main culprits: Hallucinations and word mismatches. A more detailed analysis with statistics beyond what is shown in __Pitfalls of Existing Evaluation Schema__ could bring more insight into this.
674.llm_review: Methodology, Analysis: (1) The same learned evaluator is used both as the training reward and as the primary test-time metric (Human Prox.), creating a risk of circularity or reward overfitting; more blinded human evaluation on held-out test sets would mitigate this. (2) The binary valid/invalid scheme may obscure useful granularity (e.g., partially correct extractions, boundary quality, relation correctness vs. span correctness), limiting diagnostic power and potentially conflating error types. (3) Methodological details of PPO are thin (e.g., reward normalization, KL coefficient sweeps, update stability), and there are no statistical significance tests to support improvements. (4) Error analysis is limited; more qualitative breakdowns (e.g., hallucination types, number/attribute errors, boundary shifts) and prompt details for GPT baselines would strengthen the analysis.

675.human_review: It is unclear on how the initial model extractions to train the reward function where obtained. Did you use FLAN-T5 without fine tuning to generate the data for human feedback?
675.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: (1) The approach presumes span-from-source outputs and requires a gold reference at evaluation time; it does not extend to trigger-based or free-form event representations, reducing applicability. (2) The evaluator’s reliance on references (and its degraded performance without them) restricts deployment in settings without gold labels or where references may be noisy. (3) Transfer is only demonstrated across similar English span datasets; cross-domain/language robustness and real-world settings without references remain untested. (4) Although weak supervision reduces labeling, initial human annotation costs and domain adaptation effort can still be substantial.

676.human_review: The paper presents a good framework for empirically experimenting with LLMs hidden states in the context of comparing ICL and IT. I appreciate the authors performing multiple experiments to reduce the variance of their estimates and performing significance testing when required to highlight experimental results.
676.llm_review: Methodology, Experiment, Comparison: The paper proposes a clean, controlled analysis framework that operationalizes three comparable conditions (h_anchor, h_ICL, h_IT) and measures their pairwise relationships via cosine similarity. The experimental design carefully aligns ICL and IT by using identical demonstrations and inference examples, and it controls for confounds such as number of parameter updates when scaling to few-shot (adjusting epochs to keep updates constant). The study includes diverse, well-motivated manipulations (varying demo–query semantic similarity, number of shots, wrong labels, cross-task demonstrations), cross-layer analyses revealing a structured U-shaped convergence pattern, and per-token loss analysis that triangulates the representational findings. Comparisons extend across model sizes (7B/13B) and training regimes (IT vs classic supervised), supporting the central claim with multiple, mutually reinforcing perspectives.

677.human_review: The authors perform a well ablated analysis of the relationship between in context learning and instruction tuning and present various empirical findings on how they compare by varying a) semantic similarity between demonstration and inference examples , b) number of provided demonstrations, c) demonstrating with wrong labels, d) demonstration with different tasks. These findings are also relevant for actual practical uses, such as using ICL for identifying redundant data in instruction tuning.
677.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, Analysis: The work evaluates across three representative tasks (SST-2 sentiment classification, WMT16 EN–CS translation, XSum summarization), and two LLaMA-2 sizes plus LLaMA-2-Chat, supporting generality beyond a single dataset/model. Results consistently show high ICL–IT representational convergence (≈0.9 similarity for SST-2 final-layer states), increasing with demo–query semantic similarity and number of shots, and persisting—though with different anchor relations—on generative tasks. The analysis is careful: semantic similarity is binned with a sentence-transformer, the same inference instances are used across bins, and statistical tests (Wilcoxon) verify that ICL–IT similarity exceeds Anchor–ICL/Anchor–IT on generative tasks. The layer-wise and per-token loss analyses add interpretability and align with the main findings.

678.human_review: Although I appreciate the author's attention to detail and being rigorous in their experiments, I am a bit concerned about the generalizability of these findings on LLMs. In the paper, results on the Llama2 13B model show that the similarity between ICL-IT, Anchor-IT and Anchor-ICL all seem to converge, compared to the baseline Llama2 7B model. This fact alone seems to point that IT/ICL do not have a “significant” impact on the model performance compared to the anchor. However, we’ve seen in literature that Instruction Tuning LLMs does improve instruction following abilities quite a lot (ChatGPT, Llama-2), so this experimental setup seems a bit counter intuitive in this scenario.
678.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment: (1) The central evidence rests almost entirely on cosine similarity of the last-token hidden state; this single metric and locus may be sensitive to prompt formatting, positional effects, and anisotropy, and may not capture behavioral equivalence. Complementary representational metrics (e.g., CKA/CCA, RSA), coverage of multiple token positions, and logit/KL comparisons would strengthen the claim that ICL acts as implicit IT. (2) The causal link between representational convergence and task behavior is not thoroughly tested: performance metrics and their correlation with s_ICL–IT are only partially reported (e.g., wrong-label IT), and more systematic accuracy/quality evaluations across manipulations would contextualize the representational results. (3) Some controls are underexplored: ablations over LoRA ranks/target modules, optimizer/lr sensitivity, prompt templates/length, and decoding settings are limited; the 13B finding where Anchor–ICL/Anchor–IT are high suggests instruction-only zero-shot capability confounds the interpretation, but this is not isolated via additional controls. (4) The cross-task demonstration result (translation demos for sentiment inference) is interpreted as no effect, but the convergence of all three similarities may indicate saturation or insensitivity of the chosen metric rather than a true null effect. Additional causal interventions (e.g., shuffling/masking demo tokens) and reporting confidence intervals for all conditions would make the experimental conclusions more robust.

679.human_review: This paper focuses on the zero-shot relation extraction task, which is significant for real-world relation extraction. The proposed method could have a high potential to solve relation extraction in low-resources.
679.llm_review: The paper tackles a timely and practical problem: relation extraction with only natural-language relation definitions and an unlabeled corpus. The proposed REPAL framework smartly leverages LLMs for seed synthesis and a small NLI-style classifier for efficient inference, and it shows substantial empirical gains over zero-shot baselines across two benchmarks.

680.human_review: The proposed method overall makes sense to me. Simply leveraging the LLMs for relation extraction could lead to low-quality RE results so the authors change the role of LLMs to produce some seed data. Further iterative improvement and fine-tuning are conducted to ensure the quality of the SLM-based RE model.
680.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: The work introduces a realistic definition-only zero-shot RE setting and a well-motivated three-stage methodology: (i) definition-driven positive seed generation (with prompt variants to cover brief/medium/implicit patterns) plus unlabeled-corpus negatives; (ii) fine-tuning a bidirectional SLM (NLI-style) for task specialization; (iii) feedback-driven iterative refinement that uses both SLM inference on unlabeled data and synthesis history to expand positive pattern coverage and to craft targeted/near-miss negative definitions and instances. The evaluation protocol over DefOn-FewRel and DefOn-Wiki-ZSL (constructed from FewRel/Wiki-ZSL with Wikidata-derived definitions and an unlabeled corpus) is appropriate for the setting, and ablations substantiate the contribution of each component.

681.human_review: Overall, this paper is well-written and easy to follow.
681.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is clearly written and well organized, with an intuitive overview figure of the pipeline, explicit prompt templates, and detailed ablations (effects of templates, seed sizes, and feedback). The motivation linking few-shot coverage limitations to definition-driven synthesis is articulated clearly, and the Limitations/Ethics sections are transparent about assumptions and trade-offs.

682.human_review: I have concerns about the sensitivity of the proposed method. Due to the wide applications of LLMs in the proposed method, it is applied to generate positive instances and improve the predicted inferences. The performance may rely heavily on the designed prompt and the generation quality of LLMs. I suggest the authors include a section discussing the generalization of different LLMs as backbones for the proposed method.
682.llm_review: Methodology: The approach relies on several assumptions that may introduce bias or confounds. (1) Negative sampling from the unlabeled corpus assumes a low positive rate and can inject mislabeled positives; although feedback aims to mitigate this, the noise rate is not quantified, and probability-range sampling choices are not rigorously justified. (2) The framework depends on proprietary GPT-3.5/4 for both positive and negative definition/instance synthesis, raising reproducibility and controllability concerns; there is limited analysis of how performance varies with open-source LLMs or different prompt/cost budgets. (3) Baseline comparisons mix settings: multi-way zero-shot baselines are not evaluated under the same definition-only binary setting, and the Macro-F1 comparison uses REPAL-synthesized data, which can confound fairness. (4) The SLM choice (NLI-style RoBERTa) is reasonable but not contrasted against alternative extractors or calibration strategies; error analysis focuses on seed size and prompts but less on failure modes (e.g., entity-type confusions) and label quality of synthesized data.

683.human_review: The authors could show more about the potential usage of REPAL on low-resource relation extraction to strengthen its significance.
683.llm_review: Significance: While the definition-only zero-shot RE setting is interesting, the broader impact is tempered by evaluation on repurposed datasets with modified definitions and sentence-level scope; it is unclear how well the gains transfer to real-world, noisier, or document-level RE scenarios where definitions may be incomplete or unavailable. The reliance on proprietary LLMs may limit adoption, and without a standardized benchmark for this setting, it is difficult for the community to compare methods fairly. Improvements on the noisier Wiki-ZSL variant are smaller, suggesting sensitivity to annotation noise.

684.human_review: The introduction of the McMarket dataset provides a valuable resource for research in multilingual and cross-market product-based question answering. This dataset covers a wide range of languages and marketplaces, significantly enhancing the scope of research in this area.
684.llm_review: The paper defines a clear and timely task (MCPQA) that formalizes multilingual cross-market product QA, where information from a resource-rich auxiliary market supports answering questions in a resource-scarce main market. On the data side, McMarket is a substantial contribution: it spans 13 marketplaces and 8 languages, includes questions and reviews (with translations for non-English content), and supports two concrete subtasks (review-based answer generation and product-related question ranking). This pairing of a well-motivated task with a large, realistic dataset fills a gap in multilingual, cross-market PQA.

685.human_review: The paper provides in-depth analysis of the dataset and the performance of different models. It includes human evaluation of LLM-generated data, which adds credibility to the quality of the annotations and the effectiveness of the proposed methods.
685.llm_review: Data/Task: McMarket is large-scale (millions of questions and reviews across 13 markets, 8 languages), includes both questions and reviews, and provides two LLM-labeled subsets tailored to answer generation (McMarket_r) and question ranking (McMarket_q). Result: Across both subtasks, cross-market methods consistently outperform single-market baselines, and LLMs (e.g., Llama-2/Flan-T5) outperform lexical and non-LLM neural baselines, demonstrating clear utility of the proposed setting. Evaluation: The authors report standard text generation metrics for AG (BLEU-4/ROUGE-L) and ranking metrics for QR (MRR/P@3), compare single vs cross-market and Exact vs non-Exact settings, and validate GPT-4 labels via human assessment (e.g., 0.76/0.83 IAA; 97.6% F1 on QR labels; 61.8% of GPT-4 AG answers judged better than human ground truth). Analysis: The paper provides informative temporal and answerability analyses (showing cross-market resources increase answerability, especially in low-resource markets), hyperparameter sensitivity (K retrieval size), and multilingual comparisons (translated vs non-translated), which together strengthen the claims and offer guidance for future work.

686.human_review: While human assessments are used to evaluate the quality of annotations, there is a lack of direct user feedback on the actual usefulness and relevance of the generated answers in practical e-commerce settings.
686.llm_review: Data/Task, Evaluation: The evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE) for AG, which are known to be weak proxies for factuality and usefulness in PQA; there is no dedicated human evaluation of model-generated answers beyond validating GPT-4 labels. For QR, the test labels are produced by GPT-4, which can introduce bias and evaluation circularity (e.g., models optimized toward LLM-friendly outputs may score better). Moreover, LLM annotations are done on English-translated content, potentially conflating translation quality with task difficulty and limiting insight into true multilingual performance. Statistical significance testing and detailed error analyses are limited.

687.human_review: The paper mentions the use of professional translation tools and LLMs for data annotation, but there is a risk of inconsistency and quality issues in the translated and annotated data, which could impact the overall performance of the models.
687.llm_review: Data/Task: The dataset is restricted to the Electronics category on Amazon and excludes three marketplaces (es/it/de) from the main benchmarks, which constrains generalizability across domains and languages. The reliance on machine translation (DeepL for QA, fine-tuned NLLB for reviews) introduces noise and domain-specific biases that may unevenly affect languages and marketplaces; while some translation assessment is mentioned, its impact on task performance is not systematically quantified. There is also some ambiguity around data licensing statements, which should be clarified for downstream use.

688.human_review: The use of large, complex models like LLMs might lead to overfitting, especially given the size and specificity of the dataset. The paper could benefit from a discussion on strategies to prevent overfitting and ensure robust performance.
688.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task: Several pipeline choices may affect validity but are under-specified or insufficiently ablated: (i) the retrieval of "similar items" in cross-market settings (and the distinction between Exact vs non-Exact) may admit subtle leakage or mismatches; (ii) the pre-filtering of answerable questions using a prior classifier can introduce selection bias into AG results; (iii) GPT-4 annotations performed only on translated English undermine the multilingual nature of the task and may obscure challenges specific to non-English content; and (iv) the approach does not explore stronger cross-lingual alignment or domain adaptation techniques that could better leverage multilingual signals, especially for non-Latin languages.

689.human_review: The design of the hybrid framework is comprehensive and meticulous, and it adopts an innovative proxy method of symbolic reasoning to elevate the quality of explanation. The utilization of Isabelle/HOL theorem prover and Neo-Davidsonian event semantics deserves acknowledgment, which enhances the entire process.
689.llm_review: Methodology and exposition are strong and well-structured. The paper introduces a clear neuro-symbolic pipeline that combines LLM-generated explanations with Isabelle/HOL proofs, using Neo-Davidsonian event semantics to preserve predicate–argument structure in formalization. It concretely specifies how premises/hypotheses become theorems, explanations become axioms, and how proof tactics (e.g., blast) are orchestrated. The syntax refiner is explicitly scoped to type-unification vs. other syntax errors, and the iterative feedback loop is carefully described (error extraction, failed steps mapping to axioms, pruning redundancy, targeted refinement). Overall, the definitions, architectural choices, and step-by-step description make the approach interpretable and replicable.

690.human_review: The authors have conducted a series of experiments to show that the proposed method can effectively improve the logic validity of existing annotated explanations. Ablation studies are also presented to discuss the impact of autoformalisation on performance.
690.llm_review: The motivation is compelling (limitations of crowd-sourced explanations and surface-level language metrics), and the validation is multifaceted. Experiments span three datasets with rising reasoning complexity (e-SNLI, QASC, WorldTree) and five LLMs, complemented by ablations that isolate the autoformalization component (using GPT-4) and show clear gains. The study reports iteration dynamics, syntax-error reductions, and human judgments of factuality/triviality, and provides quantitative improvements in logical validity (e.g., GPT-4 from 36%→84% on e-SNLI, 12%→55% on QASC, 2%→37% on WorldTree), substantiating the claimed benefits of theorem-prover feedback for refinement.

691.human_review: It should be stated clearly what language generation metrics are used in previous studies, why they could be flawed for this task, and how they would be correlated with the proposed metrics.
691.llm_review: Evaluation scope leaves several gaps. (1) The sample size (300 items) and selection strategy may limit statistical power and generalizability; there are no statistical significance tests or uncertainty estimates on key metrics. (2) The main metric (provability) conflates explanation quality with autoformalization quality; while the ablation helps, stronger controls or gold logical forms would better disentangle these factors. (3) Human evaluation is limited to factuality and triviality for two models and does not assess faithfulness to a model’s internal reasoning or the completeness/minimality of explanations from a human perspective. (4) Efficiency is underreported: wall-clock time, prover timeouts, and cost per iteration are not quantified, making it hard to assess practicality.

692.human_review: This paper is missing some baseline experiments. As stated in the paper, existing work possesses inherent issues, and the paper appears to be deficient in certain effect comparisons. The most straightforward notion is to conduct a comparison with the baseline of directly employing LLM for refinement and additionally using the feedback based on the metrics used in previous studies.
692.llm_review: Limited comparative analysis weakens the empirical case. There is no head-to-head comparison with alternative verification/refinement baselines (e.g., LLM self-critique without a prover, self-consistency/majority voting, differentiable logic reasoners, SMT/ASP checks) or with other proof assistants (Lean/Coq) to justify Isabelle/HOL as the backbone. The choice of Neo-Davidsonian semantics is not compared against simpler FOL templates or other semantic formalisms. Experimental controls across models (e.g., token budgets, prompting budgets, repeated runs) are not detailed, and there is no statistical comparison to prior neuro-symbolic explanation-verification systems, making it difficult to place the gains w.r.t. state of the art.

693.human_review: The introduction of the Structure Guided Prompt is innovative, providing a systematic approach to improve LLMs’ multi-step reasoning.
693.llm_review: Methodology: The paper presents a clear three-stage prompting framework (graph construction, task-specific planning, and execution) that operationalizes structured reasoning within LLMs. By explicitly inducing a concept graph from text and then guiding traversal with a plan, the approach mirrors human graph-based reasoning and provides a principled decomposition of multi-step reasoning.

694.human_review: The framework is tested on diverse datasets (CLUTRR, BBH, HotpotQA, and Entailment Bank), demonstrating its robustness and versatility.
694.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result: The framework is instantiated across diverse reasoning task categories—relation prediction (CLUTRR), entity prediction over dynamic KGs (BBH tracking shuffled objects), complex entity prediction (HotpotQA bridging), graph sorting (BBH logical deduction), graph query (BBH tables/colored objects), and logical inference (EntailmentBank). Using a unified template with task-specific planning strategies, the method yields consistent improvements over zero-shot CoT on both GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, with especially large gains on CLUTRR (longer-hop relations) and dynamic tracking where explicit state updates are beneficial.

695.human_review: The experimental results show substantial performance gains in various reasoning tasks compared to baseline methods.
695.llm_review: Result, Experiment: The empirical evaluation spans four benchmarks and multiple sub-tasks, with analyses stratified by path length (hops) and number of objects. The plots show the method scales more gracefully as reasoning depth increases and substantially boosts accuracy on dynamic state-tracking (the paper cites up to 146% improvement over GPT-4 w/ 0-CoT). The authors include prompts, case studies, and an error analysis noting conclusion-phase mistakes, increasing transparency of the experimental setup.

696.human_review: The three-stage prompting framework is well-explained, making it easy to understand.
696.llm_review: Methodology: Avoiding reliance on external KGs while still leveraging graph structure is a pragmatic design choice that reduces the risk of irrelevant information injection. The planning stage provides reusable strategy templates (e.g., path tracing, temporal updates, decomposition into sub-questions), making the approach modular and adaptable across tasks in a zero-shot setting.

697.human_review: The main paper lacks detailed descriptions of the experimental settings with GPTs and the specific prompts used in the reasoning tasks, which are crucial for reproducibility and understanding the methodology.
697.llm_review: Methodology, Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Experiment: Critical implementation details of the graph induction step are underspecified: how entities/relations are extracted (schema, canonicalization, coreference resolution), how temporal updates are represented, and how ambiguity is resolved. The experiments lack quantitative evaluation of induced graph quality, ablations isolating each stage’s contribution, and reporting of decoding settings (temperature, sampling, self-consistency), number of trials/seeds, or significance testing. Without these, reproducibility and robustness are hard to assess.

698.human_review: Appendix Length: The appendix is more than double the length of the main content of the paper, indicating that a significant portion of important details may/can not be included in the main sections of the paper.
698.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: The exposition overstates “task-agnostic” while relying on task-specific planning prompts, without a precise definition of what is shared vs. specialized. The paper does not formalize the graph representation (relation inventory, handling of attributes/events) or clearly distinguish it from existing semantic structures (e.g., AMR, dependency graphs). The taxonomy of task categories and the mapping from natural language questions to planning strategies would benefit from more rigorous definitions and examples.

699.human_review: Complexity in Real-World Scenarios: Constructing and maintaining Knowledge Graphs can be complex and expensive, which may limit the practical applicability of the proposed framework.
699.llm_review: Methodology: The approach hinges on the LLM’s ability to accurately construct KGs from long inputs; errors or omissions (admitted for HotpotQA) propagate and degrade performance. There is no iterative repair/verification of the KG or the final conclusion beyond a suggested future idea, and no mechanism like self-consistency, retrieval augmentation, or tool use to mitigate extraction errors. The absence of ablations (e.g., graph vs. no-graph, planning variants) and of automated planning selection leaves uncertainty about the method’s core drivers.

700.human_review: The framework struggles with tasks requiring precise, logical order and distinguishing between premises and conclusions.
700.llm_review: Methodology: Scalability concerns are unaddressed. The framework’s multi-stage prompts increase token budget and latency, and long inputs (e.g., HotpotQA) already stress context windows, leading to incomplete graphs. There is no measurement of computational or inference cost, nor an automated method to choose planning strategies for new tasks, which weakens the claim of generality and raises questions about deployment feasibility.

701.human_review: The methodology and dataset used for different contributions need to be presented in a better manner.
701.llm_review: Methodology, Contribution, Data/Task: The contribution appears incremental relative to Tree/Graph-of-Thoughts, Least-to-Most, ReAct, and program-of-thought approaches that also impose structure and search over reasoning. The experimental comparison omits these stronger baselines and relies only on (w/ and w/o) zero-shot CoT, which limits the strength of the empirical claim. The tasks are mostly synthetic or controlled (BBH, CLUTRR), with limited real-world breadth beyond HotpotQA bridging, and evaluations use only closed-source models, further constraining generalizability and reproducibility.

702.human_review: The authors introduce LoRAN, a simple and straightforward way of adding non-linearity to LoRA based adapter methods which enhance the adapter’s ability to model the underlying finetuning function without introducing extra parameters.
702.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a simple yet broadly applicable modification to LoRA by inserting a parameter-free non-linear transformation f after the low-rank product (DeltaW = f(BA)). The specific Sinter function is identity-preserving for small amplitudes, which makes it a safe drop-in that enhances representational capacity without destabilizing training. The design is model-agnostic and integrates cleanly with existing PEFT pipelines (demonstrated with QLoRA) without adding trainable parameters or memory footprint, and with only minor compute overhead. This is a clear, practical methodological contribution likely to be adopted by practitioners.

703.human_review: To highlight the effectiveness of their method, the authors also introduce an example for a nonlinearity which can be used for LoRAN - $\mathbb{S}inter$ - and show that their method leads to improvements on top of the QLoRA baseline on summarization and classification tasks.
703.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Comparison: The method is evaluated across multiple LLM backbones (Flan-T5-Large, Falcon-7B, Llama-2 7B/13B) and two tasks (SAMSum summarization, 20 Newsgroups classification), consistently outperforming the QLoRA baseline. The gains, while modest at rank 64, are consistent (e.g., up to +0.76 ROUGE-L on SAMSum and +1.22 accuracy on 20 Newsgroups), and become more pronounced at lower rank (r=8, +1.95 accuracy), supporting the methodological claim that non-linear transformation helps when adapter capacity is tight. An ablation comparing Sinter against Identity (reducing to QLoRA) and Swish variants shows that the choice of non-linearity matters and that Sinter is the strongest among those tested. The class-wise analysis on 20 Newsgroups further suggests the approach improves fine-grained discrimination among closely related classes, adding interpretive value beyond aggregate scores.

704.human_review: In experimental section 3.1, the authors mention using $A = 5e-5$ and $\omega = 1e-4$. However, it is not clear from the paper how these hyperparameters were chosen. Specifying how the parameters were swept, or how different values influence performance would be very useful for users of LoRAN.
704.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment: The central claim that the non-linear transformation can "match the full-rank model capacity" is not theoretically substantiated and is not empirically demonstrated by comparison to full fine-tuning; the argument about rank post non-linearity remains informal. Experimental support is limited to two datasets with relatively small improvements at r=64, and there is no statistical significance analysis or variance reporting across seeds, making it hard to rule out noise for several small deltas (e.g., +0.06 ROUGE-2). The hyperparameters governing the non-linearity (A, omega) are fixed without sensitivity analysis or learning strategies, and it is unclear how robust results are to these choices. Finally, the evaluation is conducted only within the QLoRA setting; it would strengthen methodological claims to disentangle benefits from 4-bit quantization and to include plain LoRA and full-precision LoRA baselines.

705.human_review: In experimental section 3.2, the authors mention that LoRAN enhances the performance of downstream tasks significantly. However, it is not clear how the significance of these improvements has been calculated. It would be great if the authors could use different seeds for the QLoRA experiments to estimate the variance of downstream metrics and estimate the statistical significance of these improvements.
705.llm_review: Result, Experiment: The empirical scope is narrow: only SAMSum and 20 Newsgroups are used, with no instruction-following, reasoning, or multilingual tasks to demonstrate broader utility. Comparisons omit several strong and relevant PEFT baselines such as AdaLoRA, DyLoRA, DoRA, LoKr/IA3 variants, and full fine-tuning, so it is unclear how competitive the results are against the current state of the art. The paper does not report multi-run averages, standard deviations, or significance tests, and some reported gains are very small or even negative on specific metrics (e.g., ROUGE-L on Flan-T5-Large), limiting confidence in the generality of the improvement. Reporting of training cost and latency differences is minimal and could better quantify the practical trade-offs.

706.human_review: This paper proposes a new self-jailbreaking method called IRIS, which enables a single language model to act as both the attacker and the target. The iterative refinement and self-explanation steps are distinctive compared to previous jailbreaking methods.
706.llm_review: Methodology: IRIS is a simple yet effective pipeline that unifies attacker and target, leveraging self-explanation during iterative prompt refinement and a rate-and-enhance stage to push responses to maximum harmfulness. The method is fully black-box, uses interpretable prompt manipulations rather than opaque suffixes, and achieves strong query efficiency with minimal hyperparameter tuning. The algorithmic structure (feedback loop with explicit EXPLAIN and MODIFY queries, followed by RATE+ENHANCE) is well-articulated and operationally clear.

707.human_review: IRIS achieves near-perfect jailbreak success rates (98% on GPT-4, 92% on GPT-4 Turbo) with significantly fewer queries (under 7 on average) compared to state-of-the-art methods like TAP and PAIR. The experiments comprehensively validate the effectiveness of IRIS.
707.llm_review: Intuition/Motivation/Validation and Experiment: The paper is well-motivated by two underexplored ideas—self-jailbreaking (can capable models help subvert their own guardrails?) and refinement of generated outputs (not just prompts). Validation is convincing within scope: IRIS substantially outperforms PAIR and TAP on AdvBench Subset with far fewer queries; a transfer study probes cross-model behavior; and ablations separate the contribution of iterative refinement versus RATE+ENHANCE. Human evaluation (rather than LLM-as-judge) is a thoughtful choice aligned with recent critiques.

708.human_review: The paper is well-organized and clearly written. The figures, such as the diagram of the IRIS method in Figure 1, effectively illustrate the proposed approach. Notations and formulations are properly defined, enhancing the readability of the paper.
708.llm_review: Presentation: The exposition is clear and accessible. The paper provides an intuitive diagram, concrete pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and unambiguous definitions of metrics and success criteria. Experimental settings (model versions, decoding parameters) are specified, aiding reproducibility. The narrative flow from motivation to method, experiments, and limitations is coherent and easy to follow.

709.human_review: While IRIS introduces a new self-jailbreaking method, the paper does not provide a clear justification for why and how the proposed modifications, such as the iterative refinement and self-explanation steps, effectively address the limitations of existing jailbreaking methods.
709.llm_review: Intuition/Motivation/Validation: (1) The core mechanism—why self-explanation helps bypass guardrails—is asserted but not deeply analyzed; there is little cognitive or alignment-oriented explanation beyond empirical observation. (2) The rejection heuristic (e.g., classify as reject if <20 words) is ad hoc and not justified; it could misclassify safe-but-long refusals or short-but-harmful outputs, undermining the conceptual validity of the loop. (3) Validation rests on a small dataset (50 prompts) with a single in-house annotator and no reported inter-annotator agreement on the full set, limiting confidence in generality. (4) The threat model and ecological validity of instructing the model to rate its own harmfulness and then maximize it are under-justified; the paper could clarify how this maps to realistic attacker behaviors and guardrail designs.

710.human_review: The experiments in this paper only compare IRIS with TAP and PAIR. More recent and stronger baselines need to be added to reflect the comprehensiveness of the experiments. The authors should also provide a more detailed discussion about the intended incremental contributions of IRIS above and beyond existing research.
710.llm_review: Contribution, Experiment, Comparison: (1) The claimed near-perfect success is demonstrated on a narrow benchmark and older closed-source model snapshots; broader coverage (newer checkpoints, open-source models, and diverse safety layers) is limited, tempering the generality and impact. (2) Comparisons rely partly on results reported from prior work rather than re-running baselines under identical settings and query budgets, which risks unfairness; no statistical significance or variance is reported. (3) The evaluation omits stronger or more recent baselines/defenses and does not assess robustness to provider-side mitigations or detection mechanisms (e.g., prompt-template filtering), despite the method’s templates being fixed. (4) The RATE+ENHANCE step inflates ASR by explicitly instructing the target to produce maximally harmful content—arguably an unrealistic attacker affordance—yet the paper does not provide alternative, more naturalistic evaluation protocols or costs analyses to contextualize the contribution.

711.human_review: The paper shows that the models enhanced with DEFT show improved alignment capabilities and generalization abilities compared to previous methods. This suggests that DEFT can effectively maintain or improve a model’s performance while better adhering to desired human values.
711.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The paper proposes a simple, model-agnostic distribution reward that can be plugged into existing fine-tuning methods (PRO, DPO) to guide optimization at the distribution level while simultaneously enabling data filtering. Empirically, this yields consistent improvements over the corresponding baselines on HH-RLHF across reward-model scores, BLEU/BART, and human evaluation, and it preserves or improves generalization on MT-Bench, especially when combined with DPO.

712.human_review: One significant advantage noted is the reduction in training time when using DEFT. This can make the process more efficient
712.llm_review: Methodology: The discrepancy distribution (positive–negative token-frequency subtraction) and the resulting distribution reward are conceptually clean and easy to implement. They require only forward passes to precompute per-sample scores for filtering and add a single scalar term to the training loss. The ablation study cleanly separates the gains from the high-quality subset and from the distribution-guidance term, and the reward-trajectory analysis illustrates how the guidance steers the model during training.

713.human_review: Data filtering is quite important and this paper proposes new method on automatic filtering instead of labor intense human filtering
713.llm_review: Methodology and Data/Task: The data filtering strategy is well-motivated and practical: ranking samples by the distribution reward identifies preference-dense, harder examples, and the data-volume study shows that a small subset (top 5% lowest scores) balances diversity and noise, reducing training cost while improving alignment metrics. Demonstrating applicability across pairwise (DPO) and listwise/contrastive (PRO) settings supports the frameworks generality.

714.human_review: How are the positive and negative distributions, Q_{+} and Q_{-}, derived? Are these distributions based on word frequencies from the data? Can you provide a more detailed explanation?
714.llm_review: Data/Task and Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: The study is limited to HH-RLHF (helpfulness/harmlessness) and a single base model (Llama3-8B), which constrains claims of broad applicability. Several definitional and implementation details need clarification: whether the discrepancy distribution is computed per-sample or aggregated, how tokenization choices and sequence-length normalization affect frequency subtraction, how negative values in the distribution are scaled, how the averaging of log-probabilities over positions approximates a stable output distribution, and how c is selected and tuned. Without these details, reproducibility and interpretability are reduced.

715.human_review: It would be beneficial to elaborate on how word frequency effectively addresses distributional rewards. Considering that the context in which words are used may be more critical than the words themselves, do you have any insights or statistical evidence to support this approach?
715.llm_review: Result: While overall improvements are reported, some subset-level results are mixed (e.g., on D3 the harmless reward decreases for DEFT-DPO), and no statistical significance, confidence intervals, or multi-seed variance are provided. Efficiency claims (e.g., significantly reduced training time) are not quantified in wall-clock hours or GPU-days. Heavy reliance on proxy metrics (reward models, BLEU/BART for dialogue) limits the strength of the conclusions.

716.human_review: I wonder if the proposed framework is more effective when applied to reinforcement learning-based alignment methods such as PPO, beyond just comparing it with DPO or PRO.
716.llm_review: Methodology and Comparison: The comparison set is narrow. There are no head-to-head results against strong contemporary alignment and preference-learning baselines (e.g., IPO, KTO, ORPO, RLAIF variants) and no comparisons to established data selection/filtering strategies (random subsets, loss- or margin-based selection, diversity-aware or influence-based sampling). This makes it difficult to attribute gains specifically to the proposed distribution-guided approach.

717.human_review: As mentioned in Appendix A, the inference length is set to 128. Were the MT Bench results also based on this length? It seems that a length of 128 might be insufficient for obtaining good score in the MT Bench evaluation.
717.llm_review: Data/Task, Result, and Evaluation: The pipeline risks circularity and bias: a reward model is used to construct/score training data and another reward model is used for evaluation; references are augmented by ChatGPT; GPT-4 is used as a judge only on D3; and human evaluation lacks details on annotator training, guidelines, and inter-annotator agreement. These choices can inflate apparent gains and complicate cross-method fairness. Additional independent evaluations (e.g., Arena-style pairwise battles, safety benchmarks, or human studies with rigorous protocols) would strengthen claims.

718.human_review: Have you considered using larger or more advanced reward models? If so, is there any notable difference in performance?
718.llm_review: Methodology and Result: The discrepancy distribution is based on token-frequency differences, which may overemphasize stylistic markers (e.g., sorry, refusal phrases) rather than substantive preference reasoning. The inner product with averaged log-probabilities could incentivize superficial token-level shortcuts, potentially explaining some gains while risking degraded robustness. The paper lacks tests controlling for stylistic tokens, stopword/subword effects, or rephrasing robustness, and does not report safety-specific stress tests to verify that improvements are not just surface-level.

719.human_review: The difficulty of evaluation NFQA lies in the lack of clear borderline of correctness. Putting too many criteria or constitutions in the evaluation prompts would hinder LLMs from upvoting the better answers due to commonly known problems such as recency bias and limitations in prompts lengths. **LINKAGE tackles this by transferring these onerous meta-instructions into multi-grade ground truths or synthetic reference answers, which forms a clear spectrum for LLMs to rank the candidate answers.**
719.llm_review: Methodology and Evaluation: The paper introduces a clear and practical listwise LLM-as-judge framework (LINKAGE) for NFQA, where a candidate is ranked among a curated list of varied-quality references. The formulation is well-motivated by learning-to-rank literature and cleanly subsumes pairwise when the list has a single reference. The reference-list construction is carefully specified for three realistic scenarios (multi-grade GT, single-grade GT, and no GT). Evaluation is thorough across three NFQA datasets (ANTIQUE, TREC-DL-NF, WebGLM) and two evaluator families (Mistral and ChatGPT), with consistent improvements over strong baselines (automatic metrics, pointwise, pairwise) measured via Kendall’s tau, Spearman, and Pearson. The study also controls for pairwise position bias and shows that providing references helps even pointwise scoring, supporting the central premise that multiple graded references clarify evaluation criteria.

720.human_review: Comprehensive experiments, ablation study and case study could to some degree support their claims.
720.llm_review: Ablation and Experiment: The paper includes informative ablations: (a) few-shot vs zero-shot prompting (few-shot generally helps), (b) reference list composition (length and grade distribution), showing uniform sampling across grades works best, and that list length interacts with dataset quality/noise, (c) robustness to randomization with small standard deviations, and (d) scenarios with single/no ground truth where LINKAGE still outperforms alternatives. Additional analyses—accuracy of identifying best/worst answers on WebGLM and a qualitative case study—illustrate concrete failure modes of similarity metrics and pairwise judging, and the gains from listwise ranking. The experiments also compare different evaluator models (Mistral vs ChatGPT), highlighting generality.

721.human_review: The proposed method is a LLM-based evaluation method. LLM-as-Judge is biased in evaluating predictions from different LLMs. Analysis should be added with different (open-weight) models, **which could be more appreciated by the open-source community**.
721.llm_review: Methodology, Evaluation, and Analysis: (1) The approach relies on LLM-generated references when single/no gold exists; there is limited quality control or human validation of these synthetic references beyond indirect correlation measures, risking circularity if the judge favors the generator’s style. (2) Potential evaluator bias is insufficiently mitigated: the same family of models is involved in generating references (GPT-4/3.5, Llama) and judging (Mistral/ChatGPT), and self-enhancement or cross-model stylistic bias could influence rankings; cross-judge evaluation or human tie-breaks would strengthen claims. (3) Empirical scope is narrow: TREC-DL-NF has only 55 NF questions and WebGLM uses 50 annotated cases; significance testing and inter-annotator agreement for human labels are not reported, making it hard to assess the reliability of observed gains. (4) Cost/latency and context-length scaling are not analyzed; listwise prompts grow with |R| and candidate length, yet the method’s efficiency claims vs pairwise are not backed by runtime/token-usage measurements or sensitivity to longer candidate lists. (5) Prompt sensitivity (temperature 0.8) and calibration from ranks to final scores are under-explored; guidance on stable prompting, reference-list size selection, and how to map ranks into actionable metrics for system development would help adoption.

722.human_review: The proposed method is, to some degree, **lack of novelty**. From the first point of the strength part, this could be perceived as a choice of engineering method in evaluation question answering with more subjectiveness, which is believed to be mentioned in prior works. Besides, I do not see the essential difference between LINKAGE and the pointwise approach with references as they are both input with sorted lists of references.
722.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty, and Related Work: While the listwise framing is well-motivated, the conceptual novelty appears incremental—adapting established listwise LTR ideas to LLM-as-judge for NFQA. The paper could better position itself relative to prior LLM evaluation frameworks that employ ranking/tournament or discussion/debate mechanisms and synthetic preference data, clarifying how LINKAGE differs in assumptions, bias mitigation, and scalability. The generation of varied-quality references via prompting echoes existing synthetic preference construction; a deeper comparison and justification for the specific design choices (e.g., using GPT-4 to seed golden answers, multi-model reference generation, chosen grade scales) would strengthen the novelty and related-work positioning. A brief theoretical or empirical rationale for why listwise prompting improves calibration beyond increased context could also sharpen the contribution.

723.human_review: This paper introduces the first pitch-based similarity representation, a novel and innovative approach that will significantly facilitate tone research.
723.llm_review: The paper proposes a novel representation, Tone2Vec, that maps five-scale tone transcriptions to smooth pitch-trajectory curves and uses the area between curves as a principled similarity measure. This enables the first automatic approach to tone transcription (predicting five-scale strings rather than coarse categories) and unsupervised tone clustering across dialects. The integration into a practical toolkit (ToneLab) further strengthens novelty by turning the idea into an accessible workflow for field linguistics and cross-dialectal analysis.

724.human_review: The authors have collected data from Jianghuai Mandarin, thereby extending the toolkit to achieve better dialectal coverage.
724.llm_review: The work addresses an important, under-served task suite for tonal languages: cross-dialect tone transcription and clustering. It assembles two relevant datasets in Jianghuai Mandarin: a speech dataset with expert five-scale labels across 11 dialects (2,238 recordings, stratified by speaker demographics) and a large transcription-only dataset spanning 31 dialect areas (31,000 tokens) for clustering/variance analyses. The tasks are carefully scoped to realistic fieldwork constraints (low resources, cross-regional generalization, few samples per speaker) and the evaluation acknowledges relative-pitch ambiguities inherent to five-scale transcription.

725.human_review: The authors present a lightweight framework for practical use, making it highly beneficial to a group of researchers.
725.llm_review: Methodologically, the paper is simple yet effective: (i) represent transcriptions via parametric curves (linear for two-digit, quadratic for three-digit) and compute distances to derive comparable features; (ii) train transcription models with a pitch-based loss that directly penalizes deviations in the five-scale space; (iii) infer length (two vs three digits) via a linearity threshold; and (iv) perform tone clustering using intermediate embeddings and DBSCAN. The approach improves dialect clustering over a categorical baseline and yields consistent transcription gains over an F0-fitting heuristic across multiple CNN backbones, while providing interpretable analyses (MDS, multiple linkage criteria).

726.human_review: The authors placed most of the implementation and design details of Tone2Vec into the appendix. While I understand the constraints of page limits, this makes it challenging to grasp the complete picture when reading the main text. I suggest including more details in the camera-ready version.
726.llm_review: Methodology; Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: (1) The evaluation protocol for transcription accuracy is under-specified given the acknowledged ambiguity of absolute levels (e.g., whether (55) and (44) are considered equivalent). The Variance metric is introduced but not clearly tied to the reported Accuracy; a formal definition of Accuracy, matching criteria, and tolerance for near-equivalent contours is needed. (2) There are apparent equation errors/typos that affect clarity: L_pitch is written with a negative sign, which would maximize rather than minimize the loss; and the case distinctions for two- vs three-digit targets are duplicated/mislabeled. (3) The decision threshold beta for linearity is fixed (0.5) without describing how it was chosen, whether it is tuned on validation, or how sensitive results are to this choice. (4) Important implementation details are missing (e.g., MFCC configuration, normalization, data augmentation, segment lengths), and the clustering evaluation reports a 71% rate for recovering the number of categories without defining the metric or providing aggregate statistics (e.g., ARI/NMI, per-speaker/per-dialect breakdowns).
