Computational overhead of the mitigation (MTCNN + gender classifier + face replacement) is not quantified beyond a qualitative "lightweight" claim, and potential adverse effects (artifacts, distribution shift, or reduced performance under different operating points) are not analyzed.

816.human_review: The paper is clearly structured and includes figures that effectively clarify and illustrate the central concepts.
816.llm_review: Clear and well-structured presentation. The paper motivates the problem, defines notation early, and provides a concise algorithm description for the ranking procedure. Prompts for hypothetical query generation and implementation details (retrieval top-100, re-rank top-30, LLM settings, lambda per embedding model) are included, and figures (pipeline diagram, ICA visualization) aid understanding. Appendices give additional prompts and derivations, improving reproducibility.

817.human_review: Experimental results show that applying HyQE consistently improves the performance of most combinations of retrieval models, embedding models, and LLMs used for generating hypothetical questions, demonstrating its effectiveness in ranking retrieved contexts given input queries.
817.llm_review: Methodologically, the idea of ranking contexts via LLM-generated hypothetical queries conditioned on each context—combined with a simple similarity-based scoring—offers a practical and training-free alternative to LLM re-rankers and query-expansion approaches. The variational inference framing provides a unifying perspective and yields two concrete scoring variants. Empirically, the method consistently increases NDCG@10 across multiple datasets (DL19, DL20, COVID, NEWS, Touche) and across diverse retrievers/embedders and LLMs (from Mistral-7B to GPT-4o). The study includes ablations on the lambda hyperparameter, sensitivity to K, an alternative VI-derived scoring, and compatibility with HyDE—demonstrating robustness and plug-and-play applicability.

818.human_review: The proposed method can reduce the computational overhead of generating hypothetical queries by generating them once and storing and reusing them when needed. This addresses the limitations of other baselines, which have to expand queries every time input queries are given.
818.llm_review: The methodological contribution is positioned clearly relative to existing families: unlike HyDE (query expansion) it conditions on contexts and reuses hypothetical queries, and unlike LLM re-rankers it avoids concatenating query+contexts and fine-tuning. Comparisons span sparse (SPLADE) and dense retrievers and multiple embedding backbones, showing additive gains and complementarity (including combined HyDE+HyQE). This breadth of comparisons supports the claim that the approach is model- and pipeline-agnostic.

819.human_review: While the authors emphasize the need for their proposed methods in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems multiple times in the Abstract and Introduction, they only perform experiments in document retrieval tasks and skip the experiments in RAG. Including experiments in RAG would strengthen the authors' claims.
819.llm_review: Methodology–Experiment gap on efficiency and scalability. While the approach is designed to amortize LLM calls by storing hypothetical queries, the paper does not quantify preprocessing cost, storage footprint, indexing strategy for H(c), or end-to-end latency at inference. The number of hypothetical queries per context and its impact on quality vs. cost are not systematically explored. Experimental evaluation focuses on retrieval metrics only; there is no end-to-end RAG task evaluation to confirm downstream gains. Statistical significance is not reported, and the hyperparameter tuning protocol (e.g., validation split vs. test tuning) is not fully specified.

820.human_review: Although they address their efficiency in theory compared to other query expansion methods, including a quantitative analysis of their superiority in complexity in practice would make the authors' claims even stronger.
820.llm_review: The theoretical/causal–VI analysis is suggestive but not rigorous. The prior p(c) is defined as proportional to exp(sim(q,c)) and thus depends on q, which is unconventional for a prior and undermines the probabilistic interpretation of the ELBO. The claim that generating hypothetical queries from c avoids LLM prior knowledge is debatable, as the LLMs parametric knowledge can still shape outputs even when conditioned on c. The softmax-to-max approximation and adoption of cosine similarity as a proxy for p(q|q^) lack error bounds or calibration checks, and no controlled analysis is provided to substantiate the causal/spurious correlation claims (e.g., robustness under distribution shift).

821.human_review: While the authors mention that their method can avoid hallucinations seen in the previous work HyDE (Gao et al., 2023), they do not perform a direct comparison with HyDE in the experiment table. Showing a direct comparison between HyQE and HyDE would strengthen the authors' claims further.
821.llm_review: Comparative coverage is incomplete. The study does not include strong cross-encoder re-rankers (e.g., monoT5/monoBERT, bge-reranker-large) or late-interaction models (e.g., ColBERTv2), nor classic document expansion baselines (e.g., docTTTTTquery/doc2query). Recent zero-shot LLM-based listwise re-rankers (e.g., RankZephyr) are discussed but not evaluated. Benchmarks are limited to five datasets rather than the broader BEIR suite, and no significance testing is provided. Some results rely on proprietary models (GPT-4o, OpenAI embeddings), which affects reproducibility and cost realism.

822.human_review: The proposed dataset effectively incorporates a range of media types, including text, images, videos, and audio, contributing to the advancement of multimodal fact-checking systems.
822.llm_review: Clear motivation and well-scoped task: the paper defines fine-grained claim verification over multimodal, multi-document evidence and operationalizes it via AMR-level node/tuple entailment labels. The new M3DC benchmark is large (over 400K claims across 10K+ topics) and explicitly targets cross-document, cross-media reasoning with long, realistic claims. The synthesis pipeline ties claim pieces to evidence, improving interpretability and enabling supervision at sub-claim granularity, which is a valuable step beyond coarse, sample-level fact-checking datasets.

823.human_review: This paper offers detailed insights by labelling and predicting the logical relationship of each claim aspect, enhancing the utility and interpretability of fact-checking beyond binary true/false classification.
823.llm_review: The paper provides detailed descriptions of the task setup, data construction, and model, making the contributions interpretable. It explains how AMR trees from text, image, video, and audio are linked into a cross-document, cross-media KG; how claims are generated via DFS traversal and then manipulated with target label control; and how the hierarchical transformer and GCN fuse multimodal encoders with AMR structure for node/edge entailment. Figures and equations clarify the flow from multimedia inputs to fine-grained predictions and sample-level outputs, helping readers understand what aspects are being verified and why.

824.human_review: Experimental results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on M3DC, indicating the efficacy of the approach in multimodal fact-checking tasks.
824.llm_review: Empirically, the method outperforms baselines on M3DC at both sample-level and fine-grained levels, and shows competitive fine-grained performance on MOCHEG in a zero-shot transfer setting. The study reports per-class F1s, highlighting improved neutral handling compared to LVLM baselines. Ablations across modalities, and text-only vs. multimodal configurations, probe the contribution of each modality. Qualitative analyses illustrate consistent, localized contradictions at specific AMR nodes/tuples, supporting the claim of providing actionable, fine-grained evidence.

825.human_review: The process of dataset construction is not described clearly and the introduction of the fine-grained claim labeling is missing.
825.llm_review: Data/Task validity and presentation clarity raise concerns. Although the dataset is large, most fine-grained labels are synthetic and derived from automatic models, with only a very small human-annotated subset (30 samples), limiting confidence in label quality. The manuscript alternates between stating that manipulation-level supervision is available and that labels come from a trained entailment classifier, which can confuse readers about the true source of fine-grained supervision. Ablations show limited gains from non-text modalities, suggesting the benchmark may be text-dominant and not convincingly demonstrating multimodality as essential.

826.human_review: The presentation of the methodology proposed in this paper is not very clear. For example, how to initialize the GCN? How to get and use the Joint Representation in Figure 3?
826.llm_review: Methodologically, the pipeline compounds errors from multiple components (AMR parsing, cross-modal grounding, captioning, audio summarization), yet the paper provides limited analysis of error propagation or robustness. The training labels for the verifier are produced by the paper's own entailment classifier used in the manipulator reward, risking circularity and bias. Presentation-wise, important training details (e.g., hyperparameters, model variants, annotation protocol and IAA, baseline adaptation procedures) are under-specified, making it hard to assess experimental rigor and to reproduce results.

827.human_review: The method proposed in this paper does not perform well on the MOCHEG dataset. The gap with LLaVA and MiniGPT in sample-level prediction is relatively large.
827.llm_review: There are open questions about the realism and soundness of the RL-based claim manipulation and the resulting task difficulty. The manipulator is steered by an NLI-style reward and filtered by another LLM, which may induce distributional artifacts that models can exploit. Potential leakage between generated captions/summaries and claims is not addressed. Results show especially low neutral F1 on human fine-grained labels, and ablations indicate text alone carries most of the signal, undermining the central claim that multimodal, multi-document reasoning is crucial. A stronger human evaluation and stress tests would be needed to validate the methodology and the benchmark's intended properties.

828.human_review: The paper is well-written, easy to read and understand.
828.llm_review: The recall–detect–predict pipeline is presented clearly, with a concise architectural figure and step-by-step equations that make the flow of information easy to follow. The narrative connection to cognitive theory provides intuitive motivation and improves readability.

829.human_review:
The final experimental results of the paper are very good and competitive.

The strengths of the paper in this cycle:
829.llm_review: Results are strong and consistent across three benchmarks: on IEMOCAP the model achieves ~76% Acc/Weighted-F1/Macro-F1, surpassing strong baselines; on DailyDialog it achieves higher Acc and Micro-F1 than prior work; and on EmoryNLP it reports the best Acc and Weighted-F1 among compared systems. Multiple metrics are reported to capture class imbalance.

830.human_review: The paper is well-written, easy to read and understand.
830.llm_review: Related work is well structured into sequence-, PLM-, and graph-based lines, situating the contribution within the ERC literature. Dataset statistics and training details are provided to aid reproducibility.

831.human_review: The final experimental results of the paper are very good and competitive.
831.llm_review: The experimental coverage includes both multimodal (IEMOCAP) and text-only (DailyDialog, EmoryNLP) settings, indicating the approach’s applicability across modalities and conversation structures. The qualitative case study illustrates improved handling of emotional inertia relative to DialogueRNN/DialogueCRN.

832.human_review: The paper includes new analytical experiments and provides some interpretable analysis through feature visualization, which is of certain value.
832.llm_review: The paper complements quantitative results with analyses: heatmap visualizations expose internal representations in the detection and classification layers, and the case study explains prediction behavior. The ablation overview attempts to attribute gains to recall and detection components, improving interpretability of the design choices.

833.human_review:
The use of ablation analysis and case studies makes it difficult to prove that the capabilities claimed by the method are consistent with the actual capabilities of the model. The former can only show that the module contributes to the results, while the latter makes it hard to generalize the conclusions.

The  weaknesses of the paper in this cycle:
833.llm_review: The ablation study and its analysis are insufficiently precise and somewhat contradictory. The toggles for intra-context dependency, recall, and detection are not rigorously defined, and reported numbers conflict with claims (e.g., removing both recall and detection on IEMOCAP still yields 70.40 Acc, which is not a substantial drop relative to the full model). There is no sensitivity analysis (e.g., number of encoder blocks/heads, context length), no per-class breakdowns, and no statistical significance testing, limiting confidence in the component-wise conclusions.

834.human_review: The visual analysis is conducted on individual cases, which might result in conclusions that are not generalizable.
834.llm_review: Methodological novelty appears incremental: the cognitively framed ‘recall–detect–predict’ maps onto standard bi-GRU encoders, transformer self-attention, and cross-attention, without a clear, unique mechanism beyond established architectures. Comparative analysis may be confounded by mixed reproduced vs. reported baselines and differing feature backbones/modalities; computational cost, parameter counts, and efficiency are not analyzed. Including stronger contemporary PLM/LLM baselines under matched inputs and a cost–performance analysis would strengthen methodological claims.

835.human_review: The proposed SCA method is model-independent, plug-and-play, and does not require training or fine-tuning.
835.llm_review: Methodology: The paper proposes a clear, general KV-cache compression scheme that is training-free and model-agnostic. The greedy selection objective explicitly minimizes an additive redundancy proxy computed jointly over keys and values, increasing the chance that compressed caches preserve diverse, representative token information. Important implementation details are carefully considered: adding RoPE to keys before similarity computation for faithfulness to attention, token-level selection by concatenating heads to preserve token integrity, and retaining most-recent tokens to protect recency effects. The selection cost is parallelizable across candidates, and sharing selections across layers further improves practicality.

836.human_review: Preliminary experiments are conducted to provide a reasonable basis for removing redundant vectors to compress the KV cache.
836.llm_review: Experiment: The empirical study is broad and convincing. It spans short-text tasks (IMDB, RACE, AG News, Cosmos QA) under a substantial 50% KV compression, long-text language modeling on PG19 and ArXiv up to 64k tokens, synthetic passkey retrieval (7B/13B chat models), and real long-context closed-ended tasks from L-Eval, with consistent comparisons against StreamingLLM, Sparse attention, and H2O. SCA consistently matches or closely tracks full attention on short tasks, delivers the lowest or tied perplexities in most long-context LM settings, maintains high passkey retrieval accuracy under large extensions, and improves accuracy on L-Eval at 8k/16k, even outperforming fine-tuned long-context models. The ablation on sharing selections across layers adds useful insight into efficiency-accuracy trade-offs.

837.human_review: The extensive experiment verifies the performance of SCA in modeling long text, while retaining the long context capabilities of the model better than other methods.
837.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment: The central design choice—selecting representative token vectors to minimize redundancy growth in the joint K/V space—translates into strong empirical outcomes. Compared with eviction or fixed-sparsity baselines, SCA better preserves information: near-parity with full attention at 50% compression on short tasks, lower perplexities when extending context by up to 16x, 100% passkey retrieval in challenging long-context settings, and tangible gains on L-Eval when expanding 4k models to 8k/16k without training. These results substantiate the method’s core intuition that maintaining the diversity of retained vectors in the KV cache is a more faithful and robust compression criterion than recency-only or attention-score heuristics.

838.human_review: SCA employs cosine similarity to identify redundant vectors and employs a greedy algorithm to select the most representative vectors for compressing the KV cache. While these measures aim to minimize information loss during compression, they may overlook subtle semantic differences that can impact the model's performance in nuanced tasks.
838.llm_review: Methodology, Result: The approach requires computing pairwise similarities and per-candidate additive increases, which is O(n^2) in the number of cached tokens per compression event. The paper does not quantify runtime or wall-clock overhead, nor report end-to-end throughput/latency, making it hard to assess practical efficiency gains in real deployments. Claims about reducing memory footprint and improving efficiency are supported indirectly (by enabling longer contexts) but not with concrete measurements of GPU memory, bandwidth, or speed. Furthermore, the decision to compute selections only on the last layer and share them across all layers is justified empirically but may introduce mismatches across layers; the impact on exact attention fidelity is not deeply analyzed.

839.human_review: The evaluation of SCA was confined exclusively to the Llama2 and Vicuna model architectures. The generalizability of SCA's effectiveness remains unvalidated across a broader range of LLMs.
839.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Evaluation: The redundancy metric—maximum cosine similarity over concatenated multi-head token vectors—as a proxy for information is heuristic and lacks theoretical grounding connecting it to attention quality or downstream loss. It also ignores potential head-specific structure and positional interactions in the value cache. While the preliminary redundancy analysis is suggestive, stronger validation (e.g., linking the metric to attention output error or task loss) would bolster the motivation. On evaluation, several choices limit conclusiveness: relatively small sampled subsets for short-text tasks, reliance on a synthetic passkey benchmark, and missing comparisons to other KV-compression strategies (e.g., clustering/merging, token pooling, KV quantization) and recent long-context methods beyond StreamingLLM/H2O. The specific hyperparameters (e.g., always retaining a fixed number of recent tokens) may favor SCA but are not systematically stress-tested across alternatives.

840.human_review: Customized Knowledge Base (MatSciKB): The creation of a high-quality, structured materials science knowledge base represents a substantial contribution to the field, providing a reliable and up-to-date resource for scientific inquiry.
840.llm_review: Clear and timely contribution: the paper introduces HoneyComb as (to my knowledge) the first LLM-based agent system purpose-built for materials science, combining a curated domain knowledge base with a tool hub to tackle computational and knowledge-intensive tasks. The work targets a high-impact niche where general LLMs underperform, and demonstrates consistent gains on two established benchmarks, suggesting practical value to the *ACL community interested in scientific NLP and agentic systems.

841.human_review: Sophisticated Tool Hub (ToolHub): The introduction of ToolHub, with its Inductive Tool Construction method, offers a new paradigm for enhancing LLMs with specialized computational capabilities, which is a significant methodological contribution.
841.llm_review: Methodology and contribution are well-aligned: the architecture couples a structured MatSciKB, a unified ToolHub (with both domain-specific and general tools), and a hybrid retriever, wrapped in a two-phase assessor/executor decision loop. The Inductive Tool Construction pipeline and embedded Python REPL concretely extend an LLM’s capabilities beyond text-only reasoning. Together, these choices constitute a coherent agent design that materially advances tool-augmented LLMs for a specialized domain.

842.human_review: Broad Applicability: The adaptable framework of HoneyComb is showcased to have potential for extension to other scientific domains, suggesting broader impacts beyond the specific focus on materials science.
842.llm_review: Methodology: the hybrid retrieval strategy (BM25 for speed + Contriever for semantic precision) is a sensible and practical design for scientific QA, and the agent’s two-stage tool-selection (assessor to shortlist tools, executor to plan/iterate) addresses common issues of tool overload and poor action grounding. The unified interface for both general and materials tools promotes modularity and extensibility.

843.human_review: Interdisciplinary Relevance: The work bridges the gap between AI and materials science, appealing to an interdisciplinary audience and fostering collaboration across fields.
843.llm_review: Methodology: the system design explicitly supports up-to-date information access (Google/Scholar/arXiv/Wikipedia/YouTube) and numerics via a Python REPL, which are often failure modes for LLMs in scientific domains. The Inductive Tool Construction approach—LLM-generated functions with human verification and decomposition into atomic APIs—provides a principled path to grow reusable domain tools over time.

844.human_review: Lack of Comprehensive Analysis: The paper could provide more comprehensive comparative analysis with other state-of-the-art systems in the field to better position HoneyComb's contributions and performance.
844.llm_review: Result and analysis: (1) Reporting irregularities (e.g., MaScQA GPT-4 baseline differs between Table 3 and the ablation table; minor discrepancies like 96.54 vs. 96.56 on SciQA) undermine confidence in the results. (2) No statistical tests, confidence intervals, or variance estimates are provided despite agentic runs often exhibiting stochasticity. (3) Baseline coverage is limited—there is no direct comparison against strong agent/tool-augmented baselines (e.g., ChemCrow/Coscientist-style setups) or standard RAG baselines with web search. (4) Evaluation focuses on multiple-choice QA; there is no analysis of tool-call correctness, latency/cost, or end-to-end task success on concrete computational workflows typical in materials science. (5) The observed topic-wise regressions for GPT-3.5 when using HoneyComb are not deeply analyzed, leaving unclear when the framework helps or hurts.

845.human_review: Reliance on LLM Quality: The performance of HoneyComb is contingent on the quality and capabilities of the underlying LLMs used for knowledge base construction, tool development, and retrieval processes. This reliance may introduce limitations if the LLMs have inherent biases or knowledge gaps.
845.llm_review: Methodology and result: the MatSciKB appears very small for a comprehensive resource (table suggests on the order of a few dozen entries), and its construction/coverage are insufficiently detailed to justify claims of breadth. The Inductive Tool Construction pipeline lacks critical specifics (size and nature of Dtrain, number and types of atomic tools, coverage analyses, failure modes), raising concerns about generalization and potential leakage if tools are derived from the same distributions as the evaluation sets. Prompting, tool-use policies, and safeguards for web-based retrieval (to avoid label leakage or answer copying) are not specified, and reproducibility details (release of tools/KB, prompts, hyperparameters, run-time budgets) are missing. These issues limit interpretability of the reported gains and hinder replication.

846.human_review: The article is clear and logical, making it easy to read.
846.llm_review: The paper is clearly written and well-structured. The decomposition into planner/caller/summarizer is introduced with intuitive motivation and supported by helpful figures (workflow and GLPFT pipeline) that make the execution loop and decision points easy to follow. The evaluation setup, metrics, and dataset splits (in-domain vs. out-of-domain) are presented coherently, and references to appendices for prompts and dataset details aid navigability.

847.human_review: The proposed concept is valuable; if smaller models can replace larger ones, it will lower the implementation threshold for deploying large models in various business applications.
847.llm_review: Methodologically, the modular multi-LLM design is well-motivated by capacity constraints of small LLMs, and the two-stage GLPFT strategy is a principled way to leverage global context before specializing. The local fine-tuning with gradient masking on sub-spans (rationale/action/answer) is a sensible training objective to enforce role specialization, and the paper examines alternatives (direct one-stage multi-LLM, multi-task single-LLM, and LoRA vs. full fine-tuning), strengthening the case for the chosen approach.

848.human_review: The authors demonstrate that using only three Llama2-7B or Llama2-13B models can achieve results comparable to GPT-4, which is quite impressive. They also analyze the characteristics of the α-Umi framework from various perspectives, providing valuable insights for industrial implementation.
848.llm_review: The empirical study is broad and informative: results span both offline (step-wise) and real-time ToolBench evaluations, multiple model sizes (7B/13B), and several baselines (ChatGPT, GPT-4, ToolLLaMA). The analysis goes beyond raw scores, including data scaling laws, instruction reuse vs. non-reuse, LoRA vs. full fine-tuning, and loss-curve tracking to explain why GLPFT + modularization helps. Improvements are consistent on planning, action accuracy, and reduced hallucinations, and the 7B multi-LLM surpassing a 13B single-LLM baseline highlights the practical value of specialization.

849.human_review: The authors do not provide specific advantages of the α-Umi framework in terms of resource consumption for model training and deployment.
849.llm_review: Methodology: The fairness of comparisons is not fully addressed. The multi-LLM agent effectively deploys three copies of an LLM (e.g., 3x7B), which increases total parameters and inference compute relative to a single-LLM baseline. Claims that a 7B multi-LLM outperforms a 13B single-LLM could be confounded by aggregate capacity and repeated invocations. The paper lacks a parameter/FLOPs/latency/cost analysis and does not compare against parameter- or compute-matched baselines (e.g., larger single-LLM with equal total params, or ensembles). Reporting throughput, memory, and end-to-end latency for real-time runs would clarify practical trade-offs.

850.human_review: The article proposes a multi-LLM framework but does not adequately discuss the increased complexity of the models and how to manage this complexity.
850.llm_review: Methodology: The evaluation relies heavily on ToolBench and an LLM-as-judge for the real-time pass/win metrics, with no human evaluation or statistical significance testing. The offline Rouge-L and step-wise metrics may not fully capture user-perceived answer quality. Out-of-domain is defined by tool exposure, but broader generalization (e.g., unseen tool schemas, different tool ecosystems) is not assessed. Including more datasets beyond ToolBench (main text), human judgments, agreement analyses, and significance tests would strengthen the validity and generality of the findings.

851.human_review: The authors do not clearly explain why they chose to define the split models as Planer, Caller, and Summarizer. What specific basis do they have for these definitions?
851.llm_review: Methodology; Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: Important training details are under-specified in the main text. The GLPFT masking strategy is only briefly described ("gradients from other text spans are stopped") without precise objective formulations, loss weights, or pseudocode. The exact prompt templates, label construction for planner decisions (Next: Caller/Summarizer/Give up), and the procedure for creating sub-task datasets (sizes, distributions, split seeds) are deferred to appendices or not fully quantified. Providing explicit training objectives, data statistics per sub-task, and releasing prompts would improve clarity and reproducibility.

852.human_review: The paper presents a splitting method that has certain reference significance for the industry, as it allows for better and more cost-effective deployment. However, it inherently leads to error accumulation, similar to traditional pipelines. How to strike a balance is worth a more detailed discussion.
852.llm_review: Methodology: Ablations isolating design choices are limited. It remains unclear how much of the gain comes from (a) passing explicit rationales from planner to caller vs. alternative interfaces, (b) the specific three-way split versus other decompositions (e.g., planner+summarizer combined), or (c) decoding choices (greedy-only). Additional ablations removing rationale inputs, varying the decision granularity, or exploring different component combinations and decoding strategies would better substantiate the causal factors behind the improvements.

853.human_review: One issue of image generation models is generating images that accurately align with the given text input. In this paper, the authors evaluate image captions based on precision and recall metrics and analyze their impact on the text alignment of T2I models. This direction is interesting and should be explored further.
853.llm_review: Methodology and evaluation are well aligned: the paper formalizes caption quality along two interpretable axes (precision as the proportion of correct/positive sentences and recall as the number of subcaptions/submasks) and then trains/fine-tunes competitive diffusion backbones (PixArt-b for the human-caption analysis; SD2.1 and SDXL for synthetic captions) to test compositional alignment. The use of T2I-CompBench with category-wise reporting (color, shape, texture, spatial, non-spatial) provides a task-relevant, multi-faceted evaluation that directly reflects text-image alignment, and the observed trends are consistent across datasets and models, lending credibility to the methodological conclusions.

854.human_review: The authors conducted an ablation study, demonstrating that utilizing LVLMs for caption generation can yield comparable results to captions written by human evaluators.
854.llm_review: The ablation design is thorough and informative: a grid sweep over precision levels (0% to 100%) and recall (093 submasks) clearly isolates their individual and joint effects on compositional performance, revealing that precision dominates while recall offers diminishing returns as precision increases. A second ablation across LVLM captioners (LLaVA, BLIP2, uform) combined with a decomposed faithfulness proxy (entities, shape, color, texture, spatial, non-spatial) ties measured caption precision/recall to downstream T2I performance, reinforcing the main claim through converging evidence.

855.human_review: The analysis demonstrates that the precision of the caption is more critical than the recall when training T2I. One of its primary use cases is to establish a methodology for enhancing the text-image alignment of T2I based on these findings. It would be beneficial to present some experiments in this direction.
855.llm_review: Methodology/Experiment/Analysis: (1) The operationalization of precision via the proportion of positive vs. LLaMA2-modified negative sentences is coarse and mixes error types; negative sentences are often mostly correct with a few incorrect elements, which confounds precision with error severity and may not reflect real-world caption noise. (2) Recall is equated with the number of subcaptions (093), which conflates information coverage with verbosity and redundancy; token budget is not held constant, so gains could be due to longer inputs rather than true coverage. (3) The human-caption experiments rely on a relatively small dataset (8k images) with LoRA fine-tuning and report no variance across seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, limiting the robustness of conclusions. (4) The analysis does not control for several potential confounds (e.g., total token length, noun density, or content overlap between main and subcaptions), making causal attribution to precision vs. recall less definitive.

856.human_review: The measurement of text alignment for ‘Attribute binding’ and ‘Object relationship’ was conducted using various methods. It would be good to demonstrate that it aligns with human evaluation, even on a small portion of the samples.
856.llm_review: Methodology/Evaluation: The synthetic-caption evaluation pipeline uses GPT-3.5 for decomposition and LLaVA-13B as the final judge, while LLaVA is also one of the caption generators; this likely introduces evaluator bias toward LLaVA and inflates its measured precision. Only 1k captions are sampled for this assessment, and no human evaluation or cross-judge validation is provided. Downstream alignment is assessed solely via T2I-CompBench (BLIP2/CLIP/detector-based automatic metrics) without complementary human studies or general-purpose quality metrics (e.g., FID, aesthetic/human preference), and training budgets/token lengths across captioners are not matched or controlled, weakening the methodological validity of the evaluation conclusions.

857.human_review: The paper identifies an important problem called "speech anchor bias" that arises when directly fine-tuning LLMs with speech instructional data. This is a valuable contribution to understanding the limitations of current approaches.
857.llm_review: Clear contribution: the paper diagnoses and names the instruction-following failure in speech-text LMs as "speech anchor bias," and proposes a practical remedy via self-powered instruction augmentation. On the data/task side, the work shows that abundant ASR-only corpora (LibriSpeech, GigaSpeech, Common Voice) can be repurposed into multi-task instruction data that unlocks broader capabilities (ASR, ST, SLU, QA) without expensive multimodal pretraining, and it promises to release the augmentation dataset for community use.

858.human_review: The proposed self-powered data augmentation method is an innovative solution to address the speech anchor bias. Generating and using the model's own instructional data is a clever way to better align the speech and text modalities.
858.llm_review: Methodologically, the self-powered pipeline is simple and effective: use the LLM to generate task-specific outputs conditioned on instructions plus ASR transcripts, pair them with the original speech, freeze the speech encoder, and fine-tune the Q-Former and LLM for alignment. From a data/task perspective, this leverages widely available ASR data to synthesize diverse supervision (e.g., translation, intent, sentiment, keywords, QA), enabling capability expansion without collecting new labeled multimodal datasets.

859.human_review: The paper provides a thorough evaluation of the self-powered LSM across a diverse range of speech-based tasks, showcasing the approach's effectiveness in improving instruction-following and multimodal integration.
859.llm_review: Strong empirical methodology and evaluation: the paper includes ablations (no LLM fine-tuning, LoRA), scaling across Whisper encoder sizes, cross-backbone validation with Llama3, and a cascade vs end-to-end comparison including speed. It further analyzes layer-wise attention dynamics and representation alignment (T-SNE), tying the measured increase in instruction salience to observed gains across tasks. Results consistently improve over vanilla instruction tuning and an in-house BLSP reproduction, with competitive performance vs Qwen-Audio and faster end-to-end inference.

860.human_review: While the paper introduces a self-powered data generation process, the overall size and diversity of the final training dataset is still limited compared to other large-scale speech datasets used in prior work. Also, all the tasks are semantic understanding tasks where text LLMs can be used for generation of synthetic data but there is no discussion on how to generate the data for paralinguistic/acoustic tasks such as speaker/gender recognition etc.,
860.llm_review: Methodology and data/task design raise robustness concerns: self-powered targets are generated by the LLM from transcripts without quality control, so label noise, hallucinations, and stylistic drift may propagate. The paper does not analyze the impact of noisy pseudo-labels, filtering, or instruction diversity, nor provide sensitivity to the proportion of 230k vanilla samples mixed with generated data. The instruction pool is created with GPT-4 but concrete counts and diversity per task are limited, leaving open risks of overfitting to template artifacts and uneven task coverage.

861.human_review: While the self-powered LSM shows strong performance improvements, there are some task-specific gaps compared to specialized models or cascaded pipeline approaches, as hinted at in the paper's discussion.
861.llm_review: Methodology and data/task details, as well as definitions and results reporting, need sharpening. The formalism around speech anchor bias relies on attention-derived proxies and informal objective approximations (e.g., L ≈ −log P(t|s)), without causal analyses or statistical testing. Key dataset and instruction-pool details (exact template counts per category/language, sampling policies, mixing ratios) are unclear; Table 1 is hard to parse. Reported metrics lack variance estimates/confidence intervals, and claims of generalization (e.g., on ST) rest on small average gains with trade-offs (ASR lags specialized systems), making the empirical case less conclusive.

862.human_review: The novelty of the work is limited given that the prior work (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.02248) also uses similar techniques to generate synthetic data but applies on specific tasks like ASR and Translation.
862.llm_review: Novelty and positioning: while naming the phenomenon is useful, the core technique is close to known self-instruction/self-training with pseudo-labels and to continuation-style augmentation (e.g., BLSP). The paper would benefit from deeper comparisons and discussion relative to recent audio-LLMs and instruction-augmentation approaches, as well as the broader self-training literature, and from stronger baselines/datasets beyond Qwen-Audio and an internal BLSP replication. As a result, the incremental novelty over existing data augmentation paradigms can feel limited.

863.human_review: The author takes the previously retrieved passages into consideration when judging whether to retrieve or not. This idea is quite a novel perspective. Besides, the author gives a comparison results on retrieval frequency to demonstrate its effectiveness.
863.llm_review: Methodology, Novelty, Comparison: The paper introduces a clear and novel multi-turn extension of SELF-RAG that explicitly learns when to retrieve, what to summarize for retrieval, and how to assess responses via reflection tokens. The 3-way retrieval decision (retrieve / no retrieve / continue to use evidence) and the use of conversation summaries as retrieval queries, rather than single-question rewrites, are well-motivated innovations for conversational QA. Empirically, the approach is compared against single-turn SELF-RAG variants trained on similar data distributions, showing consistent improvements in critic accuracy (e.g., retrieval and relevance judgments) and downstream response quality. The ablations comparing summary vs. rewrite query formulations and the retrieval effectiveness gains (e.g., +13.5% R@5 on average vs. rewriting) provide convincing comparative evidence that the proposed components matter.

864.human_review: It is a beneficial try that the author summarizes the conversation for better retrieval recall. The author also conductes experiment to demonstrate its superiority over other rewriting methods.
864.llm_review: Methodology, Experiment: The end-to-end design—training a critic (to produce reflection tokens for retrieval necessity, passage relevance, groundedness, and utility) and a generator (to emit reflection tokens and produce conversation summaries for retrieval)—is coherent and aligns well with the multi-turn setting. The experiments are reasonably thorough: three datasets (QReCC, UltraChat, MT-Eval), both automatic (BERTScore, UniEval coherence/groundedness) and human evaluations, and targeted analyses such as handling previously retrieved passages, retrieval-on/off decisions over turns, and query representation ablations. The consistent human-rated gains (~13% over SELF-RAG on conversational datasets) and improved groundedness when retrieval is called support the methodological choices.

865.human_review: In table 6 and table 7, the author didn't compare their pipeline in MT-Eval dataset. I think it's critical to add this out-of-domain benchmark result, to demonstrate that the superiority of usage of summary and previously retrieved passages.
865.llm_review: Data/Task, Comparison: The empirical scope is constrained: training and evaluation are limited to English tasks and primarily to QReCC/UltraChat, with MT-Eval as out-of-domain. The retrieval corpus (54M Wikipedia + Common Crawl) and a single retriever (Contriever) may not reflect diverse real-world sources or retriever choices. Comparisons focus on SELF-RAG variants and a T5-based rewriter; missing are stronger contemporary conversational RAG baselines (e.g., retrieval controllers/filters, rerankers, compressive RAG, or recent RL-based reformulators) and richer query-rewriting systems reported in the related work. Efficiency/cost comparisons (latency, token/bandwidth savings) are only discussed qualitatively and not measured, limiting task-level and system-level comparability.

866.human_review: In line 281 and line 325, the author mentions that the special token from critic model is used for response generation. Can you give more explanation for how the special token is used during generation? It's a bit confusing.
866.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Presentation: Several core elements would benefit from clearer, front-and-center descriptions: (i) the exact decision procedure that converts multiple reflection signals into a final selection ("highest score") lacks a formal definition or weighting scheme; (ii) details on the summarization objective, supervision, and decoding constraints are mostly in appendices; (iii) retrieval configuration (k, re-ranking if any, fusion across turns, deduping) and hyperparameters are under-specified; (iv) training set sizes per task, prompt templates, and sampling policies are dispersed or deferred to appendices. Figures could be more legible (e.g., decision flow with precise inputs/outputs), and some table captions/labels (Ret. w/ vs w/o passages, single vs multi-turn splits) are hard to parse without cross-referencing. These presentation gaps make it harder to fully interpret the mechanisms and to reproduce the pipeline.

867.human_review: In line 322, how to measure which passage ‘score’ the highest?
867.llm_review: A broader concern is potential bias and circularity: GPT-4 provides both critic training labels (reflection tasks) and is used as an automatic evaluator, which can overstate gains aligned with GPT-4 preferences. Statistical significance is not reported for human/automatic metrics, and there is limited error analysis on failure cases (e.g., when summaries hurt retrieval or when grounding fails). Finally, the study uses a single 7B backbone and offline retrieval; generalization across model scales, other LLMs/retrievers, and online retrieval dynamics is untested, which may limit robustness claims.

868.human_review: The proposed algorithm is quite simple and intuitive in itself and it really can help to create LMs for low resource languages, at least judging by the results of the experiments conducted in the paper
868.llm_review: Methodology and Experiment: The paper proposes a simple, resource-lean lexical-level transfer method (TEMA) that maps token embeddings from a high-resource L1 model to a low-resource L2 model using a bilingual dictionary, followed by a light fine-tuning step via an added embedding layer. The approach is architecturally minimal (no changes to the transformer backbone), tokenizer-aware (evaluates both BPE and linguistically motivated DeepSpin), and is tested across multiple language pairs including a morphologically complex low-resource language (Quechua). Experiments include intrinsic (pseudo-perplexity) and extrinsic (XTREME tasks and SuperGLUE) evaluations, with consistent hyperparameters and comparisons against strong baselines (eB-BERT, eB-BERT+linear_unsup, mBERT, XLM-R), demonstrating consistent gains attributable to the proposed mapping.

869.human_review: The authors conduct several experiments with the use of benchmarks such as SuperGLUE and they do a thorough evaluation of their results, including some visualisation
869.llm_review: Experiment, Data/Task, Evaluation: The experimental design covers both intrinsic and extrinsic endpoints, using pseudo-perplexity for masked LMs and a broad set of downstream tasks from XTREME (XNLI, PAWS-X, POS, NER, XQuAD) and SuperGLUE (BoolQ, CB, COPA, RTE, WiC). The study considers realistic low-resource settings by training L2 models on 10M-token corpora and includes a particularly challenging target (Quechua), strengthening the claim of applicability to morphologically rich languages. It also probes tokenizer effects (BPE vs. DeepSpin), provides statistical testing for SuperGLUE improvements, and reports large perplexity reductions and downstream gains, lending credibility to the evaluation.

870.human_review: The paper is written in a quite clear manner
870.llm_review: Presentation: The paper is well-motivated and situates TEMA clearly within related work on multilingual transfer, vocabulary extension, and cross-lingual embedding alignment. The inclusion of an illustrative figure, qualitative fill-mask examples, and a concrete limitations section helps readers grasp both the intuition and practical constraints of the method. The narrative linking improved embedding geometry to semantic task gains (e.g., WiC) is accessible and persuasive.

871.human_review: You should say at least something about the metrics you use. Table 3 doesn't even mention which metric is presented (F1?)
871.llm_review: Presentation and Evaluation: The mathematical exposition of the mapping (e.g., the projection equations and the use of a single reference token 1 across languages) is unclear and appears dimensionally ambiguous, which hampers reproducibility. Evaluation reporting lacks detail in places: pseudo-perplexity comparability across tokenizers is not discussed; significance testing is reported only for SuperGLUE but not XTREME; and error bars/confidence intervals are missing. Some comparisons confound architecture/tokenizer choices (e.g., RoBERTa for TEMA vs. BERT for eB-BERT) and differ in vocabulary handling, complicating fairness. The procedure for adding sentences to introduce missing tokens (and its potential impact on results) is insufficiently quantified, making it hard to isolate TEMAs contribution from ancillary data augmentation.

872.human_review: There are several repetitions across the text: instead of repeating the same thing twice, you could probably use the space for metric descriptions.
872.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation: Core algorithmic details are under-specified. The function T for identifying translation-equivalent tokens, handling of polysemy, and subword alignment (especially with BPE) are not rigorously described. The choice of using the digit 1 as the anchor for an affine mapping is not justified, and there is no ablation on the number/type of anchor pairs or on alternative mappings (e.g., orthogonal Procrustes). The process for creating and selecting tgt_sent sentences, the quantity/quality of added examples per token, and their sources lack detail. Sensitivity to dictionary size/coverage, tokenizer design, domain mismatch between L1/L2 corpora, and stability of the added embedding layer fine-tuning are not explored, leaving important implementation and robustness questions unanswered.

873.human_review: The structure of the paper definitely could be improved (concerning repetitions)
873.llm_review: Result: While gains are consistent, some claims are overstated. The paper asserts state-of-the-art or better results for the most semantic tasks, yet TEMA does not surpass fully multilingual models on English SuperGLUE, and evidence of SOTA status is limited to selected tasks/languages (notably Quechua). Results on European languages are derived from artificially low-resource subsets, which may not reflect real low-resource conditions. There is no analysis of failure cases or when TEMA might underperform, nor broader comparisons to recent cross-lingual adaptation methods beyond eB-BERT variants. The mixing of vocabulary expansion with embedding mapping also blurs attribution of the observed improvements.

874.human_review: Achieve the objective of cultivating a model that can distinguish between information that can be openly shared and information that demands strict confidentiality.
874.llm_review: Methodology: The paper introduces a comprehensive CPPLM framework that operationalizes contextual PII protection through multiple, complementary post-training strategies (instruction-tuning with positive/negative pairs, a lightweight PII classifier, penalty-based unlikelihood, corpus curation, and DPO). The design choices are pragmatic (e.g., LoRA-based updates, SFT-compatible pipelines) and the methodology is motivated by a clear design intent: preserve domain utility while suppressing sensitive outputs without resorting to costly RLHF. The instruction-based paradigm is particularly well-scoped and practically deployable, requiring only labeled contrastive examples rather than specialized infrastructure.

875.human_review: Address the challenge of balancing privacy protection with maintaining data quality and model performance using the model CPPLM they offered.
875.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result: The study benchmarks several methods across two LLaMA-2 scales (7B/13B) and multiple biomedical datasets and a synthetic PQA set, providing a broad comparison under a consistent training protocol. Results consistently show that instruction tuning with positive/negative examples achieves strong privacy leakage reductions (often ~40–60% SPriv decrease) while maintaining ROUGE/BERTScore close to or better than vanilla SFT, and frequently lies on the reported Pareto frontier. The inclusion of DPO, classifier, penalty, removal, and substitution baselines clarifies trade-offs and supports the central claim that instruction-based tuning is a strong, cost-effective alternative.

876.human_review: Comprehensive datasets and evaluation methods, such as the Pareto frontier, are very suitable for this experiment. Moreover, the analysis for each method is very complete.
876.llm_review: Data/Task, Evaluation, Analysis: The paper evaluates utility (ROUGE-1/2/L, BERTScore) and a privacy metric (SPriv) across three biomedical QA datasets and a synthetic PQA dataset with multiple PII categories (names, emails, addresses, SSNs), enabling per-type analysis. The comparative evaluation spans many strategies and instruction variants (PN/NP), with scale-sensitive reporting (7B vs 13B) and a Pareto frontier view to contextualize trade-offs between utility and privacy. The appendices add training details and step-wise curves, which, together with the main tables, provide a reasonably thorough empirical picture of method behavior.

877.human_review: There is an unclear definition of personally identifiable information. The whole experiment and test are based on the scrubadub toolkit, which includes basic PII.
877.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation, Experiment: The notion of “contextual PII” is central but insufficiently specified and operationalized—most annotations and the evaluation metric rely on scrubadub detectors for names/organizations/addresses, which do not capture contextuality (e.g., the combination of identity and condition) nor user-specific privacy norms. The paper would benefit from clearer definitions, labeling schemas, and discussion of edge cases (e.g., quasi-identifiers, templated contexts, thresholds for detection). Experimental descriptions omit details that matter for interpretation—prompt templates for QA, detector precision/recall on the generated text, handling of false positives/negatives, and how contextual labels are derived beyond simple entity tagging—making it hard to assess how well the setup reflects contextual privacy rather than entity scrubbing.

878.human_review: There is no experiment on the performance of this model in other user-customized privacy preferences.
878.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment: The privacy evaluation is limited: SPriv counts tokens flagged as PII in generated text, but does not measure memorization or extraction risk (e.g., canary exposure, membership inference) or robustness under adversarial/red-team prompts. Comparisons lack stress tests that are standard in privacy work and may overstate protection. Baselines like removal/substitution predictably harm utility, while instruction methods still leave non-trivial SPriv; yet the paper suggests there is no privacy–utility trade-off. Results lack statistical rigor (no confidence intervals, multiple seeds) and do not examine sensitivity to decoding strategies, prompt attacks, or dataset shifts, weakening the strength of the empirical claims.

879.human_review: The labeling process for user-customized privacy preferences may be more flexible and adaptable.
879.llm_review: Methodology: Several components are underspecified or potentially brittle. The penalty-based unlikelihood depends on n-grams extracted from the training set, limiting generalization to unseen entities or paraphrases and risking distortions to content words beyond PIIs. The PII classifier’s architecture, training data balance, thresholds, and calibration are insufficiently detailed, and its performance under domain shift is untested. Instruction-based tuning uses negative examples containing PII; without careful filtering or control, these could reinforce memorization or be surfaced by jailbreak prompts. DPO setup may require sizable preference data to be effective; data scale and sampling strategy are not deeply analyzed.

880.human_review: The connection between theoretical analysis of the information loss during corpus curation and further five strategies could have been explained better. This analysis only implies that the model with the "correct" information is more effective and informative than imposing constraints to selectively forget previously acquired knowledge. Four of the five ways to manage information by imposing some form of constraint or adjustment are different from the view advocated in theoretical analysis.
880.llm_review: Theory, Analysis: The theoretical section primarily applies a data-processing inequality argument to assert that learning from (s, p) is more informative than learning from masked sequences; this does not constitute a privacy analysis nor a formal guarantee about contextual PII protection. The link from the inequality to the conclusion that instruction-based approaches avoid a privacy–utility trade-off is not rigorous, and there is no modeling of adversaries, leakage channels, or bounds on exposure. Analytical depth is limited—no error analysis of failure cases, no ablation isolating the effect of instruction content vs ordering, and the Pareto frontier plots lack methodological details (e.g., variability across runs), making the theoretical and analytical support for the main claims weaker than desired.

881.human_review: The introduction of DMPO, which adapts DPO for multi-turn tasks, is a significant contribution. The use of SAOM and length normalization provides a robust solution to the challenges posed by multi-turn scenarios.
881.llm_review: Clear, focused contribution: the paper introduces DMPO, a direct multi-turn preference optimization objective that (i) replaces the policy-KL constraint with a state-action occupancy measure (SAOM) KL constraint and (ii) introduces length normalization in the Bradley–Terry model to enable cancellation of the partition function for multi-turn trajectories. This addresses a well-known limitation of DPO in multi-turn settings and targets compounding-error reduction in language agents, making the contribution relevant and timely for agent tuning.

882.human_review: The work offers a solid theoretical foundation for the proposed DMPO loss, including a detailed explanation of the length normalization technique and its impact on the partition function.
882.llm_review: Methodologically and theoretically grounded: the derivation shows that optimizing under a SAOM-KL constraint yields a closed-form optimal occupancy proportional to the reference occupancy times an exponentiated reward, which makes the partition function state-independent and thus cancelable in the preference likelihood when combined with length normalization. The paper provides useful interpretive corollaries (early-step reweighting via a discounting function and reduction to single-turn DPO as gamma approaches zero) and a rationale for the empirical success of length normalization, offering an interpretable bridge between theory and practical design choices.

883.human_review: The extensive experiments on multiple datasets validate the effectiveness of the DMPO loss function, demonstrating its superiority over existing methods in various multi-turn agent tasks.
883.llm_review: Good methodological intuition validated on representative agent tasks: the motivation to emphasize early steps (to mitigate compounding errors) and to normalize for trajectory-length mismatch is coherent with agent dynamics, and the experiments on WebShop, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld with two base LLMs (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct) under both noisy and clean preference-pair constructions provide empirical support. The inclusion of seen vs. unseen splits, as well as ablations on the discount factor and on the effect of trajectory length, help justify design decisions and demonstrate robustness relative to DPO and other tuning baselines.

884.human_review: While the experiments are extensive, they are limited to three multi-turn agent task datasets. Including more diverse tasks and datasets could strengthen the generalizability claims.
884.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Experiment: the construction of preference data fixes expert trajectories as winners and uses model-generated trajectories as losers (noisy vs. filtered), which risks biasing the preference signal toward imitation of available experts rather than reflecting diverse or human-in-the-loop preferences. The environments are all simulated and the ALFWorld section appears incomplete (table values truncated; very small reported training size), limiting external validity. Important experimental details (e.g., clearer statistics for all tasks, more thorough dataset descriptions, and consistent reporting for ALFWorld in both settings) are missing or unclear, and the noise model (e.g., repeated actions and meaningless words) may not reflect realistic failure modes.

885.human_review: Missing results with different sizes of LLMs. Adding these results strengthens the proposed method's efficiency as the model size increases.
885.llm_review: Methodology/Result: several derivational steps need clarification or stronger justification, especially the form and estimation of the occupancy measure and its ratio, and the transition from likelihoods over occupancies to per-step policy ratios without instability (using raw ratios rather than log-ratios could be brittle). Some reported gains over DPO are modest and not uniform across seen/unseen splits; there is no statistical significance analysis or confidence intervals to support the strength of the improvements.

886.human_review: The work could benefit from a more detailed comparative analysis with other state-of-the-art methods, including a discussion of scenarios where DMPO might not perform as well.
886.llm_review: Result/Comparison/Analysis/Explanation/Methodology: comparisons omit closely related single-stage preference-learning baselines such as IPL and CPL, and there is no ablation isolating the contributions of SAOM vs. length normalization. The analysis lacks discussion of computational overhead and training stability relative to DPO/PPO, and sensitivity analyses for beta, the choice of reference model, and alternative discount schedules are limited. Presentation issues (typos, missing equation references such as "Eq (??)", and truncated tables) hinder interpretability; equations defining the occupancy decomposition and weighting deserve a more precise, self-contained exposition to fully support the claimed theoretical properties.

887.human_review: The authors presents SyncToD as an "alternative RAG approach" to incorporate LLMs to solve specific tasks, and shows experimentally that it outperforms prior work in training specific models or directly using RAG.
887.llm_review: Methodology, Result, Experiment: The paper introduces a simple yet effective pipeline (hint predictors for entity types, response length, and dialog closure + hint-aware exemplar retrieval/reranking) that directly targets style alignment while preserving LLM reasoning. Experiments across three TOD benchmarks (MultiWOZ2.1, SMD, BiTOD) show consistent gains, especially in the low-data regime where SyncTOD outperforms both vanilla few-shot LLM prompting and strong supervised baselines (e.g., MAKER) on Entity F1. Human evaluations further corroborate improved appropriateness and fluency, lending credibility to the reported quantitative results.

888.human_review: (compared to the previous submission) the authors included detailed motivations of their approach - why hints about response length, entity types, and dialogue closure would be beneficial for an LLM to improve ToD response.
888.llm_review: Methodology, Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation: The motivation is clear and compelling—LLMs tend to be verbose and misaligned with TOD response style, which is problematic in constrained settings (e.g., in-car assistants). The chosen hints are well-justified: entity types capture the core informational intent; response length directly addresses verbosity; dialog closure helps enforce dataset-appropriate endings. The alignment analysis (average length and entity count) validates that these hints move outputs closer to gold style, supporting the core intuition.

889.human_review: the authors conducted careful ablation studies and human evaluations, demonstrating the importance of using the designed hint prediction modules to perform re-ranking
889.llm_review: Ablation, Evaluation: The ablation study is informative, demonstrating that removing hint prediction, retrieval, or reranking degrades performance—highlighting each component’s contribution. The inclusion of human evaluation (appropriateness and fluency with inter-annotator agreement) strengthens the evidence beyond BLEU, which is known to be brittle for style. Evaluations cover both full-data and low-data settings and multiple datasets, improving robustness of the claims.

890.human_review: One limitation of the proposed approach is that it requires both training (for the hint prediction modules) and prompting an LLM. This should be included in the Limitation section, as I believe most people would either opt-for either 1) easy setup that simply pays for calling an LLM, or 2) fully finetune a local model to avoid monetary cost. This method incurs both a monetary requirement from 1) and a compute requirement from 2).
890.llm_review: Methodology: The approach depends on auxiliary predictors that require dataset-specific entity-type schemas and labels derived from gold responses, which may limit generality across domains with different or evolving schemas. The RS (response length) constraint relies on LLM compliance and may be brittle across models/prompts; no analysis of compliance or failure modes is provided. The exemplar reranking uses a very simple score (indicator for closure + Jaccard on entity types) and selects only two exemplars; more principled state proxies or adaptive exemplar counts could yield stronger or more stable gains. Additionally, the paper does not report the accuracy of the hint predictors or the computational/latency overhead introduced by training and running them, which is important for practical TOD deployment.

891.human_review: the specific version of MultiWoZ is not mentioned. In the previous submission, the authors used MultiWoZ 2.1 which contains errors in the test set and has less baselines compared to MultiWoZ 2.2. It is unclear whether MultiWoZ 2.1 or 2.2 is used in this submission.
891.llm_review: Comparison: While the paper compares to supervised SoTAs and few-shot/RAG LLM baselines, it omits several relevant comparisons that affect interpretability: (i) standard MultiWOZ Inform/Success metrics commonly used for TOD; (ii) stronger LLM prompting/control baselines (e.g., style-controlled instructions, constrained decoding, self-consistency/CoT for reasoning with style constraints); (iii) alternative demonstration selection methods beyond semantic similarity (e.g., label/case-based or state-aware selection). Reporting variance/CI and more comprehensive LLM baselines (e.g., GPT-4 with RAG) would further clarify the relative advantage.

892.human_review: Innovative Multi-Aspect Encoding: MARE introduces a Multi-Aspect Multi-Head Attention mechanism, which allows the model to encode multiple aspects of the text simultaneously. This is a significant improvement over traditional uni-aspect models.
892.llm_review: Methodology + Result: The paper introduces a clear architectural innovation for unsupervised rationale extraction in multi-aspect settings. The Multi-Aspect Multi-Head Attention (MAMHA) with hard deletion and a Multi-Aspect Controller (MAC) enforces aspect-wise isolation while allowing within-aspect interactions, and special aspect tokens + Gumbel-softmax provide a principled way to assign tokens to aspects. Empirically, these design choices translate into consistent gains over strong baselines: on BeerAdvocate, MARE improves average token-level F1 by about 2.3 points (high-sparse) and 3.6 points (low-sparse) vs. YOFO, with per-aspect gains up to 5.4 points; on Hotel Review, it improves average F1 by 0.7 points while remaining competitive per aspect.

893.human_review: The experimental results show that MARE achieves state-of-the-art performance on unsupervised rationale extraction benchmarks. Specifically, it outperforms previous methods in token-level F1 scores and accuracy metrics.
893.llm_review: Data/Task + Result + Evaluation + Experiment: The work targets the realistic multi-aspect rationale extraction task and evaluates on two standard datasets (BeerAdvocate and Hotel Review), including the decorrelated and correlated BeerAdvocate variants and both high- and low-sparsity regimes. Evaluation uses token-level F1 and classification accuracy, and the experimental suite is comprehensive: comparisons to a range of prior unsupervised rationale methods, ablations on deletion strategy (hard vs. AMD), training strategy (multi-task vs. multi-aspect collaborative), and special-token initialization, plus case studies. The multi-task training analysis quantifies efficiency gains (−17.9% memory, −25.2% time) without hurting performance, which strengthens the practicality of the approach.

894.human_review: The multi-task training strategy reduces memory usage and training time by 17.9% and 25.2%, respectively, compared to multi-aspect collaborative training. This efficiency gain is crucial for practical applications.
894.llm_review: Methodology: The formulation P(y1, z1, ..., yk, zk | x; θ) and the MAC mechanism that derives aspect-specific masks via Gumbel-softmax and applies an outer-product hard deletion are well-motivated and address incomplete deletion in prior attention-mask approaches. The straight-through estimator for binarization, aspect-specific query/key mappings, and prepended aspect tokens together provide a coherent mechanism for simultaneous aspect encoding and rationale selection within an encoder-based PLM, constituting a novel and technically sound contribution.

895.human_review: The results of baseline methods are all collected from YOFO, while YOFO has not been formally publised yet. This can lead to some potentially inconsistent setups, which can produce unfair comparisons. For example, the authors are encouraged to reimplement BERT-RNP themselves.
895.llm_review: Methodology + Result + Comparison: (1) The comparison set, while broad, relies on numbers reported in YOFO and does not fully control backbone and training parity (e.g., multi-task variants of strong baselines or shared-encoder multi-label baselines). A direct comparison to training k uni-aspect YOFOs with a shared encoder or parameter-efficient adapters would better isolate the benefit of MAMHA/MAC. (2) Gains are modest on Hotel Review (avg +0.7 F1), and MARE underperforms YOFO on two aspects there, which raises questions about robustness across domains and aspect distributions. (3) The approach is currently tied to encoder-based PLMs and requires prepending multiple special tokens, which increases sequence length and compute; the paper claims generality but does not provide decoder-only or long-context results. (4) No statistical significance testing is reported for the improvements.

896.human_review: There are some details that are in need of proofreading, for example, I do not find the experiment the authors mention in L330-332.
896.llm_review: Definition/Description/Detail/Discussion/Explanation/Interpretation + Experiment: Important implementation details that affect reproducibility and interpretation are insufficiently specified in the main text (left to appendices or omitted): the Gumbel-softmax temperature schedule and annealing, the exact layers/heads where MAMHA is applied, the interaction between hard deletion and residual connections, sensitivity to the number of aspects k and to sparsity targets, and stability across random seeds. The hard-deletion gradient path is briefly referenced via straight-through but lacks discussion of variance/stability. Experimental analysis focuses on token-level F1 and accuracy; broader interpretability metrics (e.g., sufficiency/comprehensiveness, human evaluation) and significance tests are missing. Finally, details on preprocessing, tokenization with special tokens, and hyperparameters (batch sizes, learning rates, early stopping) should be centralized for full reproducibility.

897.human_review: The paper resolves previous concerns regarding the harmonic mean with other metric pairs, experiments on the temperature setting, and overfitting to specific metrics, and lack of consistency in model/data/metric usage.
897.llm_review: Methodology/Data/Task/Evaluation: The paper introduces a simple yet effective in-context diversification (ICD) framework that combines a two-step diversified prompting scheme with a lightweight subset selection over Sdef ∪ Sdiv using a user-chosen diversity metric. The approach is well grounded in the GCR setting and evaluated on three representative benchmarks (CommonGen, ComVE, DimonGen), covering concept-constrained generation and explanation tasks. Evaluation is multi-faceted: it reports lexical and semantic diversity (self-BLEU, Distinct/Entropy, self-cosSim, self-BERTScore), quality (BLEU, SPICE, BERTScore), and combined measures (Harmonic Mean, FBD). The study also probes LLM diversity judgements with a small human study (κ=0.409), and ablates the choice of diversity metric f, showing ICD is robust across self-BLEU-3, self-cosSim, and self-BERTScore. ICD consistently improves the diversity–quality balance over default/diversified prompts, with notable HM gains (e.g., CommonGen: 72.7 vs. 65.4/39.6; ComVE: 69.0 vs. 67.4/54.9; DimonGen: 58.2 vs. 55.9/52.1).

898.human_review: The paper is well-organized and easy to read, with a valid experimental design and proofs.
898.llm_review: Experiment/Presentation: Experiments are thorough, spanning two LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo and Vicuna-13B) for reproducibility, with clear prompt templates, algorithmic pseudocode, and detailed metric reporting. Comparisons include default/diversified prompts, a fine-tuned baseline, and a downstream MoE setting where ICD-generated data boosts diversity and yields competitive quality against KG-augmented systems. Runtime and cost estimates, stability notes, and ablations (LLM choice, f-selection) are presented, and examples illustrate qualitative gains in diversity without severe quality degradation.

899.human_review: As shown in the experiments in Table 5, increasing the temperature alone can achieve the highest level of quality while securing diversity. This also raises the question of whether maintaining high diversity is necessarily beneficial. Isn't it ideal to achieve high quality with moderate diversity? ICD clearly demands high computational costs and adjusting only the temperature as the default decoding parameter can yield high-quality results with moderate diversity.
899.llm_review: Experiment: Human evaluation is limited to a small-scale diversity judgement (35 items) with no human assessment of grammaticality, coherence, or concept coverage, leaving quality claims primarily supported by automatic metrics. Statistical significance is not reported, and decoding baselines are somewhat narrow: stronger or better-tuned alternatives (e.g., diverse beam search, typical sampling, controlled temperature/top-k/top-p sweeps) are not systematically compared. The trigger for Step 2 relies on detecting exact duplicates, which may miss low semantic diversity; max response length (25 tokens) could bias both quality and diversity metrics. Experiments are confined to English datasets and a fixed small number of in-context examples, limiting generality.

900.human_review: The approach appears vulnerable to the decoding strategy, necessitating further analysis.
900.llm_review: Methodology/Analysis: The subset search objective optimizes only a diversity metric f, while quality is assumed to come via Sdef; there is no explicit quality or constraint satisfaction term in the selection criterion, creating a potential mismatch with the reported combined metrics. The Step-2 trigger based on exact duplication overlooks near-duplicate or semantically similar outputs; a similarity-based trigger could be more principled. Reliance on self-BLEU (or similar) as f risks incentivizing superficial lexical variation; the method does not enforce concept coverage or factuality during selection. The analysis lacks deeper error typology, sensitivity to N and prompt formats, or formal justification of why the two-pool union and greedy selection should reliably attain the desired diversity–quality trade-off.

901.human_review: TOCSIN uses a token cohesiveness as a plug-and-play module to improve existing zero-shot detectors, token cohesiveness module adds only minimal additional time and space consumption compared to the detector
901.llm_review: The paper tackles a timely and important problem in zero-shot detection of LLM-generated text and presents a simple, broadly applicable idea that integrates cleanly with existing detectors. The exposition is generally clear, the related work is well-situated, and the experimental study is comprehensive enough to inform practice.

902.human_review: Zero-shot classifiers need to extract a variety of statistical features as a basis for identifying LLM-generated text, for black-box models, these features can only be extracted by surrogate models, TOCSIN uses token cohesiveness as substitute and does not rely on the source LLM, which is suitable for black-box model scenarios.
902.llm_review: Methodology: The introduction of token cohesiveness—estimated via random token deletion and a semantic difference metric (BARTScore)—is conceptually neat, training-free, and well-aligned with black-box constraints. The dual-channel "plug-and-play" design is generic, imposes modest additional compute/memory overhead, and shows hyperparameter insensitivity, which enhances practicality and reproducibility.

903.human_review: Two current state-of-the-art base detectors with TOCSIN achieve meaningful improvements across four diversified datasets with passages generated from seven different source LLMs, demonstrating the the effectiveness and generality of TOCSIN.
903.llm_review: Methodology, Data/Task, Result: The method is validated across four diverse datasets (XSum, SQuAD, WritingPrompts, PubMedQA) and seven source models (including GPT-4), under both white-box and black-box settings, demonstrating consistent AUROC gains over two strong base detectors (LRR and Fast-DetectGPT). Improvements are especially notable in black-box conditions, and the authors further analyze hyperparameters, runtime/memory, and the effect of passage length, supporting the claimed generality and efficiency.

904.human_review: In section 4.2, the same detector shows a performance degradation in the black-box settings compared to the white-box setup, and the text suggests that this is due to the fact that the black-box setup is not able to use the source model, without further justification.
904.llm_review: Intuition/Justification/Motivation/Validation, Result: The central hypothesis—causal attention induces higher token cohesiveness in LLM text—remains largely intuitive and correlational. Validation relies on a single semantic metric (BARTScore) and shows weakened effect on short texts, which suggests potential confounds (e.g., length, redundancy, stylistic homogeneity) rather than a uniquely causal-attention-driven signal; more controlled studies or alternative semantic metrics would better substantiate the claim.
